According to Sauvages, this distemper begins with a laxitude of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMBS">limbs</a>, transient colds and shiverings, pain of the head, and anxieties of the precordia. Then come on spasmodic startings of the fingers and feet; also of the tendons and muscles, conspicuous... spicuous below the skin. The disease is attended with heat, fever, delirium, stupor, constriction of the breast, suffocating dyspnea, loss of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-VOICE">voice</a>, horrid convulsions of the limbs, preceded by a formication, or <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SENSATION">sensation</a> as of ants or other small insects creeping on the parts. In this state of the disease, the convulsive paroxysms are attended with most violent pains in the limbs, vomiting, or diarrhea, with the passing of worms, thirst, and in young people as unnatural <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HUNGER">hunger</a>. It continues from ten days to three months. About the eleventh or twentieth day, some are relieved by copious sweats, or purple exanthemata; while others <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> into a tabes, with stupor, or stiffness of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JOINTS">joints</a>. Causes, &c. This disease is frequently epidemic in Swabia and other parts of Germany; where it is said to be produced by seeds of radishes, which are often mixed with rye in that country; and from this supposed cause the disease takes its name. It is also, however, a very common opinion, that this disease depends on the rye used in diet being of a bad <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, and particularly containing a large proportion of what is called spurred rye. Cure. In this affection, also, the cure, as far as it has yet been discovered, is very much the same with that of epilepsy, the disease next to be considered. GENUS LIII. EPILEPSIA.

MAGALESIA

and MAGALENSIS LUDI, feasts, and games in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of Cybele <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> Rhea the mother of the gods, kept on the 12th of April by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, and famous for <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> rejoicings and diversions of various sorts. The Galli carried the image of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> along the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CITY">city</a>, with <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> of drums and other music.

MEASLES

Pages 215-227

Rubeola, Sauv. gen. 94. Lin. 4. Sag. 293. Fehris morbillofa, Vog. 36. Hoffm. II. 62. Morbilli, Funk. 76. Sp. I. The Regular Measles. Rubiola vulgaris, Sauv. fp. 1. Morbilli regulares, Sydenb. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">Sect</a>. iv. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 5. Var. 1. The Anomalous Measles. Rubeola anomala, Sauv. fp. 2. Morbilli anomali, Sydenb. Sect. v. cap. 3. Var. 2. The Measles attended with Quinsy. Var. 3. The Measles with Putrid Diathesis of the Blood. Sp. II. The Variolodes. In Scotland <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called the Nirles. Rubeola variolodes, Sauv. fp. 3. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">Description</a>. This <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a> begins with a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COLD">cold</a> stage, which is soon followed by a hot, with the ordinary symptoms of thirst, anorexia, anxiety, sickness, and vomiting; and these are more <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> less considerable in different <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CASES">cases</a>. Sometimes from the beginning the fever is sharp and violent; often, for the first two days, it is obscure and inconsiderable; but always becomes violent before the eruption, which commonly happens on the fourth <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>. This eruptive fever, from the beginning of it, is always attended with hoarseness, a frequent hoarse dry cough, and often with some difficulty of breathing. At the same <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a>, the eye-lids are somewhat swollen; the eyes are a little inflamed, and pour out tears; and with this there is a coryza, and frequent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SNEEZING">sneezing</a>. For the most <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">part</a>, a constant drowsiness attends the beginning of this disease. The eruption, as we have said, commonly appears upon the fourth day, first on the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FACE">face</a>, and successively on the lower parts of the body. It appears first in small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RED">red</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-POINTS">points</a>; but, soon after, a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of these appear in clusters, which do not arise in visible pimples, but, by the touch, are found to be a little prominent. This is the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CASE">case</a> on the face; but, in other parts of the body, the promiscuity, or roughness, is hardly to be perceived. On the face, the eruption retains its redness, or has it increased for two days; but on the third, the vivid redness is changed to a brownish red; and in a day or two more the eruption entirely disappears, while a mealy desquamation takes <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. During the whole time of the eruption, the face is somewhat turgid, but seldom considerably swollen. Sometimes, after the eruption has appeared, the fever ceases entirely; but this is seldom the case; and more commonly the fever continues or is increased after the eruption, and does not cease till after the desquamation. Even then the fever does not always cease, but continues with various <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DURATION">duration</a> and effect. Though the fever happen to cease upon the eruption's taking place, it is <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMON">common</a> for the cough to continue till after the desquamation, and sometimes much longer. In all cases, while the fever continues, the cough also continues, generally with an increase of the difficulty of breathing; and both of these symptoms sometimes arise to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> which denotes a pneumonic affection. This may happen at any <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of the disease; but very often it does not come on till after the desquamation of the eruption. After the same period, also, a diarrhoea frequently comes on, and continues for some time. It is common for measles, even when they have not been of a violent kind, to be followed by inflammatory affections, particularly ophthalmia and phthisis. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> blood be drawn from a vein in the measles, with circumstances necessary to favour the separation of the gluten, this always appears separated, and lying on the surface of the cranium, as in inflammatory diseases. For the most part, the measles, even when violent, are without any putrid tendency; but in some cases, such a tendency appears both in the course of the disease, and especially after the ordinary course of it is finished. Cautions. The measles are occasioned by a peculiar kind of contagion, the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of which is not understood; and which, like that of the small-pox, affects a person only once in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. Prognosis. From the description of this distemper already given, it appears that the measles are attended with a catarrhal affection, and with an inflammatory diathesis to a considerable degree; and therefore the danger of them is to be apprehended chiefly from the coming on of a pneumonic inflammation. Cure. In measles, as well as in small-pox, the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> from its nature must necessarily run a determined course; and therefore the sole aim of a practitioner is to conduct this course in the earliest manner, by preventing and obviating urgent symptoms. From the consideration mentioned in the prognosis, it <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WILL">will</a> be obvious, that the remedies especially necessary are those which may obviate and diminish the inflammatory diathesis; and therefore, in a particular manner, blood-letting. This remedy may be employed at any time in the course of the disease, or after the ordinary course of it is finished. It is to be employed more or less, according to the urgency of the symptoms of fever, cough, and dyspnoea; and generally may be employed very freely. But as the symptoms of pneumonic inflammation seldom come on during the eruptive fever, and as this is sometimes violent immediately before the eruption, though a sufficiently mild disease be to follow; bleeding is seldom very necessary during the eruptive fever, and may often be reserved for the times of greater danger which are perhaps to follow. In all cases of measles, where there are no marks of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PUTREFACTION">putrefaction</a>, and where there is no reason, from the known nature of the epidemic, to apprehend putrefaction, bleeding is the remedy most to be depended upon; Exanthema: but affluence may also be drawn from cooling purgatives; and particularly from blistering on the sides or between the shoulders. The dry cough may be alleviated by the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of demulcent pectorals, mucilaginous, oily, or sweet. It may, however, be observed, with respect to these demulcents, that they are not so powerful in involving and correcting the acrimony of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MASS">mass</a> of blood as has been imagined; and that their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> operation is by befriending the fauces, and thereby defending them from the irritation of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ACIDS">acids</a>, either arising from the lungs or distilling from the head. For moderating and quieting the cough in this disease, opiates certainly prove the most effectual means, whenever they can be safely employed. In the measles, in which an inflammatory state prevails in a considerable degree, opiates have indeed by some been supposed to be inadmissible; but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> abundantly demonstrates, that the objection made to their use is merely hypothetical; and even in cases where, from a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> degree of pyrexia and dyspnea, there is reason to fear the presence, or at least the danger, of pneumonic inflammation, opiates are highly useful; after bleeding, to obviate or abate the inflammatory state, has been duly employed: in such cases, while the cough and watchful ones are the urgent symptoms, opiates may be safely exhibited, and with <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> advantage. In all the exanthemata, there is an acrimony diffused over the system, which gives a considerable irritation; and, for obviating the effects of this, opiates are useful, and always proper, when no particular contra-indication prevails. When the desquamation of the measles is finished, though then there should be no disorder remaining, physicians have thought it necessary to purge the patient several times, with a view to draw off what have been called the dregs of this disease; that is, a portion of the morbid <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> which is supposed to remain <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">long</a> in the body. Dr <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CULLEN">Cullen</a> does not reject this supposition; but at the same time cannot believe that the remains of the morbid matter, diffused over the whole mass of blood, can be wholly drawn off by purging; and therefore thinks, that, to avoid the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of the measles, it is not the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> off the morbid matter which we need to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a>, so much as to obviate and remove the inflammatory state of the system which had been induced by the disease. With this last view indeed, purging may still be a proper remedy; but bleeding, in proportion to the symptoms of inflammatory disposition, is still more so. From our late experience of the use of cold <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> in the eruptive fever of the small-pox, some physicians have been of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> that the practice may be transferred to the measles; but this point has not yet been determined by sufficiently extensive experience. We are certain, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> may be very hurtful in the measles, as in most other inflammatory diseases; and therefore, that the body ought to be kept in a moderate temperature during the whole course of the disease: but how far, at any period of the disease, cold air may be applied with safety, is still uncertain. <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANALOGY">Analogy</a>, though so often the resource of physicians, is frequently fallacious; and further, though the analogy with the small-pox might <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> to the application of cold air during the eruptive fever of the measles, the analogy with catarrh seems to be against the practice. When the eruption is upon the skin, there are many instances of cold air making it disappear, and thereby producing much disorder in the system; and there are also frequent instances of this disorder's being removed by restoring the heat of the body, and thereby again bringing out the eruption. Upwards of 20 years ago, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-INOCULATION">inoculation</a> for the measles was proposed, and practised in several instances with success, by Dr Home of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>. His method of communicating the infection was, by applying to an incision in each arm cotton moistened with the blood of a patient labouring under the measles; but with others who have made similar trials, the attempt has not yet succeeded. And attempts have been made to inoculate this disease by means of the fluid discharged under the form of tears, the squamae falling from the surface, and the like; but there is reason to believe, that where it was imagined the infection had thus been communicated, the contagion was only carried about the person inoculating, and communicated in the ordinary way. From inoculation of the measles, it is imagined that several advantages may be obtained; and among others, it is thought the forenoon of the eyes may be mitigated, the cough abated, and the fever rendered less severe. But the practice was never much in fashion, and now is scarce ever heard of. GENUS XXXI. MILIARIA. The <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MILITARY">Military</a> Fever. Miliaria, Lin. 7. Febris <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PURPUREA">purpurea</a> seu miliaris, Junk. 75. Germanis der Frielzel. God. Welsch, Hist.
