Whenever the tenesmus or mucus stools were thought worth the taking notice of, warm milk and oil generally gave immediate relief. If purging was necessary, the lenient purges, such as mallow with oil, were, in this particular case, made use of: rhubarb was found too stimulating.—But, in general, the most useful purge, and which therefore was most usually taken, was cinnabar and rhubarb, of each half a drachm: this powder seldom failed to bring away a mucus as transparent as the white of an egg, and in this many *ascarides* were moving about. The cinnabar frequently adhered to this mucus, which did not come off in large quantities, when a purge was taken without cinnabar. Calomel did no more than any other purge which operates briskly would have done; that is, it brought away *ascarides*, with a great deal of mucus. Oil given as a clyster sometimes brought off these animals: the oil swam on the surface of the mucus, and the *ascarides* were alive and moving in the mucus itself, which probably hindered the oil from coming in contact with them and killing them. The Doctor also observes, that mucus or slime is the proper nest of the *ascarides*, in which they live, and is perhaps the food by which they are nourished; and it is this mucus which preserves them unhurt, though surrounded with many other liquors, the immediate touch of which would be fatal. It is hard to satisfy ourselves by what instinct they find it out in the human body, and by what means they get at it; but it is observable in many other parts of nature, as well as here, that where there is a fit soil for the hatching and growth of animals and vegetables, nature has taken sufficient care that their seeds should find the way thither. Worms are said to have been found in the intestines of infants born dead. Purgers, by lessening this slime, never fail to relieve the patient; and it is not unlikely, that the worms which are not forced away by this quickened motion of the intestines, may, for want of a proper quantity of it, languish, and at last die; for if the avaricaries are taken out of their mucus, and exposed to the open air, they become motionless, and apparently die in a very short time. Dr Heberden supposes that the kind of purge made use of is of some consequence in the cure of all other worms as well as avaricaries; the animals being always defended by the mucus from the immediate action of medicines; and that therefore those purges are the best which act briskly, and of which a repetition can be most easily borne. Purging waters are of this sort, and jalap especially for children; two or more grains of which, mixed with sugar, are most easily taken, and may be repeated daily. From the case above-mentioned, and from Dr Heberden's observations, we may easily see why it is so difficult to destroy these animals; and why anthelmintics, greatly celebrated for some cures, are yet far from being specifics in the disease. As the worms which reside in the cavities of the human body are never exposed to the air, by which all living creatures are invigorated, it is evident, that in themselves they must be the most tender and easily destructible creatures imaginable, and much less will be requisite to kill them than any of our common infects. The most pernicious substances to any of the common infects are oil, caustic fixed alkali, lime, and lime-water. The oil operates upon them by shutting up the pores of their bodies; the lime-water, lime, and caustic alkali, by dissolving their very substance. In the case of intestinal worms, however, the oil can have very little effect upon them, as they are defended from it by the moisture and mucus of the intestines; the like happens with lime-water; and therefore it is necessary that the medicine should be of such a nature as to destroy both mucus and infects together; for which purpose the caustic fixed alkali is at once safe and efficacious; nor is it probable that any cafe of worms whatever could reflect the proper use of this medicine. A very large dose of any salt indeed will also destroy the mucus and destroy the worms; but it is apt to inflame and excoriate the stomach and intestines, and thus to produce worse distempers than that which it was intended to cure. Dr Heberden gives the following remarkable case of a patient cured of worms by enormous doses of common salt, after trying many other remedies in vain. In February 1757, the patient was seized with uncommon pains in his stomach, attended with nausea, vomiting, and constipation of bowels, and an almost total loss of sleep and appetite. He soon became much emaciated, and could neither stand nor walk upright; his belly grew small and hard, and closely retracted, insomuch that the sternum covered the navel, and the latter could scarce be discovered or felt by the finger; his urine was always milky, and soon deposited a thick white sediment; his excrements were very hard and lumpy, resembling those of sheep, only of a brown colour; nor had he ever a stool without some medicine or other to procure it. In this situation he continued four years; during which time he had been in an infirmary, attended by eminent physicians, but was dismissed as incurable. At last he was advised by a neighbour to drink salt and water, as he said he knew one cured by it who had for many years been afflicted with the same kind of pains in the belly and stomach. As his distemper was now almost insupportable, he willingly tried the experiment. Two pounds of common salt were dissolved in as little water as possible, all which he drank in less than an hour. Soon afterwards he found himself greatly oppressed at the stomach, grew extremely sick, and vomited violently; on the fourth strain he brought up about half a pint of small worms, part avaricaries, and the rest resembling those worms which are called the botts, and frequently met with in the stomach of horses, but much smaller, and about the size of a grain of wheat. The salt soon began to operate downwards, and he had five or six very copious fetid stools, tinged with blood; and in them discharged near an equal quantity of the same kind of worm he had vomited. Being greatly fatigued with the violence of the operations, he fell into a calm sleep, which lasted two hours, during which he sweated profusely, and awoke much refreshed. Instead of his usual pains, he now only complained of a rawness and soreness of his gullet, stomach, and bowels, with an almost unquenchable thirst; to allay which, he drank large quantities of cold water, whey, butter-milk, or whatever he could get. The urine he now passed was small in quantity, and rendered with very great difficulty, being highly saturated with the salt, from whence arose a most troublesome dysuria and strangury. However, these symptoms gradually abated by a free use of the liquors above-mentioned; and on the third morning he was so well recovered, that he took two pounds more of salt, dissolved in the like quantity of water. The effects were nearly similar to the former; only that most of the worms were now burnt, and came away with a considerable quantity of slime and mucus. The drought, strangury, &c., returned with their former violence, but soon yielded to the old treatment. He sweated very copiously for three days, slept easily, and by that time could extend his body freely: on the fifth day he left his bed, and, though very weak, could walk upright; his strength and appetite soon returned, and he became robust and well. The anthelmintic medicines which have been recommended by one person or other, are in a manner innumerable; but the principal are, 1. Quicksilver. This is very efficacious against all kinds of worms, either taken in the form of calomel or corrosive sublimate. Even the crude metal boiled in water and the water drunk, has been recommended as an almost certain cure. But this, it is evident, can receive no impregnation from the mercury. If, therefore, it have any effect, it must be from some foreign and accidental impregnation. In most instances there can be no objection to mercury, but only that it is not endowed with any attenuating quality whereby the mucus in which these infects resides can be dissolved. It therefore fails in many cases, though it will most certainly destroy worms where it can get at them. 2. Powder of tin. This was for some time celebrated as a specific, and indeed we may reasonably expect good effects from it; as by its weight and... Worms grittiness it rubs off the mucus and worms it contains from the coats of the intestinal canal, in which case they are easily evacuated by purgatives. In order to produce any considerable effects, it must be given in a large dose. 3. Geoffrea inermis, or cabbage bark. This remedy is used by the inhabitants of Jamaica. The first account of it which appeared in this country was published in the Physical and Literary Essays, vol ii, by Mr Duguid surgeon in that island. He acquaints us, that the inhabitants of Jamaica, young and old, white and black, are much infested with worms, especially the long round sort; the reason of which, he thinks, is the quantity of sweet succulent vegetables which they eat. On dissecting a child of seven months old, who died of vomiting and convulsions, twelve large worms were found; one of them filled the appendix vermiformis, and three of them were entwined in such a manner as to block up the valvula Tulpia, so that nothing could pass from the small to the great guts.—The cabbage-bark, however, he tells us, is a safe and effectual remedy, and the most powerful vermifuge yet known; and that it frequently brings away as many worms by stool as would fill a large hat. He owns that it has sometimes violent effects; but this he attributes to the negroes who make the decoction (in which form the bark is used), and not to the remedy itself. Mr Anderson, surgeon in Edinburgh, has also given an account of this bark and its operation, in a letter to Dr Duncan, published in the Edinburgh Medical Commentaries, volume iv. p. 84. From this account it appears, that there are two different kinds of bark; the one much paler than the other: the pale kind operates much more violently than the other. It often occasions loose stools, great nausea, and such like symptoms, attended with great uneasiness in the belly: in one or two instances it was suspected of inducing syncope. The darker coloured kind resembles the cassia lignea, though it is of a much coarser texture. This kind, Mr Anderson thinks, may be exhibited in any case where an anthelmintic is necessary; the dangerous symptoms might have followed either from the use of the first kind, or from an over-dose of the second. The usual method of preparing the medicine is by boiling two ounces and a half of the bark in two quarts of water to a pint and a half. Of this a tea-spoonful may be given at first in the morning, gradually increasing the quantity till we come to four or five table-spoonfuls in a day. When exhibited in this manner, Mr Anderson informs us, that he never saw it produce any violent symptoms, and has experienced the best effects from it as an anthelmintic. After the use of this decoction for eight or nine mornings successively, a dose of jalap with calomel must be given, which seldom fails to bring away the worms, some dead, some alive. If at any time the decoction produce more than one or two loose stools, a few drops of liquid laudanum may be given; and, in general, Mr Anderson gave 15 or 20 drops of the spirit of lavender with each dose. In a letter from Dr Ruth, professor of chemistry at Philadelphia, to Dr Duncan of Edinburgh, the following account is given of another preparation of this medicine. "It has long (says he) been a complaint among physicians, that we have no vermifuge medicine which can be depended upon. Even calomel fails in many cases where there are the most pathognomonic signs of worms in the bowels. But this complaint, it is hoped, is now at an end. The physicians of Jamaica have lately found, that the cabbage-bark, as it is called in the West Indies, made into a syrup with brown sugar, is an infallible antidote to them. I have used above 30 pounds of it, and have never found it fail in one instance. The syrup is pleasant; it sometimes pukes, and always purges, the first or second time it is given." Notwithstanding these encomiums, however, the cabbage-bark (A) hath not come into general use in Britain. But diseases from the teretes, or lumbrici as they are often called, the species of worm against which this bark is employed, much less frequently occur than in some other countries. When they do occur, in almost every instance they readily yield to more gentle and safe anthelmintics; and the worms may not only be expelled by calomel, but by the vegetable bitters; as the powder of the semen fantanum, or the like. 4. Coughwort, or cow-itch. This is the Dolichos urens or pruriens of Linnaeus; and the principles on which it acts have been already explained under the article Dolichos. It is somewhat similar to the powder of tin, but bids fair for being more efficacious. It might at first appear to occur as objections to this medicine, that by the hairs of it entangling themselves with one another, calculi might be formed in the intestines, or obstructions equally bad; or if the sharp points and hooks with which it abounds were to adhere to the nervous coats of the intestines themselves, they might occasion a fatal irritation, which could not be removed by any means whatever. But from the experience of those who have employed it extensively in practice, it would appear, that these objections are entirely theoretical; and that it may be employed with perfect safety. The spiculae, gently scraped off from a single pod, and mixed with syrup or molasses, are taken for a dose in the morning fasting. It is repeated in this manner for two or three days without any sensible operation; but even a very slight purgative taken afterwards has been found to discharge an almost incredible quantity of worms. And according to Dr Bancroft, who has given a very particular account of its use in his Natural History of Guiana, it is one of the safest and most certain anthelmintics yet discovered; but, as well as the bark of the Geoffrea, it has hitherto been very little used in Britain, probably from its not being necessary. 5. Indian pink. This plant, which in the Spigelia marilandica (A) The most accurate account of this vegetable, and its effects, has been given by Dr Wright in the Philosophical Transactions, of which the reader will find a short view under the article Geoffrea, in the order of the alphabet. Worms, marilandica of Linnæus, is also an American plant, and was first recommended in the Edinburgh Physical and Literary Essays by Dr Garden of Charlestown in South Carolina. He is of opinion that a vomit ought always to precede the use of it; and informs us, that half a drachm of it purges as briskly as the same quantity of rhubarb. At other times he has known it produce no effect on the belly though given in very large quantity: In such cases it becomes necessary to add a grain or two of sweet mercury, or some grains of rhubarb; but then it is less efficacious than when it proves purgative without addition. The use of it, however, in small doses, is by no means safe; as it frequently produces giddiness, dimness of sight, convulsions, &c. The addition of a purgative, indeed, prevents these effects; but at the same time, as already observed, it diminishes the virtue of the medicine. The Doctor therefore recommends large doses, as from them he never knew any other effect than the medicine's proving emetic or violently cathartic. The dose is from 12 to 60 or 70 grains of the root in substance, or two, three, or four drachms of the infusion, twice a day. This medicine has also had its day, and is now very far from being considered as a specific. From what has been already observed, it must pretty clearly appear, that powder of tin, cow-itch, or fixed alkaline salts, bid fairest for destroying worms in all the variety of cases in which they can occur. Alkalies indeed have been but little tried. We have known one case in which all the complaints have been removed by a single dose: we have also an instance of their efficacy, in an extraordinary case of a worm bred in the liver, mentioned in the 2d volume of the Medical Observations. The patient had a violent pain in the side, and sometimes in the shoulder, as the worm shifted its place; but, on the application of a lixivial poultice, the pain went out of the side entirely, and kept in the shoulder for some weeks. The long round worms seem to be the most dangerous which infest the human body, as they often pierce through the stomach and intestines, and thus bring on a miserable death. The common symptoms of them are nausea, vomiting, looseness, fainting, slender intermittent pulse, itching of the nose, and epileptic fits. By the consumption of the chyle they produce hunger, paleness, weakness, coliciveness, tumor of the abdomen, eructations, and rumbling of the intestines; but it is from the perforation of the intestines that the disease proves so frequently fatal. A child may be known to have worms from his cold temperament, paleness of the countenance, livid eye-lids, hollow eyes, itching of the nose, voracity, startings, and grinding of the teeth in sleep; and more especially by a very fetid breath. Very frequently, however, they are voided by the mouth and anus, in which case there is no room for doubt. In the Medical Commentaries, vol. II. we have an account of the intestines being perforated by a worm, and yet the patient recovered. The patient was a woman troubled with an inflammation in the lower part of the abdomen. The pain was so violent, that for six days she slept none at all; the tumor then broke, discharged upwards of a pound of thin watery faeces, immediately after which the excrements followed. The next day she was extremely low; her pulse could scarcely be felt; the extremities were cold; and there was a considerable discharge from the wound, which had already begun to mortify. She got a decoction of the bark with wine, which alleviated the symptoms; but in removing the mortified parts a worm was found among them nine inches long, and as thick as an eagle's quill. By proper applications, the discharge of excrements ceased, and she recovered perfect health. She was sensible of no accident giving rise to the inflammation; so that in all probability it arose entirely from the worm itself. The tenia, or tape-worm, as it is called, is one of those most difficult to be removed from the human body. It is of two kinds, tenia folium and tenia lata; for a description of which see the article Tænia.—The reason of its being so difficult to cure, is, that though portions of it are apt to break off and be discharged, it is endowed with a power of reproduction, so that the patient is little or nothing better. The symptoms occasioned by it are not different from those above described. A specific against the tenia lata hath been lately so much celebrated in France, that the king thought proper to purchase it from the proprietor (Madam Nouffer), and the account of it has been translated into English by Dr Simmons. The patients are required to observe no particular regimen till the day before they take the specific. That day they are to take nothing after dinner till about 7 o'clock; after which, they are to take the following soup: "Take a pint and an half of water, two or three ounces of good fresh-butter, and two ounces of bread cut into thin slices; add to this salt enough to season it, and then boil it to the consistence of panada." About a quarter of an hour after this, they take a biscuit and a glass of white-wine, either pure or mixed with water; or even water alone, if they have not been accustomed to wine. If the patient has not been to stool that day, (which, however, is not usual with patients in this way), the following clyster is to be injected. "Take a small quantity of the leaves of mallows, and boil them in a sufficient quantity of water, mixing with it a little salt, and when strained off add two ounces of oil olive." Next morning, about eight or nine hours after the supper above mentioned, the specific is to be taken. This is no other than two or three drachms of the root of male fern, polyodium filix mas of Linnæus, gathered in autumn, and reduced to fine powder. It is to be taken in any distilled water, or in common water. This medicine is apt to occasion a nausea: to avoid which, Madam Nouffer allows her patients to chew any thing that is agreeable, but forbids anything to be swallowed; or they may smell to vinegar, to check the tickness: but if, notwithstanding this, the specific be thrown up, a fresh dose must be swallowed as soon as the tickness is gone off, and then they must try to sleep. About two hours after this, the following bolus is to be taken. "Take of the panacea of mercury 14 times sublimed, and select resin of scammony, each ten grains; of fresh and good gamboge, five or seven grains: reduce each of these substances separately into powder, and then mix them with some conserve into a bolus." This composition is to be swallowed at two different times, walking it down with

MEDICINES

Pages 369-369

whatever substances serve to restore <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> — Medicines are either simple <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a>; the former being prepared by <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> alone; and the latter owing to the industry of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MAN">man</a>, by variously mixing the simple together. See <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PHARMACY">PHARMACY</a>. Medicines are likewise distinguished from the manner of using them, into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> and internal; and with regard to their effects, they are said to be emetic, cathartic, astringent, &c. See <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">MATERIA Medica</a>. Pocket Medicines, in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SURGERY">surgery</a>, those which a surgeon ought always to carry about with him, in a box or convenient <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CASE">case</a>. Those, according to Heister, are the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DIGESTIVE">digestive</a> ointment, and some detergent ointment, for cleansing and digesting foul ulcers; to which must also be added a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLASTER">plaster</a> or two fitted for defense or <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADHESION">adhesion</a>, since one or other of these is almost constantly wanted. Neither should there be wanting a piece of blue vitriol for the taking <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DOWN">down</a> luxuriant <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>, and to stop hemorrhages; but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> vitriol is wanting, burnt <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALUM">alum</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RED">red</a> precipitate, the infernal <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, or any other corrosive medicine, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WILL">will</a> supply its <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in corrosive intentions; and the last will also serve to open abscesses, to make ulcers, and perform many other operations of that kind. With these there should always be kept in readiness also a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of scraped lint, that the surgeon may be able to give immediate assistance to wounded persons; since, if he is unprepared for this, they may easily be taken off by an hemorrhage; a circumstance which ought also to prevail with him to be always provided with suitable bandages.

MEDICIS

Pages 371-371

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LAW">law</a>, signifies a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JURY">jury</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> inquest impaneled, of which the one half are natives of this <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LAND">land</a> and the other foreigners. This jury is never used except where one of the parties in a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PLEA">plea</a> is a stranger and the other a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DENIZEN">denizen</a>. In petit-<a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TREASON">treason</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MURDER">murder</a>, and felony, foreigners are allowed this privilege; but not in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>-treason, because an alien in that <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CASE">case</a> shall be tried according to the rules of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMON">common</a> law, and not by a medicis lingua. A <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> jury ought not in any case to be of a medicis lingua; and the person that would have the advantage of a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> in this way, is to pray the same, otherwise it <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WILL">will</a> not be permitted on a challenge of the jurors.

MEDINA

Pages 372-372

a very eminent painter, was son of Medina de L'<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASTURIAS">Asturias</a>, a Spanish <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a> who had settled at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BRUSSELS">Brussels</a>, where the son was born in 1560. He was instructed in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> by du Chatelet under whose <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> he made good progress; and applying himself to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of Rubens, made that eminent <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MASTER">master</a> his <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MODEL">model</a>. He painted both <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PORTRAIT">portrait</a>; and was held in extraordinary esteem by most of the princes of Germany, who distinguished his merit by several marks of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>. He married young, and came into England in 1686, where he drew portraits for several years with <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> reputation; as he painted those subjects with remarkable freedom of touch, a delicate management of tints, and strong resemblance of the persons. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Leven encouraged him to go to Scotland, and procured him a subscription of 500l. worth of business. He went, carrying a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of bodies and postures, to which he painted heads. He returned to England for a short <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a>; but went back to Scotland, where he died, and was buried in the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>-yard of the Greyfriars at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a> in 1711, aged 52. He painted most of the Scotch <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>; but was not rich, having 20 children. The portraits of the professors in the surgeon's <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HALL">hall</a> at Edinburgh were painted by him, and are commended. At Wentworth-castle is a large piece containing the first <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Argyle and his sons, the two late dukes John and Archibald, in Roman habits; the style Italian, and superior to most <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> performers. In surgeon's hall are two small histories by him. The duke of Gordon presented Sir John Medina's head to the great duke of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TUSCANY">Tuscany</a> for his collection of portraits done by the painters themselves; the duke of Gordon too was drawn by him, with his son the marquis of Huntley and his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> Lady Jane, in one piece. Medina was knighted by the duke of Queensberry, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LORD">lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSIONER">commissioner</a>; and was the last <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KNIGHT">knight</a> made in Scotland before the union. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINTS">prints</a> in the octavo edition of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MILTON">Milton</a> were designed by him; and he composed another set for Ovid's Metamorphoses, but they were never engraved.

MEDINA-TALNARI

Pages 371-372

a famous town of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a> Petraea, between Arabia Deserta and Arabia the Happy; celebrated for being the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BURIAL">burial</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of Mahomet. It stands at a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>'s journey from the port of Iambo. It is of moderate size, surrounded by wretched walls, and situated in the midst of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a> plain. It belongs to the Sherif of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MECCA">Mecca</a>, although it had of late times a particular sovereign of the family of Dacii Barkad. At present, the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> is confided by the Sherif to a vizir, who must be taken from the family of the sovereign. Before Mahomet, this <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CITY">city</a> was called Iatbreh; but it got the name of Medinet en Nebbi, "the City of the Prophet," after Mahomet, being driven from Mecca by the Koreishites, had taken refuge there, and passed in it the rest of his days. The <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a> of Mahomet at Medina is respected by Mussulmans, but they are under no obligation to visit it for the purposes of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARAVANS">caravans</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a> alone, which on their return from Mecca <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> near Medina, go a little out of their way to see the tomb. It stands in a corner of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, whereas the Kaba is situated in the middle of that at Mecca. That the people may not perform some superstitious worship to the relics of the prophet, they are prevented from approaching the tomb by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRATES">grates</a>, through which they may look at it. It consists of a piece of plain mason-<a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> in the form of a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHEST">chest</a>, without any other monument. The tomb is placed between two others, where the ashes of the two first caliphs repose. Although it is not more magnificent than the tombs of the greater <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">part</a> of the founders of mosques, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> that covers it is decorated with a piece of green <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SILK">silk</a> stuff embroidered with <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, which the pacha of Damacus renewes every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years. It is guarded by 40 <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EUNUCHS">eunuchs</a>, who watch the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a> said to be deposited there. It is seated in a plain abounding with palm-trees, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 39° 53' N. Lat. 25°. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of Arabia. MEDINA-Celi, an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, in Old Castile, and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of the same name; seated near the river Xalon, in W. Long. 2° 9' N. Lat. 41° 15'. MEDINA-de-las-Torres, a very ancient town of Spain, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-ESTREMADURA">Estremadura</a>, with an old castle, and the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of a duchy. It is seated on the confines of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANDALUSIA">Andalusia</a>, at the foot of a mountain near Bajadoz. MEDINA-del-Campo, a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LARGE">large</a> rich, and ancient town of Spain, in the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Leon. The great square is very fine, and adorned with a superb fountain. It MEDINA is a trading place, enjoys great privileges, and is seated in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> abounding with corn and wine. W. Long. 4° 20' Nat. Lat. 41° 22'. MEDINA-del-Rio-Secco, an ancient and rich town of Spain, in the kingdom of Leon, with the title of a duchy; seated on a plain, where there are fine pastures. E. Long. 4° 33'. N. Lat. 42° 8'.

MEDINE

Pages 372-372

an Egyptian piece of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-IRON">iron</a> silvered over, and about the size of a silver threepence.

MEDIOLANUM

Pages 372-372

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CITY">city</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the Insubres, built by the Gauls on their settlement in that <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>. A municipium, and a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> strength. The seat of the liberal arts; whence it had the name of Novae Athene. Now <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MILAN">Milan</a>, capital of the Milanese, situated on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Olona and Lombro, E. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 9° 30'. N. Lat. 45° 25'. MEDIOLANUM Aulercorum (anc. geog.), a town of Gallia Celtica, which afterwards took the name of the Eburovicum Civitas (Antonine); corrupted to Civitas Eburocorum, and this last to Eburoica; whence the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> appellation <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EVREUX">Evreux</a>, a city of Normandy. E. Long. 1° 12'. N. Lat. 49° 21'. MEDIOLANUM Gugenorum (anc. geog.), a town of Mediolanum <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELGICA">Belgica</a>; now the village Moyland, not far from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOGNE">Cologne</a>. MEDIOLANUM Ordovicum (anc. geog.), a town of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, now Llan Vethin, a market-town in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MONTGOMERYSHIRE">Montgomeryshire</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>. MEDIOLANUM Santonum (anc. geog.), which afterwards taking the name of the people, was called Santonica Urbis; also Santones and Santoni: A town of Aquitain. Now <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-SAINTES">Saintes</a>, capital of Saintonge in Guienne, on the river <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARENTE">Charente</a>.

MEDIOMATRICI

Pages 372-372

anciently a territory of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELGICA">Belgica</a>. Now the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METZ">Metz</a>.

MEDITATION

Pages 372-372

an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> by which we consider anything closely, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> wherein the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> is employed in the search or consideration of any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>. In our <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, it is used to signify a consideration of the objects and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> truths of the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>. Mythic divines make a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between meditation and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONTEMPLATION">contemplation</a>: the former consists in discursive acts of the soul, considering methodically and with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MYSTERIES">mysteries</a> of faith and the precepts of morality; and is performed by reflections and reasonings, which leave behind them manifest impressions on the brain. The pure contemplative have no need of meditation, as seeing all things in God at a glance, and without any reflection. When a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MAN">man</a>, therefore, has once quitted meditation, and is arrived at contemplation, he returns no more; and, according to Alvarez, never resumes the oar of meditation, except when the <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> of contemplation is too weak to fill his sails.

MEDITERRANEAN

Pages 372-372

something inclosed within <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LAND">land</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> that is remote from the ocean. MEDITERRANEAN is more particularly used to signify that <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SEA">sea</a> which flows between the continents of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, entering by the straits of Gibraltar, and reaching into <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, as far as the Euxine Sea and the Palus Maeotis. The Mediterranean was anciently called the Grecian Sea and the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> Sea. It is now cantoned out into several divisions, which bear several names. To the west of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> it is called the Liguric or Tuscan Sea; near <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, the Adriatic; towards <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, the Ionic and Aegean; between the Hellespont and the Bosporus, the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WHITE">White</a> Sea, as being very safe; and beyond, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BLACK_SEA"><a class=</a>"xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">Black</a> Sea, its <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a> being dangerous.

MEDITRINALIA

Pages 372-372

a Roman festival in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> Meditrina, kept on the 30th of September. Both the deity and the festival were so called a mendendo, because on this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> they began to drink new wine mixed with old by way of medicine. The mixture of wines, on this festival, was drank with much form and solemn <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a>.

MEDITULLIUM

Pages 372-373

is used by anatomists for that spungy. Medium. Spungy substance between the two plates of the cranium, and in the interstices of all laminated <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BONES">bones</a>. See Anatomy, no. I, II.

MEDIUM

Pages 373-373

in logic, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> middle <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TERM">term</a> of a syllogism, being an argument, reason, or consideration, for which we affirm or deny anything; or, it is the cause why the greater <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> is affirmed or denied of the less in the conclusion. Medium, in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARITHMETIC">arithmetic</a>, or arithmetical medium or mean, called in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a> medium rei; that which is equally distant from each extreme, or which exceeds the lesser extreme as much as it is exceeded by the greater, in respect of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a>, not of proportion; thus 9 is a medium betwixt 6 and 12. Geometrical Medium, called in the schools medium persona, is that where the same ratio is preserved between the first and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SECOND">second</a> as between the second and third terms; or that which exceeds in the same ratio or quota of itself, as it is exceeded: thus 6 is a geometrical medium between 4 and 9. Medium, in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, that space or region through which a body in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> passes to any point: thus <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ETHER">ether</a> is supposed to be the medium through which the heavenly bodies move; <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a>, the medium wherein bodies move near our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WATER">water</a>, the medium wherein fishes live and move; and glass is also a medium of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, as it affords it a free passage. That density or consistency in the parts of the medium, whereby the motion of bodies in it is retarded, is called the resistance of the medium; which, together with the force of gravity, is the cause of the cessation of the motion of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PROJECTILES">projectiles</a>. Subtile or Aetherial Medium. Sir <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> Newton considers it probable, that, beside the particular aerial medium, wherein we live and breathe, there is another more universal one, which he calls an aetherial medium; vastly more rare, subtile, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-ELASTIC">elastic</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a>, than air; and by that means freely permeating the pores and interstices of all other mediums, and diffusing itself through the whole <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CREATION">creation</a>; and by the intervention hereof he thinks it is that most of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> phenomena of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> are affected. See Aether, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-ELECTRICITY">Electricity</a>, Fire, &c. Medium, in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OPTICS">optics</a>, any substance through which light is transmitted.

MEDULLA OSSUM

Pages 373-373
or Marrow of the Bones. See Anatomy, no. 5. Medulla cerebri and cerebelli, denotes the white soft part of the brain and cerebellum, covered on the outside with the cortical substance, which is of a more dark or ashy colour. See Anatomy, no. 131—133. Medulla oblongata, is the medullary part of the brain and cerebellum, joined in one; the fore-part of it coming from the brain, and the hind-part from the cerebellum. See Anatomy, no. 134. It lies on the basis of the skull, and is continued thro' the great perforation thereof into the hollow of the vertebrae of the neck, back, and loins; though only so much of it retains the name oblongata as is included within the skull. After its exit thence, it is distinguished by the name of medulla spinalis. Ibid. no. 135.

MEDUSA

Pages 373-374

one of the three Gorgons, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Phorcys and Ceto. She was the only one of the Gorgons who was subject to mortality. She is celebrated for her personal charms and the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> of her locks. <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol7.html#article-NEPTUNE">Neptune</a> became enamoured of her, and obtained her favours in the temple of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MINERVA">Minerva</a>. This violation of the sanctity of the temple provoked Minerva; and she changed the beautiful locks of Medusa, which had inspired Neptune's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LOVE">love</a>, into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERPENTS">serpents</a>, the sight of which turned the beholders into <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-STONES">stones</a>: but Perseus, armed with <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-MERCURY">Mercury</a>'s ax with which he killed Argus, cut off Medusa's head, from whose blood sprang Pegasus and Chrysaor, together with the innumerable serpents that infest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>. The conqueror placed Medusa's head on the aegis of Minerva, which he had used in his expedition; and the head still retained the same petrifying powers as before. Medusa, in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ZOOLOGY">zoology</a>, a genus of vermes, belonging to the order of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOLLUSCA">mollusca</a>. The body is gelatinous, roundish, and depressed; and the mouth is in the centre of the under <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">part</a> of the body. Many <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, on being handled, affect with a nettle-like <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BURNING">burning</a>, and excite a redness. The <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, and some of the moderns, add that they have an aphrodisiac <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>, and in several languages they are called by an obscene name. They were known to the Greeks and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> by the names of Πλευρα θαλασσινης, and pulmo marinus, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-lungs. They attributed medicinal virtues to them. Dioscorides informs us, that, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> rubbed fresh on the diseased part, they cured the gout in the feet, and killed fleas. Aelian says, that they were depilatory; and, if macerated in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-VINEGAR">vinegar</a>, would take away the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARD">beard</a>. Their phthoric <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> is well known; nor was it overlooked by the ancients. Pliny observes, that if rubbed with a stick it <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WILL">will</a> appear to burn, and the wood to shine all over. The same naturalist observes, that when they sink to the bottom of the sea, they portend a continuance of bad <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>. On Plate CCXCIV, are figured several specimens, viz. 1. The aurita, or aurited medusa; which appears, as floating on the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WATER">water</a>, to be a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> lifeless lump of jelly. It is of a whitish <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> of bluish grey, and is of an orbiculated <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, elevated into a convexity in the middle on the upper side, flat on the under, and furnished with a fringe of fine and somewhat rigid filaments round the edge, resembling <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WHITE">white</a> hairs: on the under surface there are four cavities near the centre, each of an arcuated figure, and surrounded with an opaque line, formed of about 24 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-POINTS">points</a> or dots: from the very centre of the under side there arise four crooked appendages, which have each a row of hairy filaments on the exterior edge; and on the upper surface there is an appearance of fine vessels of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> colour. This species is frequent, floating on the surface of the sea, or adhering to rocks about our own coasts; and when the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> shines on them, they have a very beautiful lucid appearance. It is called by some the sea nettle, it being one of those animals that when touched occasions a very disagreeable tingling in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>. 2. The capillata, or capillated medusa, is a very singular and odd animal: it seems a mere lump of a whitish femi-pellucid jelly; and is as easily broken and destroyed by a touch as the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMON">common</a> jellies brought to our tables: its shape is rounded, rising into a convexity in the middle, where it is therefore thickest, and whence it becomes gradually thinner to the sides; on the under side it is plain, and on this there is visible a rough, or as it were echinated circle, within which... there run eight pairs of rays from the centre toward the circumference; and from the centre there arise also a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of curled appendages, which are sometimes reddish, but more usually whitish, and a vast number of slender filaments: the edge or the circumference of the body is regularly divided into eight portions, and each of them is marginated, so that on the whole verge there are 16 sinuses. This species is to be met with in vast abundance floating on the surface of the water about Sheppey <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KENT">Kent</a>, and elsewhere on that <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COAST">coast</a>: <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> quantities of it are destroyed by being thrown on shore with the waves, whence it has no power of getting off again; and in the open seas, many fish skim near the surface, and prey on them. This is the species called by many authors pulmo marinus, or the sea lungs. 3. The marsupials, or purple medusa, is semi-oval, with four tentacles on the edge. It inhabits the Mediterranean. 4. The waved medusa has the edges waved, with fangs on the projecting parts; four orifices beneath, between which rises a stem divided into eight <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LARGE">large</a> ragged tentacles. These animals swim in large companies in search of food, with their tentacles in continual <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>, with which they <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SEIZE">seize</a> their prey, and convey it to their mouths: they vary in size, the largest being generally about eight inches in diameter. They vary likewise in the number of their tentacles; some having only two, others four, six, and some eight, but they rarely exceed that number. So powerful is their embrace, that whatever prey comes within their reach never escapes. They subsist on insects, small fish, &c. Mr Banks, in his passage from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MADEIRA">Madeira</a> to Rio de Janeiro, discovered a new species, which, when brought aboard by the casting <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NET">net</a>, had the appearance of metal violently heated, and emitted a white <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>. With these animals were taken small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CRABS">crabs</a> of three different species, altogether new, each of which gave as much light as the glow-worm, though the creature was not so large by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NINE">nine</a>-tenths. These <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LUMINOUS">luminous</a> animals are one of the causes of that appearance to the sea which has been mentioned by many navigators, and of which various reasons have been assigned. It appeared to emit flashes of light exactly resembling those of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LIGHTNING">lightning</a>, only not so considerable, but so frequent, that sometimes eight or ten were visible at the same moment.

MEDWAY

Pages 374-374

a river of England, rises in the Weald of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SUSSEX">Sussex</a>, and entering <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KENT">Kent</a> near Ashurst, runs by <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TUNBRIDGE">Tunbridge</a>, and thence continues its course towards <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MAIDSTONE">Maidstone</a>. It is navigable for <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LARGE">large</a> ships to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-ROCHESTER">Rochester</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>, and thence for vessels and barges to Maidstone, the tide flowing up to that town. The distance between the mouth of this river, where the fort at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SHEERNESS">Sheerness</a> is erected, and Rochester bridge, is between 16 and 18 miles. In this <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">part</a> of the river, the channel is so deep, the banks so soft, and the reaches so short, that it is one of the best and safest harbours in the world; and ships of 80 guns ride afloat at low-<a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WATER">water</a>, within musket-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> of Rochester bridge. Nor is there a single instance upon record, that any of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NAVY">navy</a> ever suffered here by storms, except in that dreadful tempest which happened in November 1703, when the Royal Catharine was driven on shore, where she sunk and was lost. On the shore of this river are two castles, one at Upnor, which guards two reaches of the river, and is supposed to defend all the ships which ride above, between that and the bridge; on the other side of the river is Gillingham castle, built for the same purpose, and well furnished with cannon which commands the river. Besides these, there is a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PLATFORM">platform</a> of guns at a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLACE">place</a> called the Swan, and another at Cockham-wood. But the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> fortification on this river is the castle at Sheerness.

MEEREN

Pages 374-374
or Meer, (John Vander,) called De Jonghe, an eminent landscape-painter, is supposed to have been the son of the old John Vander Meer, and of whom he learned the first rudiments of the art; but being in his youth deprived of his instructor before he had made any great progress, he became a disciple of Nicholas Berghem, and was accounted the best of those who were educated in the school of that admired master. In the manner of his master, he painted landscapes and cattle; and his usual subjects are cottages, with peasants at their rural occupations and diversions. It is observed of him, that he very rarely introduced cows, horses, or any other species of animals, except goats and sheep; the latter of which are so highly finished, that one would imagine the wool might be felt by the softness of its appearance. His touch is scarcely perceptible, and yet the colours are admirably united. He died in 1688. The genuine works of this Vander Meer bear a very high price, and are esteemed even in Italy, where they are admitted into the best collections; but the scarcity of them has occasioned many moderate copies after his works to be passed on the unfeeling for real originals.

MEGALE POLIS

Pages 374-374

(anc. geog.) dividedly (<a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>, Pausanias); <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> conjunctly Megalopolis, (Strabo) = A town of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCADIA">Arcadia</a>, built under the auspices of Epaminondas, after the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LEUCTRA">Leuctra</a>; many inconsiderable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> being joined together in one <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CITY">city</a>, the better to withstand the Spartans. It was the greatest city of Arcadia, according to Strabo.

MEGARA

Pages 374-377

a noble <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CITY">city</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the territory of Megaris, which for many years carried on <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WAR">war</a> with the Corinthians and Athenians. It had for some <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a> a school of philosophers, called the Megaric, successors of Euclid the Socratic, a native of Megara. Their dialect was the Doric; changed from the Attic, which it formerly had been, because of Peloponnesian colonists who settled there. Megara was situated at a distance from the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. Its port was called Nysa, from Nysus son of Pacion the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, who obtained the Megaris for his portion, when the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a> was divided into four lots by his father. He founded the town, which was eighteen stadia <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> two miles and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> from the city, but united with it, as the Piraeus with Athens, by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">long</a> walls. It had a temple of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CERES">Ceres</a>. "The <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> (says Pausanias) may be supposed to have fallen through <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>." The site (as Dr Chandler informs us) is now covered with rubbish, among which are standing some ruined churches. The <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLACE">place</a> has been named from them Dode Ecclesias, "The Twelve Churches;" but the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> is reduced to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a>. The acropolis or citadel, called also Nysa, was on a rock by the sea-side. Some pieces of the wall remain, and a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> fortress has been erected on it, and also on a lesser rock near it. The village Megara (continues the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DOCTOR">Doctor</a>) consists of low <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> cottages, pleasantly situated on the slope of a brow or eminence indented in the middle. On each side of this vale was an acropolis or citadel; one named <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CARIA">Caria</a>; the other from Alcathous, the builder of the wall. They related, that he was afflicted by <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a>, who laid his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARP">harp</a> aside on a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, which, as Pausanias testifies, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> struck with a pebble returned a musical <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SOUND">sound</a>. An <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> of the wall of one citadel is seen by a windmill. The masonry is of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> called Incertum. In 1676 the city-wall was not entirely demolished, but comprehended the two summits, on which are some churches, with a portion of the plain toward the south. The whole site, except the hills, was now green with corn, and marked by many heaps of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, the collected rubbish of buildings. A few <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INSCRIPTIONS">inscriptions</a> are found, with pedestals fixed in the walls and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-INVERTED">inverted</a>; and also some maimed or mutilated <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a>. One of the former relates to Atticus Herodes, and is on a pedestal which supported a statue erected to him when <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONSUL">consul</a>, A.D. 143, by the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> and people of Megara, in return for his benefactions and good-<a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WILL">will</a> toward the city. In the plain behind the summits, on one of which was a temple of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MINERVA">Minerva</a>, is a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LARGE">large</a> basin of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WATER">water</a>, with scattered fragments of marble, the remains of a bath or of a fountain, which is recorded as in the city, and remarkable for its size and ornaments, and for the number of its columns. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> was named from the local nymphs called Sithnides. The stone of Megara was of a kind not discovered anywhere else in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HELLAS">Hellas</a>; very <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, uncommonly soft, and consisting entirely of cockle-shells. This was chiefly used; and, not being durable, may be reckoned among the causes of the desolation at Megara, which is so complete, that one searches in vain for vestiges of the many public edifices, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a>, and sepulchres, which once adorned the city. Megara was engaged in various wars with Athens and Corinth, and experienced many vicissitudes of fortune. It was the only one of the Greek cities which did not re-flourish under their <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMON">common</a> benefactor <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HADRIAN">Hadrian</a>; and the reason assigned is, that the avenging <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANGER">anger</a> of the gods purified the people for their impiety in killing Anthemocritus, a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HERALD">herald</a>, who had been sent to them in the time of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PERICLES">Pericles</a>. The Athenian generals were sworn on his account to invade them twice a-year. Hadrian and Atticus were followed by another friend, whose <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> is preserved by an inscription on a stone lying near a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> in the village:— "This too is the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> of the most magnificent <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COUNT">count</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DIOGENES">Diogenes</a> son of Archelaus, who regarding the Grecian cities as his own family, has bestowed on that of the Megarensians one hundred pieces of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> toward the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> of their towers, and also one hundred and fifty more with two thousand-two hundred feet of marble toward re-edifying the bath; deeming nothing more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> than to do good to the Greeks, and to restore their cities." This person is not quite unnoticed in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>. He was one of the generals employed by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Anastasius on a rebellion in Isauria. He surprised the capital Claudiopolis, and sustained a siege with <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> bravery, A.D. 494. Megara retains its original name. It has been much infested by corsairs; and in 1676 the inhabitants were accustomed, on seeing a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOAT">boat</a> approach in the daytime or hearing their dogs bark at night, immediately to secrete their effects and run away. The Vaiwode or Turkish governor, who resided in a forsaken tower above the village, was once carried off. It is no wonder, therefore, that Nysa has been long abandoned. The place was burned by the Venetians in 1687. MEGARIS (anc. geog.) formerly called Hybla, a town towards the east <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>; extinct in Strabo's time, though the name Hybla remained on account of the excellence of its <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>. It was a colony of Megareans from <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>. Rijus Megaricus denotes a hoarfrost.

MEGARIS

Pages 377-377

a small <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> in the Tuscan <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, joined to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a> by a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>. Now called Castello del Porto.

MEGASTHENES

Pages 377-377

a Greek historian in the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> of Seleucus Nicanor, about 300 years before Christ; He wrote about the oriental nations, and particularly the Indians. His <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> is often quoted by the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>. What now passes as his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> is spurious.

MEGIDDO

Pages 377-378

a town of Galilee, recited (Joshua xvii. 11.) among the cities of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MANASSEH">Manasseh</a>, in the tribe of Issachar <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> Asher, on the west side of Jordan. Famous for the defeat of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AHAZIAH">Ahaziah</a> and Jotham, who perished there (2 Kings xxiii. 29.) near it was Melibomius an open plain, fit for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> up an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARRAY">array</a>. It was situated to the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, contrary to its position in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMON">common</a> maps. The Canaanites, being tributary to the Israelites, dwelt in it, Joshua xvii. — It was rebuilt by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SOLOMON">Solomon</a>, I Kings ix.

MEIBOMIUS

Pages 378-378

the name of several learned Germans. — John Henry Melibomius was professor of physic at Helmstadt, where he was born, and at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LUBEC">Lubec</a>; he wrote the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">Life</a> of Maeæna, published at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a> in 4to, 1653, with several other learned works. Henry, his son, was born at Lubec in 1638; became professor of physic at Helmstadt; and, besides works in his own profession, published Scriptores rerum Germanicarum, 3 vol. folio, 1688; a very useful collection, first begun by his father. — Marcus Melibomius, of the same family, published a collection of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> Greek authors who had written upon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> music, with a Latin version by himself; dedicated to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHRISTINA">Christina</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, who invited him to her <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COURT">court</a>. But the engaging him one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> to sing an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> of ancient music, while somebody was ordered to dance to it, the immoderate mirth which this occasioned in the spectators so disgusted him, that he immediately left the court of Sweden. His edition of the Greek mythologists, and notes upon <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DIOGENES">Diogenes</a> Laertius in Menage's edition, show him to have been a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MAN">man</a> of learning; but he suffered no little raillery for his attempt to correct the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> text of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BIBLE">Bible</a>, by a kind of metre he fancied he had found out in those ancient writings.

MEISSEN

Pages 378-378

a considerable town of Germany, in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-ELECTORATE">electorate</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a>, and in the margravate of Misnia, with a castle. It formerly belonged to the bishop, but is now secularized, and the inhabitants are Lutherans. In this <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLACE">place</a> is a famous manufactory of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PORCELAIN">porcelain</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 13° 33'. N. Lat. 51° 15'.

MELA

Pages 378-378

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Latin writer, was born in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Baetica in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, and flourished in the reign of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Claudius. His three books of Cosmography, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> De situ orbis, are written in a concise, perspicuous, and elegant manner; and have been thought worthy of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> and labours of the ablest critics. <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> Vossius gave an edition of them in 1658, 4to, with very <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and copious notes. To this edition is added, Julli Honorii oratoris excerptum cosmographicum, first published from the manuscript, and Athenici cosmographia. Gronovius afterwards published another edition with illustrations by medals. In his last edition are added five books, De Geographia, written by some later author; by Jordanes, as Fabricius conjectures.

MELAENE

Pages 357-364

This is a distemper not very <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMON">common</a>, but it has been observed by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> physicians, and is described by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIPPOCRATES">Hippocrates</a> under the name of morbus nigra. It shows itself by a vomiting and purging of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> tar-like <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>; which Hippocrates, Boerhaave, and Van Swieten, supposed to be occasioned by atra bilis. But Dr Home, in his Clinical Experiments, shows that it is owing to an <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-EFFUSION">effusion</a> of blood from the mesenteric vessels, which by its stagnation and corruption assumes that strange appearance. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>, he says, frequently follows hemorrhagy; and those of a scorbutic <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> are most subject to it. It is an acute disease, and terminates soon; yet is not attended with any <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of fever. In one of Dr Home's patients the crisis happened on the eighth <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> by diarrhoea; in another, on the 14th, by sweat and urine; and a third had no evident critical evacuation. As to the cure, Dr Home observes, that bleeding is always necessary where the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PULSE">pulse</a> can bear it; nor are we to be deterred from it by a little weakness of the pulse, more than in the enteritis. Emetics are hurtful, but purgatives are useful. But the most powerful medicine for checking this hemorrhagy is the vitriolic acid; and, that this might be given in greater <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a>, he mixed it with mucilage of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GUM">gum</a> arabic; by which means he was enabled to give <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> the quantity he could otherwise have done. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COLD">cold</a> bath was tried in one instance, but he could not determine whether it was of any <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> not. The cure was completed by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> and the bark. Of the DISEASES of CHILDREN. Dr <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BUCHAN">Buchan</a> observes, that from the annual registers of the dead it appears, that about one half of the children born in Great <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> die under twelve years of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>; and this very great mortality he attributes in a great <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> to wrong management. The particulars of this wrong management enumerated by him are, 1. Mothers not suckling their own children. This, he owns, it is sometimes impossible for them to do; but where it can be done, he affirms that it ought never to be omitted. This, he says, would prevent the unnatural <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of mothers leaving their own children to suckle those of others; on which he passes a most severe censure, and indeed scarce any censure can be severe enough upon such inhumanity. Dr Buchan informs us, "He is sure he speaks within bounds, when he says not one in a hundred of these children live who are thus abandoned by their mothers." For this reason he adds, that no mother should be allowed to suckle another's child till her own be fit to be weaned. A regulation of this kind would <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-SAVE">save</a> many lives among the poorer sort, and would do no harm to the rich; as most women who make good nurses are able to suckle two children in succession upon the same <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MILK">milk</a>. 2. Another source of the diseases of children is the unhealthiness of parents; and our author insists that no person who labours under an incurable malady ought to marry. 3. The manner of clothing children tends to produce diseases. All that is necessary here, he says, is to wrap the child in a soft loose covering; and the softness of every <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">part</a> of the infant's body sufficiently shows the injury which must necessarily ensue by pursuing a contrary method. 4. A new-born infant, instead of being treated with syrups, oils, &c., ought to be allowed to suck the mother's milk almost as soon as it comes into the world. He condemns the practice of giving wines and spirituous liquors along with the food soon after birth; and says, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the mother or nurse has a sufficient quantity of milk, the child <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WILL">will</a> need little or no other food before the third or fourth <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MONTH">month</a>. But to this it may reasonably be objected, not only that the nursing would thus be very severe on the mother; but if the child be left thus <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">long</a> without food, it will not easily relish it for some <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a>, and its stomach is apt to be easily hurt by a slight change of diet after it has been long accustomed to one thing. Neither can it be shown, that the strongest and most healthy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INFANTS">infants</a> are those which get no other food but the mother's milk during the first months of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. In fact, children are evidently of a weak and lax habit of body, so that many of their diseases must arise from that cause; all directions which indiscriminately advise an antiphlogistic regimen for infants as soon as they come into the world, must of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> be wrong. Many instances in fact might be brought to show, that by the preposterous method of starving infants, and at the same time treating them with vomits and purges, they are often Diseases of often hurried out of the world. Animal-food indeed is excessively agreeable to children, and they ought to be indulged with it in moderation; and this will prove a much better remedy for those acidities with which children are often troubled, than <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MAGNESIA">magnesia</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALBA">alba</a>, crab's eyes, or other absorbents, which have the most pernicious effects on the stomachs of these tender creatures, and pall the appetite to a surprising degree. The <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> appetites of children are indeed the best rule by which we can judge of what is proper or improper for them. They must no doubt be regulated as to the quantity; but we may be assured that what a child is very fond of will not hurt it if taken in moderation. When children are sick, they refuse every thing but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>; and if their distemper be very severe, they will refuse it also; and in this <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CASE">case</a> they ought not to be pressed to take food of any kind; but when the sickness goes off, their appetite also returns, and they will require the usual quantity of food. According to Dr Armstrong, inward fits, as they are called, are in general the first complaint that appears in children; and as far as he has observed, most, if not all infants, during the first months, are more or less liable to them. The symptoms are these.
