On account of its quarrels with Weymouth, in the reign of Henry VI. its privileges as a port were removed to Pool: but in that of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a> they were restored to it by <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of parliament, which was confirmed in the next reign, on condition that Melcomb and Weymouth should make but one corporation, and enjoy their privileges in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMON">common</a>; and to this was owing the flourishing state of both. In the two reigns last mentioned, a wooden <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> with seventeen <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a> was built from hence to Weymouth; to which, as well as its <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> contributors were certain citizens of London; and upon its decay it was rebuilt in 1770. Here is a good market-<a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLACE">place</a> and town-<a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HALL">hall</a>, to which the members of the corporation of Weymouth come to attend public business, as the inhabitants do to its church for public worship. For several years past the sea has retired from it on the east, the priory formerly being bounded by the sea; but there is now a street beyond it, from which it is several paces to the high-<a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WATER">water</a> mark. The priory was situated in the east <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">part</a> of the town, in Maiden-street, whose site occupied about an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACRE">acre</a>, now covered with tenements. On the south side are the remains of the chapel, now converted into a malt-<a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>. Near it are the remains of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a>... ancient <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, formerly a nunnery. Here are three meeting-houses and a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a>-house for the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-POOR">poor</a>. The church, which is in the middle of the town, has a wooden turret for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELL">bell</a>, and had been an old chapel. It was rebuilt in 1605, and made parochial, and is a handsome fabric, with a beautiful altar-piece painted and given by Sir James Thornhill. The port, which generally goes by the name of Weymouth, is said to be the best frequented in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COUNTY">county</a>, and is defended by Sandford and Portland castles. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARKETS">markets</a> for both <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> are Tuesdays and Fridays, but there are no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a>. Melcombe-Regis is reckoned bigger, more thriving, and populous than Weymouth. They are both but one corporation and borough, consisting of a mayor, recorder, two bailiffs, an uncertain <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of aldermen, and twenty-four <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> burgesses. Whoever has been a mayor is ever after an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALDERMAN">alderman</a>. They send four burgesses to parliament, who are elected by such as have freeholds, whether they inhabit here <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> not; and the number of voters is near 700. Every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELECTOR">elector</a>, as in London, has the privilege of voting for four persons, who when chosen are returned, in two distinct indentures, as the burgesses of Weymouth and the burgesses of Melcombe-Regis.

MELDAE

Pages 382-382

a town of Gallia Celtica, (called Meldorum Civitas in the Notitia), on the Matrona. Now <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MEAUX">Meaux</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CITY">city</a> in Champaigne on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARNE">Marne</a>. MELEAGER (fab. hist.) a celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HERO">hero</a>, son of Æneas <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KING">king</a> of Calydonia, by Althæa <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Thestius. The Parcae were present at the moment of his birth, and predicted his future greatness. <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CLOTHO">Clotho</a> said that he would be brave and courageous; <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LACHESIS">Lachesis</a> foretold his uncommon strength and valour; and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATROPOS">Atropos</a> said that he should live as <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">long</a> as that firebrand which was on the fire remained entire and unconfused. Althæa no sooner heard this, than she snatched the stick from the fire, and kept it with the most jealous care, as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of her son totally depended upon its preservation. The fame of Meleager increased with his years; he signalized himself in the Argonautic expedition, and afterwards delivered his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> from the neighbouring inhabitants, who made <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WAR">war</a> against his father at the instigation of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DIANA">Diana</a>, whose altars Æneas had neglected. But Diana punished the negligence of Æneas by a greater calamity. She sent a huge wild boar, which laid waste all the country, and seemed invincible on account of its immense size. It became soon a public concern: all the neighbouring princes assembled to destroy this terrible animal; and nothing is more famous in mythological <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, than the hunting of the Calydonian boar. The princes and chiefs that assembled, and which are mentioned by mythologists, were Meleager son of Æneas, Idas and Lynceus sons of Aphareus, Dryas son of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MARS">Mars</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CASTOR">Castor</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLLUX">Pollux</a> sons of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> and Leda, Piritheus son of Ixion, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THESEUS">Theseus</a> son of Ægeus, Anceus and Cepheus sons of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LYCURGUS">Lycurgus</a>, Admetus son of Phereus, Jason son of Æson, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PELEUS">Peleus</a> and Telamon sons of Æacus, Iphicles son of Amphitryon, Eurytrion son of Aetor, Atalanta daughter of Schœ-Meleager, neus, Iolas the friend of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a>, the sons of The- Meleagris, stius, Amphiaraus son of Oileus, Protheus, Cometes, the brothers of Altæa, Hippothous son of Cercyon, Leucippus, Adrastus, Ceneus, Phileus, Echion, Lelex, Phoenix son of Amyntor, Panopeus, Hyleus, Hippafus, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NESTOR">Nestor</a>, Menestius the father of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PATROCLUS">Patroclus</a>, Amphi- chides, Laertes the father of Ulysses, and the four sons of Hippocoon. This troop of armed men attacked the boar, and it was at last killed by Meleager.—The conqueror gave the skin and the head to Atalanta, who had first wounded the animal. This irritated the rest, and particularly Toxeus and Plexippus the brothers of Althæa, and they endeavoured to rob Atalanta of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> present. Meleager defended her, and killed his uncles in the attempt. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">Mean</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a> the news of this celebrated conquest had already reached <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CALYDON">Calydon</a>, and Althæa went to the temple of the gods to return thanks for the victory which her son had gained: But being informed that her brothers had been killed by Meleager, she in the moment of resentment threw into the fire the fatal stick on which her son’s life depended, and Meleager died as soon as it was consumed. <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a> does not mention the firebrand; whence some have imagined that this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FABLE">fable</a> is <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-POSTERIOR">posterior</a> to that poet’s <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>. But he says, that the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Toxeus and Plexippus so irritated Althæa, that she uttered the most horrible curses and impreca- tions upon her son’s head.

MELEAGER

Pages 382-382

a Greek poet, the son of Eucrates, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SELEUCIA">Seleucia</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>, and flourished under the reign of Seleucus VI. the last <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KING">king</a> of Syria. He was educated at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TYRE">Tyre</a>; and died in the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Coos, anciently called Merope. He there composed the Greek epigrams called by us the Anthologia. The disposi- tion of the epigrams in this collection was often changed afterwards, and many additions have been made to them. The monk Planudes put them into the order they are in at present, in the year 1380.

MELEAGRIS

Pages 382-383

in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">ornithology</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a>; a genus of birds belonging to the order of gallinae. The head is covered with spongy caruncles; and there is likewise a membranaceous longitudinal caruncle on the throat. There is but one (a) <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, viz. the gallopavo, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NORTH">North</a> American turkey of Ray. It has a caruncle both on the head and throat; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MALE">male</a> is bearded or tufted. He lives upon grain and insects; when the cock struts, he blows up his breast, spreads and erects his feathers, relaxes the caruncle on the forehead, and the naked parts of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FACE">face</a> and neck become intensely <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RED">red</a>. Barbot informs us that very few turkeys are to be met with in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GUINEA">Guinea</a>, and those only in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the chiefs of the European forts; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEGROES">negroes</a> declining to breed any on account of their tenderness, which sufficiently proves them not to be natives of that <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a>. He also remarks, that neither the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-POULTRY">poultry</a> nor ducks are <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> to Guinea any more than the turkey. Neither is that <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BIRD">bird</a> a na- tive of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>: the first that were seen in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a> were brought (a) Two others were formerly enumerated; but in the late edition of the Synt. Nat. by Gmelin, they have been transferred to a new genus. See Penelope. Melagrís, brought from <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a> by some Armenian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a>. They are bred in Ceylon, but not found wild. In fact, the turkey, properly so called, was unknown to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> naturalists, and even to the old world, before the discovery of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>. It was a bird peculiar to the new continent; and is now the commonest wild-fowl in the northern parts of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, where they are frequently met with by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HUNDREDS">hundreds</a> in a flock: in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a> they frequent the woods, where they feed on acorns; and return at night to the swamps to roost, which they do on the trees. They are frequently taken by means of dogs, though they run faster for a time; but the dogs persisting in the pursuit, the birds soon grow fatigued, and take to the highest trees, where they <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WILL">will</a> suffer themselves to be <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> one after another <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> within reach of the marksman. This fowl was first seen in France in the reign of Francis I. and in England in that of Henry VIII. By the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DATE">date</a> of the reign of these monarchs, the first turkeys must have been brought from <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-MEXICO">Mexico</a>, the conquest of which was completed A.D. 1521. Ælian mentions a bird found in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, which some writers have suspected to be the turkey; but Mr Pennant concludes with Gellner, that it was either the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PEACOCK">peacock</a>, or some bird of that genus. The turkey-hen begins to lay early in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>, and will often produce a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of eggs, which are <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, marked with reddish or <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> spots, or rather freckles. She sits well, and is careful of her young; of which in this climate she will often have from fourteen to seventeen for one brood; but the scarce ever sits more than once in a season, except allured thereto by putting fresh eggs under her as soon as the first set are hatched; for as she is a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> fitter, she will willingly remain two months on the nest, tho' this conduct, as may be supposed, is said greatly to injure the bird. Turkeys are bred in quantities in some of the northern counties of England, and are driven up to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONDON">London</a> towards autumn for <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-SALE">sale</a> in flocks of several hundreds, which are collected from the several cottages about <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NORFOLK">Norfolk</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SUFFOLK">Suffolk</a>, and neighbouring counties, the inhabitants of which think it well worth their while to attend carefully to them, by making these birds a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">part</a> of their family during the breeding season. It is pleasing to see with what facility the drivers manage them, by means of a bit of red rag fastened to the end of a stick, which, from their antipathy to it as a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, acts with the same effect as a scourge to a quadruped. Of the turkey there are several varieties, which have arisen from domestication. The most common is dark grey inclining to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, or barred dusky white and black. There is also a beautiful variety of a fine deep <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COPPER">copper</a> colour, with the greater quills pure white, and the tail of a dirty white; it is when old a most beautiful bird. A variety with a pure white plumage is also now not unfrequent, and appears very beautiful. It was once esteemed as a great rarity, and the breed supposed originally to have arisen in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>. In the Leverian <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MUSEUM">Museum</a> is also a common turkey, with a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LARGE">large</a> tuft of feathers on its head, much resembling one figured by Albin.

MELES

Pages 383-383

a fine river running by the walls of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SMYRNA">Smyrna</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-IONIA">Ionia</a>, with a cave at its head, where <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a> is said to have written his poems. And from it Homer takes his original name <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MELAGRIS">Melagris</a>, given him by his mother Critheia, as being born on its banks. (<a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HERODOTUS">Herodotus</a>.)

MELETIANS

Pages 383-383

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, the name of a considerable party who adhered to the cause of Meletius bishop of Lycopolis, in Upper <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, after he was deposed, about the year 306, by <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a>, under the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> of his having sacrificed to the gods, and having been guilty of other heinous crimes; though Epiphanius makes his only failing to have been an excessive severity against the lafied. This dispute, which was at first a personal <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between Meletius and Peter, became a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> controversy; and the Meletian party subsided in the fifth century, but was condemned by the first <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of Nice.

MELIA

Pages 383-383

Azaderach, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> the Bead tree, in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a>: A genus of the monogynia order, belonging to the decandria clas of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 23d order Tribilatae. The calyx is quinquedentated; the petals five; the nectarium cylindrical, as <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">long</a> as the corolla, with its mouth ten-toothed: the fruit is a plum with a quinquilocular kernel. There are three <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, all of them exotic trees of the Indies, rising near 20 feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>; adorned with <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LARGE">large</a> pinnated or winged leaves, and clusters of pentapetalous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>. They are all propagated by seeds sown on <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HOT_BEDS">hot-beds</a>.

MELIANTHUS

Pages 383-383
Honey-flower, in botany: A genus of the angiosperma order, belonging to the didynamia clas of plants; and in the natural method ranking under the 24th order Corydalis. The calyx is pentaphyllous, with the lowermost leaf gibbous: there are four petals, with the nectarium under the lowest ones. The capsule is quadrilocular. There are two species. 1. Themajor hath a thick, ligneous, spreading root; many upright, ligneous, durable stalks, rising six or eight feet high; garnished with large pinnated leaves, of four or five pair of serrated lobes terminated by an odd one; and, from the sides and tops of the stalks, long spikes of chocolate-coloured flowers. 2. The minor hath a root like the former; upright, ligneous, soft, durable stalks, rising four or five feet high; garnished with smaller pinnated leaves; and from the sides and ends of the branches, long, loose, pendulous bunches of flowers tinged with green, saffron colour, and red.—Both the species flower about June: but rarely produce seeds in this country. They are very ornamental, both in foliage and flower, and merit admittance in every collection. They are easily propagated by suckers and cuttings. They thrive best in a dry soil, and in a sheltered warm exposure.

MELIBOEA

Pages 383-383

an <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>, at the mouth of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORONTES">Orontes</a>; which, before it falls into the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, forms a spreading lake round it. This island was famous for its purple dye. Thought to be a colony of Thessalians; and hence Lucretius's epithet, Thessalicae.

MELICA

Pages 383-384

Ropegrass: A genus of the digynia order, belonging to the triandra clas of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 4th order <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GRAMINA">Gramina</a>. The calyx is bivalved, biflorous, with an embryo of a flower betwixt the two florets. There are three <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>; of which the most remarkable is Meliceres the nutans. It is a native of several parts of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, and the adjacent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>; and the inhabitants of some of the western islands make <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROPES">ropes</a> of it for <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a>-nets, as it <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WILL">will</a> bear the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WATER">water</a> for a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a> without rotting.

MELICERES

Pages 384-384

in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SURGERY">surgery</a>, a kind of encysted tumors, so called when their contents are of the consistence of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>.

MELICERTA

Pages 384-384

Melicertes, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> Melicertus (fab. hist.), a son of Athamas and Ino. He was saved by his mother from the fury of his father, who prepared to dash him against a wall as he had done his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> Learchus. The mother was so terrified that she threw herself into the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SEA">sea</a> with Melicerta in her arms. <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol7.html#article-NEPTUNE">Neptune</a> had compassion on the misfortunes of Ino and her son. He changed them both into sea deities. Ino was called Leucothoe or Mutata; and Melicerta was known among the Greeks by the name of Palemon, and among the Latins by that of Portumnus. Some suppose that the Ithmian games were instituted in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of Melicerta.

MELILLA

Pages 384-384

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FEZ">Fez</a>, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Garet. It was taken by the Spaniards in 1499, but returned back to the Moors. W. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 2. 9. N. Lat. 35. 20. MELILOT. See Trifolium.

MELINDA

Pages 384-384

a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> on the east <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, situated, according to some, between the third and fourth <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of south latitude; though there is <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> disagreement among geographers as to its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>. It is allowed by all, however, that the coasts are very dangerous; being full of rocks and shelves, and the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SEA">sea</a> at some seasons very liable to tempests. The kingdom of Melinda is for the most <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">part</a> rich and fertile; producing almost all the necessaries of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> except wheat and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a>, both which are brought thither from Cambaya and other parts; and those who cannot purchase them make <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of potatoes in their stead, which are here fine, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, and in great plenty. They likewise abound with great variety of fruit-trees, roots, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, and other esculents, and with melons of exquisite <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>. They have also great plenty of venison, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAME">game</a>, oxen, sheep, hens, geese, and other <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-POULTRY">poultry</a>, &c. and one breed of sheep whose tails weigh between 30 and 40 pounds. The <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CITY">city</a> is also called Melinda.

MELINUM

Pages 384-384

in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol12.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, the name of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> famous in the earliest ages of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>, being the only <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WHITE">white</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> painters of antiquity; and, according to Pliny's account, one of the three colours with which alone they performed all their works. It is a fine, white, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MARLY">marly</a> earth, of a very <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMPACT">compact</a> texture, yet remarkably <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>; a sort of texture which must render any earth fit for the painter's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> that is of a proper <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>. It is frequently found forming a stratum in the earth, lying immediately under the vegetable mould. It is of a very smooth but not glossy surface; is very soft to the touch; adheres firmly to the tongue; is easily broken between the fingers; and stains the skin in handling. It melts readily in the mouth, and is perfectly fine; leaving not the least grittiness between the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a>; thrown into <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WATER">water</a>, it makes a loud bubbling and hissing noise, and moulders away into a fine powder. It does not ferment with <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ACIDS">acids</a>; and suffers no change in the fire. These are the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> by which the melinum of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> is distinguished from all other white earths. It is still found in the same <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLACE">place</a> from which the painters of old had it, viz. the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> of Milo <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-MELOS">Melos</a>, from whence it had its name; and is <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMON">common</a> in most of the adjacent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>. It has of late been tried here; but is found not to make such a bright paint as the other substances now employed. It is not, however, liable, like them, to turn <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>; hence it would seem to be worth the consideration of persons in the colour-trade; especially as it might be had in any quantities for the carriage.

MELISSA

Pages 384-385

Baum: A genus of the gymnospermia order, belonging to the didynamia class of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 42d order Verticillate. The calyx is arid, a little <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLANE">plane</a> above, with the upper lip having its dents nearly of equal height; the upper lip of the corolla is arched and bifid; the under one, with the middle lobe, cordated. There are several <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>; but the most remarkable are the following. 1. The officinalis, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMON">common</a> baum, has <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIBROUS">fibrous</a> perennial roots; many upright, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, branchy, annual stalks, rising two or three feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>; garnished with <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a>, indented, opposite leaves, by pairs, two or three inches <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and half as <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>; and from the upper axillas verticillate clusters of small <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> upon single footstalks. There is also a kind with variegated leaves. 2. The grandiflora, or Heturian calamint, hath fibrous perennial roots and annual stalks, rising about a foot high, garnished with oblong, oval, indented, hairy, opposite leaves; and from the upper axillas verticillate clusters of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LARGE">large</a> purple flowers on forked footstalks. 3. The calaminta, or common calamint of the shops, has fibrous perennial roots; upright, square, branchy hairy stalks, rising a foot high; roundish, indented, opposite leaves; and verticillate clusters of small bluish flowers, on forked footstalks as long as the flowers. All these species are easily propagated by offsets. Medicinal uses. The first species, when in perfection, has a pleasant smell, somewhat of the lemon kind; and a weak, roughish, aromatic <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>. The young shoots have the strongest flavour; the flowers, and the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HERB">herb</a> itself when old or produced in very rich moist soils or rainy seasons, are much weaker both in smell and taste. Baum is appropriated, by the writers on the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">materia medica</a>, to the head, stomach, and uterus; and in all disorders of these parts is said to do extraordinary <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>. So high an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> have some chemists entertained of this plant, that they have expected to find in it a medicine which should prolong <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> beyond the usual <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>. The present practice, however, holds it in no <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> esteem; and ranks it (where it certainly deserves to be) among the weaker corroborants. Infusions of the leaves in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WATER">water</a> smell agreeably of the herb, but have not much taste, though on being infusified they leave a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of a bitterish aulere extract. Infusions of baum do not, like other aromatics, offend the head, as is complained of from sage, &c. <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COLD">Cold</a> infusions in water or spirit are far better than the cohabated distilled water, and are the best preparations from the plant. On distilling the fresh herb with water, it impregnates the first running pretty strongly with its grateful flavour. When large quantities are subjected to the operation at once, there separates and rises to the surface of the aqueous fluid a small portion of essential <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, which some call ol. Syrie, and others ol. Germanis. It is of a yellowish <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, and of a very fragrant smell.

MELISSUS OF SAMOS

Pages 385-385

a Greek <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, was the son of Imagines and the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of Parmenides; and lived about 440 B.C. He pretended that the universe is infinite, immoveable, and without a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-VACUUM">vacuum</a>. Themistocles was among his pupils.

MELITE

Pages 385-385

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-IONIA">Ionia</a>, struck out of the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of Ionian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> on account of the arrogance of the people, and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SMYRNA">Smyrna</a> admitted in lieu of it. The situation not said.

MELITENSIS TERRA

Pages 385-385

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">Earth</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MALTA">Malta</a>: an earth of which there are two very different kinds; the one of the genus of boles, the other of the marles. The latter is that known by medicinal authors under this name; the former is the Malta earth now in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>: but both being brought from the same <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, are confusedly called by the same name. The Maltese marle, which is the terra Melitensis of medicinal authors, is a loofe, crumbly, and very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> earth, of an unequal and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> texture; and, when exposed to the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>, soon falls into fine soft powder: but when preserved and dried, it becomes a loofe, light mafs, of a dirty <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, with a greyish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a>: it is rough to the touch, adheres firmly to the tongue, is very easily crumbled to powder between the fingers, and stains the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>. Thrown into the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WATER">water</a>, it swells, and afterwards moulders away into a fine powder. It ferments very violently with acid menstruums. Both kinds are found in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> abundance in the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Malta, and the latter has been much esteemed as a remedy against the bites of venomous animals. The other has supplied its place in the German shops; and is used there as a cordial, sudorific, and astringent.

MELITO

Pages 385-385

bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-SARDIS">Sardis</a> in Lydia, in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SECOND">second</a> century; remarkable for the apology he presented to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Aurelius, in favour of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>; on which Eusebius and the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> writers bestow <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> praises: but that apology and all Melito's other works are lost.

MELITUS

Pages 385-385

a Greek orator and poet, the accuser of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SOCRATES">Socrates</a>. The Athenians, after the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Socrates, discovering the iniquity of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> they had passed against that <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, put Melitus to death, 400 B.C.

MELLAN

Pages 385-385

an engraver of considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a>, was a native of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABBEVILLE">Abbeville</a> in Picardy, and born in 1621. His father was the receiver of the customs in that town; and he took <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> care of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> of his son. His genius for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> discovering itself very early in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, he was sent to <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, and placed under the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of Simon Vouet in order to perfect himself in that art, and his studies promised success; but he was diverted from his application to them by the desire he had of learning the management of the graver, which he acquired with much facility. From Paris, at the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> of sixteen, he went to Rome, where he engraved a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of plates, many of which are held in great estimation; particularly those for the Juflian Gallery, the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PORTRAIT">portrait</a> of the Marquis Juflian, and that of Pope Urban VIII. Returning to France, he married at Paris, and settled there in 1654. The <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KING">king</a> of France being made acquainted with his merit, affigned him apartments in the Louvre, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of a painter and an engraver. He acquired a competent fortune, and was greatly esteemed by all who knew him. He died in 1688, aged 87. Florent le Comte tells us, "That <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II. was so much pleased with his performances, that he invited him to come into England, making him at the same <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a> very advantageous offers. But the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> (continues that author) prevented his accepting of them." It is remarked, that most of the plates which he engraved at Rome, and before he went thither, are executed in the usual manner; that is, with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> strokes, crossed with <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SECOND">second</a> and third strokes, as the depth of the shadows might require. But afterwards he adopted a new <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of working with single strokes only, without any second strokes laid upon them; and the shadows are expressed by the same strokes being made stronger and brought nearer to each other. The effect which he produced by this method of engraving is soft and clear. In single figures and small subjects he succeeded very happily; but in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LARGE">large</a> compositions, where great depth of shadow was required, he has failed. His neatest plates in this style have an unfinished appearance, by no means suitable to large engravings; but at the same time a lightness exceedingly agreeable when confined to small ones. According to Le Comte, the works of this <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MASTER">master</a> amount to 342.

MELLER

Pages 385-385

a lake of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, 80 miles <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and 30 <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>; on which stands the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-STOCKHOLM">Stockholm</a>.

MELLI

Pages 385-386

with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of the Mundingoes, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>. The country formerly called Melli, now chiefly inhabited by the Mundingoes, who still retain pretty much of the character ascribed to the people of Melli, lies to the south of the river <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-GAMBIA">Gambia</a>; on the west it borders on the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Kabo; on the south it has Melli, properly so called, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> that <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">part</a> it from <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GUINEA">Guinea</a>; and on the east it extends to the kingdom of Gago. A <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> part of this country we are little acquainted with; as is the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CASE">case</a> with regard to most of the inland territories of Africa, but towards the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COAST">coast</a> this country is a little better known. The first <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a> we meet with is Kachao, a Portuguese colony, situated on the river of St Domingo, which falls into the sea about 26 leagues below this this town.—About 26 leagues above Kachao, on the same side of the river, is another trading town called Farini, where, in the months of October and November, one may trade for about half the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of wax and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-IVORY">ivory</a> which is traded for at Kachao. Here are also some slaves to be bought.—Bot is a village near the mouth of the river Gefves, where most of the traders buy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a>; which is in great plenty there, and very good.—Gefves is a village on a river of the same name, on which the Portuguese have a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACTORY">factory</a>. At Gefves one may trade yearly for 250 slaves, 8c <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> 100 quintals of wax, and as many of ivory. Near the mouth of the river of Gefves is a village called Kurballi, where there is a considerable trade for <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-SALT">salt</a>; here are also some slaves and ivory. Rio Grande, or the Great River, runs about 10 or 12 leagues to the south of the river of Gefves. About 80 leagues from the mouth of it is a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATION">nation</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEGROES">Negroes</a>, who are good traders in ivory, rice, millet, and some slaves. They are called Analon. Over-against the mouth of Rio Grande is a cluster of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> called Biffago Isles; the most considerable of which is Cassaguit, being about five leagues <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">long</a> and two <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>; its <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> is very good, and produces millet, rice, and all kinds of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PULSE">pulse</a>, besides <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-ORANGE">orange</a> and palm-trees, and many others. This <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, with those of Carache, Canabac, and La Gallina, are the only ones where the Europeans may trade with some security. They trade, however, sometimes at the other islands, but they must be extremely cautious; and yet after all their precautions, they <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WILL">will</a> be robbed and murdered <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they venture to go ashore. The river Nunho runs 16 leagues to the south of Rio Grande; it is very considerable, and comes from a vast distance inland. One may buy here 300 quintals of ivory and 100 slaves a-year. Rice grows here admirably well, and is very cheap. There are everywhere <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>-canes which grow naturally; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIGO">indigo</a>, which might turn to good account. The trade is carried on here from <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MARCH">March</a> till August. In the river of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SIERRA_LEONE">Sierra Leone</a>, the late <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> African <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> of England had, in the year 1728, two islands; the one, called Taffo, a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LARGE">large</a> flat island, near three leagues in circumference, in which the company’s slaves had a good plantation; the rest of the island is covered with wood, among which are <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SILK">silk</a>-cotton trees of an unaccountable size. The other island is Benja, whereon stood a regular fort. It was formerly the residence of one of the English chiefs.

MELMOTH

Pages 386-386

a learned and worthy bencher of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LINCOLN">Lincoln</a>’s Inn, was born in 1666. In conjunction with Mr Peere Williams, Mr Melmoth was the publisher of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-VERNON">Vernon</a>’s Reports, under an order of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHANCERY">chancery</a>. He had once an intention of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PRINTING">printing</a> his own Reports; and a short <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a> before his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEATH">death</a> advertised them at the end of those of his coadjutor Peere Williams, as then actually preparing for the press. They have, however, not yet made their appearance. But the performance for which he justly deserves to be held in perpetual <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-REMEMBRANCE">remembrance</a> is, “The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> Importance of a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-RELIGIOUS">Religious</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">Life</a>,” concerning which it may be mentioned, to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, that notwithstanding many <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LARGE">large</a> editions had before been circulated, 42,000 copies of this useful treatise have been sold in the last 18 years. It is a somewhat singular circumstance, that the real author of this most admirable treatise should never before have been publicly known (it having been <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> attributed to Melochia, the first <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Egmont, and particularly by Mr Walpole in his Catalogue); which is the more surprising, as the author is plainly pointed out in the following short character prefixed to the book itself: “It may add <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>, perhaps, to the reflections contained in the following <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-PAGES">pages</a>, to inform the reader, that the author’s life was one uniform exemplar of those precepts which, with so generous a zeal, and such an elegant and affecting simplicity of style, he endeavours to recommend to general practice. He left others to contend for modes of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>, and inflame themselves and the world with endless controversy; it was the wiser purpose of his more ennobled aim, to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> up to those clear rules of conduct which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-REVELATION">revelation</a> hath graciously prescribed. He possessed by temper every moral virtue; by <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> every Christian <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GRACE">grace</a>. He had a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a> that melted at every distress; a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a> which not only thought no evil, but suspected none. He exercised his profession with a skill and integrity which nothing could equal but the disinterested <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTIVE">motive</a> that animated his labours, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> the amiable <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MODESTY">modesty</a> which accompanied all his virtues. He employed his industry, not to gratify his own desires; no <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MAN">man</a> indulged himself less: not to accumulate useless wealth; no man more disdained so unworthy a pursuit: it was for the decent advancement of his family, for the generous assistance of his friends, for the ready relief of the indigent. How often did he exert his distinguished abilities, yet refuse the reward of them, in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of the widow, the fatherless, and him that had none to help him! In a word, few have ever passed a more useful, not one a more blameless life; and his whole time was employed either in doing good or in meditating it. He died on the 6th <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> of April 1743, and lies buried under the cloister of Lincoln’s Inn Chapel. MEM. PAT. OPT. MER. FIL. D.C.” The son, by whom this character is drawn, is William Melmoth, Esq.; the celebrated translator of Pliny and of Cicero’s Letters; and author of those which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> under the name of Sir Thomas Fitzgiborne.

MELOCHIA

Pages 386-387

JEW’S MALLOW, in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a>: A genus of the pentandria order, belonging to the monodelphia clasps of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 37th order, Columbiferae. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPSULE">capsule</a> is quinquilocular and monoecious. There are several <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>; but the only remarkable one is the olitorius, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMON">common</a> Jew’s-mallow, which is a native of the warm parts of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>. It is an annual plant, which rises about two feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, dividing into several branches, garnished with leaves of different sizes and forms: some are spear-shaped, others are oval, and some almost heart-shaped: they are of a deep green, and slightly indented on their edges, having near their base two bristly reflexed segments. They have very <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">long</a> slender footstalks, especially those which grow on the lower <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">part</a> of the branches. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> sit <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> on the opposite side of the branches to the leaves, coming out singly; they are composed of five small <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> petals, and a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of stamens surrounding the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> germen, which is situated in the centre of the flower, and afterwards turns to a rough swelling capsule two inches long, ending in a point, and and having four cells filled with angular greenish seeds. This species is cultivated about the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEPPO">Aleppo</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>, and in the East Indies, as a pot-<a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HERB">herb</a>; the Jews <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> the leaves, and eating them with their meat. It is supposed by Rauwolf to be the olus Judaicum of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AVICENNA">Avicenna</a>, and the corchorum of Pliny.

MELODUNUM

Pages 387-387

(anc. geog.), a town of the Cenones in Gallia Celtica above Lutetia; now <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MELUN">Melun</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> of France, on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEINE">Seine</a>.

MELODY

Pages 387-388

in music, a succession of sounds arranged in such a manner, according to the laws of rhythmus and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MODULATION">modulation</a>, that it may form a sentiment agreeable to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-EAR">ear</a>. Vocal melody is called singing; and that which is performed upon instruments may be termed symphonic melody. The idea of rhythmus necessarily enters into that of melody. An <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> is not an air but in proportion as the laws of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> are observed. The same succession of sounds is susceptible of as many different <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>, as many different kinds of melody, as the various ways by which its emphatic notes, and the quantities of those which intervene, may be diversified; and the change in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DURATION">duration</a> of the notes alone, may <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISGUISE">disguise</a> that very succession in such a manner that it cannot be known. Thus, melody in itself is nothing; it is the rhythmus <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> measure which determines it, and there can be no air without <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> then we <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSTRACT">abstract</a> measure from both, we cannot compare melody with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a>; for to the former it is essential, but not at all to the latter. Melody, according to the manner in which it is considered, has a relation to two different principles. When regarded only as agreeable to the proportions of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> and the rules of modulation, it has its principle in harmony; since it is a harmonical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANALYSIS">analysis</a>, which exhibits the different gradations of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-SCALE">scale</a>, the chords peculiar to each <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MODE">mode</a>, and the laws of modulation, which are the sole elements that compose an air. According to this principle, the whole power of melody is limited to that of pleasing the ear by agreeable sounds, as the eye may be pleased with an agreeable assemblage of suitable colours. But when considered as an imitative art, by which we may affect the mind with various images, excite different emotions in the heart, inflame or soothe the passions; by which, in a word, we produce different effects upon our moral faculties, which are not to be effectuated by the influence of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> alone, we must explore another principle for melody: for in our whole internal frame there appears to be no power upon which either harmony alone, or its necessary results, can <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SEIZE">seize</a>, to affect us in such a manner. What then is the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SECOND">second</a> principle? It is as much founded on <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> as the first; but, in order to discover its foundation in nature, it <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WILL">will</a> require a more accurate though simpler observation, and a more exquisite <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SENSIBILITY">sensibility</a> in the observer. This principle is the same which varies the tone of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-VOICE">voice</a>, when we speak, according as we are interested in what we say, and according to the different emotions which we feel in expressing it. It is the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACCENT">accent</a> of languages which determines the melody of every <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATION">nation</a>; it is the accent which determines us to employ the emphasis of speaking while we sing, and to speak with more or less energy according as the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> which we <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> is more or less accented. That language whose accents are the most sensible, ought to produce a more pathetic and more lively melody; that which has little accentuation, or none at all, can only produce a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COLD">cold</a> and languid melody, without character and without <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a>. These are the true principles: in proportion as we depart from them, when we speak of the power of music upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> heart, we shall become unintelligible to ourselves and others; our words will be without meaning. If music does not impress the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> with images but by melody, if from thence it obtains its whole power, it must follow, that all musical sounds which are not pleasing by themselves alone, however agreeable to harmony they may be, is not an imitative music; and, being incapable, even with its most beautiful chords, either to present the images of things, or to excite the finer feelings, very soon cloy the ear, and leaves always the heart in cold indifference. It follows likewise, that notwithstanding the parts which harmony has introduced, and which the present <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> of music so wantonly abuses, wherever two different melodies are heard at the same time, they counteract each other, and destroy the effects of both, however beautiful each may be when performed alone: from whence it may be judged with what degree of taste the French composers have introduced in their operas the miserable practice of accompanying one air with another, as well in singing, which is the native expression of pathos and sentiment, as in instrumental performances; which is the same thing as if whimsical orators should take it in their heads to recite two orations at the same time, that the elegance of each might derive more force from the other. So much for Rousseau. The translator, however, has reason to fear, that the causes by which national melody is diversified and characterized, are more profound and permanent than the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> accentuation of language. This indeed may have <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> influence in determining the nature of the rhythmus, and the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of emphatic notes; but very little in regulating the nature of the emphasis and expression themselves. If Rousseau's principle be true in its full <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, he must of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> acknowledge, that an air which was never set or intended for words, however melodious, cannot be imitative: he must likewise confess, that what is imitative in one nation cannot be such in another; nor can it be denied upon his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HYPOTHESIS">hypothesis</a>, that the recitative, which is formed upon the mode of speaking, is the most forcible of all melodies; which is absurd. His other observations are at once judicious and profound. Though it is impossible to exhibit the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> and variety of harmony by playing the same melody at the same time upon different keys, admitting those keys to form among themselves a perfect chord, which will of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> preserve all the subsequent notes in the same intervals; yet this perfect harmony would by no means be uniformly pleasing to the ear. We must therefore of necessity introduce less perfect chords to vary and increase the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>, and these chords in any complex system of music must of necessity produce dissonances. It then becomes the business of the composer to be careful that these discords may arise naturally from, and return as naturally to, perfect harmony. mony as possible. All these causes must inevitably vary the melody of the different parts; but still, amidst all these difficulties, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a> ought to be zealous in preserving the melody of each as homogeneous with the others as possible, that the result of the whole may be in some measure uniform. Otherwise, by counteracting each other, the parts will reciprocally destroy the effects one of another.

MELOE

Pages 388-389

in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ZOOLOGY">zoology</a>; a genus of insects of the order of coleoptera. The antennae are jointed, the last <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> being oval; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a> is roundish; the elytra are soft and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FLEXIBLE">flexible</a>; and the head is inflected, and gibbous. The insects of this genus are divided into two families; one without wings, and having the elytra shorter than the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABDOMEN">abdomen</a>; the other winged, with elytra shorter than the body and wholly covering the wings.—The most remarkable <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> are, 1. The procarabaeus; the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> of which is <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, but without brightness, though intermixed with a small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of purple, especially towards the under <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">part</a> of the body. Its head, which is <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, is dotted; as is the thorax, which is narrower, round, and without a margin. The elytra are as soft as <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, shagreened, and cover but part of the abdomen. They are, as it were, cut off obliquely from the inner to the outer part, being shorter towards the future, longer on the sides. There are no wings under the elytra. The abdomen is large, especially that of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FEMALE">female</a>, in which it far exceeds the elytra.—This insect makes its abode on the side of wet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a> and in woods. Its food are insects, violet leaves, and delicate herbs. There oozes from its body a fat unctuous <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of an agreeable smell. The males are less than the females. 2. The vesicatorius, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> blistering meloe, is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NINE">nine</a> or ten <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> in length, of a shining green colour mixed with azure. It multiplies greatly. They are sometimes seen <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLYING">flying</a> in swarms. A nauseous smell, not unlike that of mice, bespeaks their approach; which scent leads to the discovery of them when they are sought for in order to make a provision. When dried, they are so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, that 50 scarce weigh one dram. They prey upon the leaves of trees and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHRUBS">shrubs</a>, and in preference take to those of the ash-tree. The odorous particles exhaled by these insects, are extremely corrosive. <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> caution should be used in picking them up. People have been known to be seized with violent <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of urine, voiding of blood, for having gathered a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of them during the heat of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> with their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> bare, or for having fallen asleep under trees where swarms of them had settled. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COPULATION">copulation</a> of these insects is performed during the most intense heat of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>. There are many other species, differing in size, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, and colour. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURE">Nature</a> has apparelled almost all of them in a splendid manner. Green, azure, and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, render them dazzling to the eyes. They are most <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMON">common</a> in the southern parts of the continent. In this genus, as well as in some others, the females <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COURT">court</a>, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> take the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of the males. The females deposit their eggs in the ground, whence proceed larvae, which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> through the state of chrysalids in order to attain to that of meloes. **Uset.** <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OIL">Oil</a> in which insects of the first species have been infused is said to be an excellent topical for wounds and the scorpion's sting. It enters also into the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of salve for <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLAGUE">plague</a> sores. The insects bruised and mixed with oil or <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>, Linnaeus says, are recommended as a remedy in the rabies canina. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SECOND">second</a> species is the cantharis of the shops; which, when bruised, is universally used as a blistering <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLASTER">plaster</a>. The largest and most esteemed of this sort come from <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CANTHARIDES">Cantharides</a> are extremely acrimonious; applied to the skin, they first inflame, and afterwards excoriate the part, raising a more perfect blister than any of the vegetable <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ACIDS">acids</a>, and occasioning a more plentiful discharge of serum. All the blistering compositions have cantharides for their basis. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> application of cantharides is often followed by a strangury, accompanied with thirst and feverish heat; this inconvenience may be remedied by soft unctuous or mucilaginous liquors liberally drank. Cantharides taken internally often occasion a discharge of blood by urine, with exquisite pain. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the dose is considerable, they seem to inflame and ulcerate the whole intestinal canal; the stools become mucous and purulent; the breath fetid and cadaverous; intense pains are felt in the lower belly; the patient faints, grows giddy, raving mad, and dies. All these terrible consequences have sometimes happened from a few grains. Herman relates, that he has known a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of a grain inflame the kidneys, and occasion bloody urine with violent pain. There are nevertheless cafes in which this stimulating fly, given in larger doses, proves not only safe, but of singular efficacy for the cure of diseases that yield little to medicines of a milder class. In <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COLD">cold</a> phlegmatic sluggish habits, where the viscera are overloaded, and the kidneys and ureters obstructed with thick viscid mucous matter, cantharides have excellent effects; here the abounding mucus defends the solids from the acrimony of the fly, till it is itself expelled; when the medicine ought to be discontinued. Groenveld employed cantharides with great success in dropsies, obstinate suppressions of urine, and ulcerations of the bladder; giving very considerable doses made into boluses with camphor; and interpolating large draughts of emulsions, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MILK">milk</a>, or other emollient liquids: by this means, the excessive irritation, which they would otherwise have occasioned, was in great <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> prevented. The camphor did not perhaps contribute so much to this effect as is generally imagined, since it has no sensible <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> that promises any considerable abatement of the acrimony of cantharides; nitre would answer all that the camphor is supposed to perform; this, with milk, or emollient mucilaginous liquors, drank in large quantity, are the best correctors. Cantharides, in very small doses, may be given with safety also in other cafes. Dr <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MEAD">Mead</a> observes, that the oblitinate gleatings which frequently remain after the cure of venereal maladies, and which rarely yield to balsamic medicines, are effectually remedied by cantharides; and that no one remedy is more efficacious in leprous disorders; in which last, proper purgatives are to be occasionally taken during the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the cantharides. The best and safest <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a> of cantharides for these purposes, is a spirituous tincture; and indeed, in all <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, the tincture is far preferable, for internal use, to the fly in substance. The virtues of cantharides are extracted by rectified spirit spirit of wine, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> spirit, and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WATER">water</a>; but do not arise in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISTILLATION">distillation</a>. The watery and spirituous extracts bliter as freely as the fly in substance; whilst the fly remaining after the several menstrua have performed their office, is to the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> insipid, and does not in the least blister or inflame the skin.

MELON

Pages 389-391

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of *Cucumis*, in the Linnean system. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> have no stamina <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> summits, but have a very <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LARGE">large</a> oval germen, situated below the flower, which turns to an oval fruit with several cells, filled with oval, acute-pointed, compressed seeds, inclosed in a soft pulp. There is a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> variety of this fruit cultivated in different parts of the world, many of them of no value, size being regarded too much in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARKETS">markets</a>. The Cantaloupe melon, so called from a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in the neighbourhood of Rome, where this fruit has been <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">long</a> cultivated, and whither it was brought from <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMENIA">Armenia</a>, is in the greatest esteem among the curious in every <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. Besides this, there are also the romana, the succado, the Zate, the small <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a> or dormer, and the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GALLOWAY">Galloway</a> melons, most of which are cultivated for an early crop. The proper management and culture of melons are as follows: the seeds should be procured from good melons, of the soundest form and highest flavour, produced, as some have advised, in a distant garden; for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> sown on the place where it was raised and ripened, it is very apt to degenerate. This seed should be kept three years before it is sown, but not more than six; and it should be sown at two seasons, or if at three it <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WILL">will</a> be still better: the first for the early crop, to be raised under frames, should be sown about the middle of February; the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, to be raised in the same manner, is to be sown about the middle of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MARCH">March</a>; and those which are designed for <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HAND">hand</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELL">bell</a>-glasses, or to be covered with <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OIL">oil</a>-papers, should not be sown till about a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a> in April. For those of the first season, the seeds may be sown on the upper side of a cucumber-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a>, if there be any; or, a proper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of new loose dung must be provided, and thrown on a heap to ferment, and turned over, that it may acquire an equal <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> must be raised and managed like cucumbers, until they are planted where they are to remain. The beds or ridges, where the plants are to remain, should be placed in a warm situation, so that they may be defended from all <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COLD">cold</a> and strong winds, and inclosed in a good reed <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FENCE">fence</a>. In preparing the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> for these plants, the Dutch and German gardeners form a mixture of a third part of hazel loam, a third part of the scouring of ditches and ponds, and the same quantity of very rotten dung; which they mix up at least once, and often two years, before they make <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of it, frequently <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> it over, so that the parts may be well incorporated; but the compost in which Mr Miller has found melon plants to succeed best in England is two-thirds of fresh gentle loam, and one-third of rotten neat's dung: if these are mixed together one year before it is wanted, so as to have the benefit of a winter's frosts and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>'s heat, observing to turn it over often, and never suffering weeds to grow upon it, this will be found equal to any compost whatever. Before the plants appear, there should be a quantity of new dung thrown in a heap, allowing about 15 wheelbarrows full to each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>; which must be turned over two or three times, and in a fortnight it will be fit for use; when the trench must be dug to receive the dung where the bed is designed to be made, which in a dry ground should not be less than a foot or a foot and a half deep. The frames should then be placed over the bed to keep out the wet; but no earth should be laid upon it for three or four days, till it is found of a proper temperature of heat. When this is the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CASE">case</a>, the earth may be laid upon it, about two inches thick, except in the middle of each light, where the plants are to be placed, which must be raised into a hill 15 inches <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> or more, terminating in a flat cone: in two or three days after the earth is put on the bed, it will be of a proper temper to receive the plants; which should be carefully taken up with a trowel, so as to preserve all the fibres of their roots; or if the beds cannot be ready for them in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a>, soon after the third or rough <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a> is put out, it will be a good method to put each plant into a small pot while they are young, and these may be plunged into the hot bed where they were raised, or in a cucumber-bed, where there is room; and when the bed is ready, the plants may be turned out of the pots, with the whole <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BALL">ball</a> of earth to their roots; and this is the best method for the Cantaloupe melon.
