When the plants are placed on the tops of the hills, they should be gently watered once or twice, till they have taken good root; and when they are well fixed in the new beds, a greater quantity of earth should be laid on the beds, pressed <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DOWN">down</a> as <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> as possible, and raised at least a foot and a half thick upon the dung all over the bed; observing also to raise the frames, that the glasses may not be too near the plants, lest the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> should scorch them. When the plants have four leaves, the top of the plants should be pinched off with the finger and thumb, that they may put out lateral branches for producing the fruit; and when two or more of these lateral shoots are produced, they must also be pinched to force out more. The management of these beds is much the same as that of cucumbers, except that melons require more <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> and very little <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WATER">water</a>. In five or six weeks the plants will spread over the bed, and reach to the frames, when the alleys between the beds should be dug out; or in case of one bed, a trench should be made on each side about four feet wide, as low as the bottom of the bed; and hot dung wheeled in for a lining, to the same height as the dung of the bed; this should be trodden down close, and covered with the same earth that was laid on the bed, to the thickness of a foot and a half or more, treading it down as close as possible. In this way the bed will be extended to the width of 12 feet, that the roots of the plants may spread quite through it; and the beds will also require a fresh warmth, which will be of great <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> in setting of the fruit. When the vines have extended so as to fill the frames, and want more room, the frames should be raised up with bricks about three inches high, to admit the shoots of the vines to run out under them. When the fruit appears, the vines should be carefully looked over three times a week; and one should be chosen upon each runner that is situated nearest the stem, having the largest footstalk, and appearing to be the strongest fruit; then pinch off all the other fruit which may appear upon the same runner, and pinch off the end of the runner at the third <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> above the fruit; and if the runner is gently pinched at the next joint. joint above the fruit, it will stop the sap and set the fruit. There is also another method practised by some gardeners to set this fruit, which is the taking off some of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MALE">male</a> flowers, whose farina is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> ripe and fit for the purpose, laying them over the female fruit, and gently striking with the nails the male flowers, to shake the farina into the female flowers; whereby they are impregnated, and the fruit will soon after swell, and manifest visible signs of being perfectly set; so that where the plants are under frames, and the <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> excluded from them, which is wanted to convey the farina from the male to the female flowers, this practice may be very necessary. The glases of the hotbed should also be raised high, to admit a large share of air to the plants, otherwise the fruit will not set; and if the season should prove very warm, the glases may be frequently drawn off, especially in an evening, to receive the dews, provided there is little wind stirring; but they should not remain off the whole night, lest the cold should prove too great. When the plants have extended themselves from under the frames, in cold <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> their extremities should be covered every night with mats, and the plants should be watered once in a week in dry warm weather, in the alleys between the beds. For those melons that are raised under bell or hand-glases, the plants should be raised in the manner already directed, and about the latter end of April, in a forward season, the beds may be made. For this purpose, a sufficient quantity of hot-dung should be provided, allowing eight or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NINE">nine</a> good wheel-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARROWS">barrows</a> of dung to each glass. For one bed extended in length, the trench should be cut out three-one-half feet wide, and of such a length, that the glases may not be placed nearer than four feet to each other; in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DIGGING">digging</a> the trench, it should be so situated, as to allow for the widening of the bed three or four feet on each side; the depth must depend on the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>; and when there is no danger of the beds being injured by the wet, the lower it is made the better. When the dung, prepared as before, is laid on the bed, there should be a hill for each plant, one foot and a half high, and the other part need not be covered more than four inches thick; the glases should then be placed over the hills, and in two or three days after the beds are made they will be fit for receiving the plants, which should be removed in the manner already directed. These plants must be watered at first, to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> the earth to their roots, and shaded every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, till they have taken new root; and if the nights prove cold, it will be proper to cover the glases with mats, in order to preserve the warmth of the bed. If several beds are made, they should be placed at eight feet distance from each other. When the plants have taken good root, their tops must be pinched off, and the pruning must be the same as for those under frames. In the daytime, when the weather is warm, the glases should be raised on the opposite side to the wind, to admit fresh air to the plants; and when they reach the sides of the glases, in favourable weather the glases must be set up on three bricks, that the vines may have room to run out under them; but when this is done, the beds should be covered all over with earth to the depth of one foot and an half, and trod down as close as possible; and in cold nights, the beds should be covered with mats. And as the vines of the Cantaloupe melons cannot bear wet without injury, it will be necessary to <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a> the beds over with props to support the mats, that they may be ready for covering at all times when they require it. If the weather should prove cold, hot dung may be laid to these beds in the manner directed for those under frames. Some have lately raised their melons with considerable success under oiled <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>; but great care must be taken not to keep these coverings too close over them. And Miller advises to bring up the plants under hand or bell glases, till they begin to extend themselves under the glases, and then, instead of the covering of mats, to put over them the paper done over with linseed oil. The farther management of melons, after their fruit is set, is to keep pulling off all the superfluous fruit, and to pinch off all weak runners; and also to turn the fruit gently twice a-week, that each side may have equal benefit of the sun and air. When the fruit is fully grown, care should be taken to cut it at a proper time; for if it is left a few hours upon the vines, it will lose much of its delicacy; therefore the vines should be looked over at least twice in a day; and if the fruit intended for the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TABLE">table</a> is cut early in the morning, before the sun has warmed it, it will be much better flavoured; but if it should be necessary to cut any afterwards, it should be put into cold <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> water or <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ICE">ice</a> to cool it, before it is brought to table; and that cut in the morning should be kept in the coolest place till it is used. The signs of this fruit's maturity is, its beginning to crack near the foot-stalk, and its beginning to smell, which never fail; but the Cantaloupe melons seldom change their <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> till they are too ripe. Mr Reynolds has communicated to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> of Arts the following method of raising melons without earth, dung, or water. About a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MONTH">month</a> before the seeds are sown, he prepares a bed of calf-off tanner's bark, four feet deep, six feet wide, and twelve feet in length: this he covers with four lights, so as not to admit <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-RAIN">rain</a> or water. March (he says) is a proper season for this purpose. When the bed becomes warm, which generally happens in about 20 days, a few melon seeds are put into warm <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MILK">milk</a> in an earthen vessel, which is pressed down into the bark-bed, where it remains 36 hours, in order to promote the vegetation of the seeds. Then, at equal distances, he directs to open four holes in the bed, each nine inches in diameter, and five inches deep; having in readiness about a peck of pounded bark, like <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAW">saw</a>-dust, some of it to be put at the bottom of the holes, to the thickness of three inches; on this bark some of the seeds are to be placed, and pressed down with the fingers; then the seeds are to be covered with two inches more of the powdered bark, pressing the whole down with the hand. When the plants are advanced to a proper size, the best are chosen and the others <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> away; those that are reserved are ordered to be properly pruned, and to have as much warm air as possible during the summer. In this way (he says) he has raised as good melons as can be desired. When a melon is perfectly fine, it is full, without any vacuity; this is known by knocking upon it; and when cut, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> must be dry, no water running out, only a little <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEW">dew</a>, which is to be of a fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RED">red</a> colour. Large melons are not to be coveted, but firm and well-flavoured ones. Our gardeners who raise melons for <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-SALE">sale</a>, sow the seeds of the larger rather than the good kinds, and they increase the size of these by much watering the roots; but this spoils the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>. Some of the French raise at this time particularly fine melons, by a method kept as a secret, but which we find, on a strict inquiry, is no other than the ingenious Mr Quintiny's of that <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, published near 80 years ago in our Philosophical Transactions. The melons particularly proper to be treated in this manner, are those which have a thin and somewhat embroidered skin, not divided by ribs, and have a red pulp, dry and mellowing on the tongue, not mealy, and of a high flavour. These are what succeed in the following method, and are greatly improved in size and flavour by it. When the seeds of this melon are placed in the ground, the first thing that appears is a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of seminal leaves, or ears, as the gardeners call them. Between these two leaves there shoots, some days after, a leaf called the first leaf or knot; and out of the same place, after some days more, there shoots another leaf, called the second knot. Out of the midst of this stalk of the second knot, there shoots a third knot; this third knot must be cut off at its insertion, without hurting the branch of the second knot from whence it grows. Out of this place there will grow, after this <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a>, a branch, which will be what the gardeners call the first arm; and this arm will, in the same manner as the first plant, shoot out, first one, then a second, and then a third knot; this third knot must be cut again as before, and thus the third knots are all along to be cut off, and arms or branches will grow up in the places of them all the way in the same manner as the first; and it is at those arms that the melons will be produced, and they will be always good, if the foot or root be well nourished in good earth, and cherished by a good hot-bed and the sun. The foot of the melon must never be suffered to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> into the dung, and the earth must not be watered but moderately, when it is seen to grow too dry; but in this case, it must be moderately moistened in time, lest the shoot suffer by it. Twice or thrice a week is often enough to water in the driest weather, and this must always be done about sunset; and when the heat of the sun is too violent, the melons must be covered with straw mats from 11 in the morning to about two in the afternoon. When it rains much, the melons must also be covered, lest it hurt them by too much moisture. (Philosoph. Trans. no. 41.)—If the root produce too many branches, the weakest are to be cut off, and only three or four left; and those which are left are to be such as have their knots closest to one another. When the plants are removed from the seed-bed to the places where they are to stand, if they are very strong, they should be planted single; but if otherwise, two are to be set in each hole. When they are planted single, the two branches, which always grow on each side from the base of the seed-leaves, are to be left on; but when two plants are set together, these branches are to be cut off, otherwise all the branches will be too numerous, and they will entangle and spoil one another. When the melons are knit, two of them only are to be left upon each foot, choosing those which are best placed, and next to the first and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> stalk, that is, to the heart of the foot. None but fair <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> are to be left, and such as have a thick and short tail; and the foot of the melon must be short, well trifid, and not far distant from the ground. Melons of a long stem, and having the stalk of the leaf too long and slender, are never vigorous. All the superfluous branches must be cut off from time to time, as they shoot out. There sometimes shoot out a branch more than is here mentioned, between the two seed-leaves or ears. If this is strong and vigorous, it is to be kept on, but if weakly, it is best to take it off, for it will never bear good fruit. Water-Melon. See Anguria.

MELOS

Pages 391-391

(anc. geog.), an <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> between <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CRETE">Crete</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PELOPONNESUS">Peloponnesus</a>, about 24 miles from Scyllaeum. It is about 60 miles in circumference, and of an <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>. It enjoyed its independence for above 700 years before the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the Peloponnesian <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WAR">war</a>. This island was originally peopled by a Lacedemonian colony, 1116 years before the Christian era. For this reason the inhabitants refused to join the rest of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> and the Athenians against the Peloponnesians. This refusal was severely punished. The Athenians took Melos, and put to the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> all such as were able to bear arms. The women and children were made slaves, and the island left desolate. An Athenian colony repeopled it, till Lygander reconquered it and re-established the original inhabitants in their possessions.

MELOTHRIA

Pages 391-391

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a>: A genus of the monogyne order, belonging to the triandra class of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 34th order, Cucurbitaceae. The calyx is quinquedent; the corolla campanulated and monopetalous; the berry trilocular and monospermous. There is only one <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, viz. the pendula, a native of Carolina, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VIRGINIA">Virginia</a>, and also many of the American <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>. The plants strike out roots at every <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JOINT">joint</a>, which fasten themselves into the ground, by which means their stalks extend to a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> distance each way. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> are very small, in shape like those of the melon, of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> sulphur <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>. The fruit in the West Indies grows to the size of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEA">pea</a>, is of an oval <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, and changes to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> when ripe; these are by the inhabitants sometimes pickled when they are green. In <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> the fruit are much smaller, and are so hidden by the leaves that it is difficult to find them. The plants are too tender to be reared in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> without <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>.

MELPOMENE

Pages 391-391

one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MUSES">muses</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> and Mnemosyne. She presided over tragedy. Horace has addressed the finest of his odes to her, as to the patroness of lyric <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>. She was generally represented as a young woman with a serious countenance. Her garments were splendid; she wore a bulkin, and held a dagger in one <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HAND">hand</a> and in the other a sceptre and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>.

MELROSE

Pages 391-393

a town of Scotland, in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Selkirk, and on the confines of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TWEEDDALE">Tweeddale</a>, feated on the south side of the river Tweed; with an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a> now in ruins. W. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 2. 32. N. Lat. 55° 32'. This abbey was founded by <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KING">king</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DAVID">David</a> I. in 1136. He peopled it with Cistercians brought from Rivale abbey in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a>, and dedicated it to the Virgin <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>. At the reformation James Douglas was appointed commendator, who took <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DOWN">down</a> much of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, in order to furnish materials for a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> to himself, which still remains, and is dated 1590. Nothing is left of the abbey excepting a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">part</a> of the cloister walls elegantly carved; but the ruins of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> are of most uncommon <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>. Part is at present used for divine <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>, the rest uncovered; but every part does <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECT">architect</a>.—Alexander II. was buried beneath the great altar, and it is also the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-INTERMENT">interment</a> of the Douglas's and other potent families.—Its situation is extremely pleasant. **MELT OF FISHES.** In the melt of a living cod there are such numbers of those animalcules said to be found in the semen of all <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MALE">male</a> animals, that in a drop of its juice no larger than a grain of sand, there are contained more than 10,000 of them; and considering how many such quantities there are in the whole melt of one such fish, it is not incredible, that there are more animals in one melt of it than there are living men at one <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a> upon the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FACE">face</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>. However strange and romantic such a conjecture must appear, a serious consideration and calculation <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WILL">will</a> make it appear very plain. An hundred such grains of sand as those <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> mentioned will make about an inch in length; therefore in a cubic inch there will be a million of such sands; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> there be 10,000 animals in each of those quantities, there must be in the whole 150,000 millions, which is a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> vastly exceeding that of mankind, even supposing the whole as populous as <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>. **MELTING CONE,** in espying, an hollow cone of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, into which melted metallic substances are thrown, in order to free them from their scoriae. When a small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> is melted, it will be sufficient to rub the inside of the cone with grease; but when the quantity is very large, especially if it contains anything sulphurous, this caution of allowing the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOULDS">moulds</a> is not sufficient. In this <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CASE">case</a> the espyer has recourse to a late reduced to thin pap with <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WATER">water</a>, which effectually prevents any injury to the cone. **MELTON-MOUBRAY,** a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEICESTERSHIRE">Leicestershire</a>, 108 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. It is a large built place, in a fertile <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>; with a market on Tuesday, the most considerable for cattle of any in this part of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>. It is almost encompassed with a little river called the Eye, over which it has two fine bridges; and has a large handsome church, with a free-school. Here are frequent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>-races, and three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a> in the year. **MELVIL (Sir James),** descended from an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> Scots family, being the third son of the laird of Kaeth, was born about the middle of the 16th century. He went to France very young, in the capacity of page to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> Mary, then married to the dauphin; and on the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of her husband, followed her to Scotland, where he was made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> of her chamber, and admitted a privy-counsellor. She employed him in her most important concerns, till her unhappy confinement in Lochleven, all which he discharged with the utmost fidelity; and, from his own accounts, there is reason to conclude, that had she taken his advice, she might have avoided many of her misfortunes. When she was prisoner in England, she recommended him strongly to her son James; with whom he <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in favour and employment until the death of Queen <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>; James would then have taken him to England; but Melvil, now grown old, was desirous of retiring from business, and in his retirement he drew up the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-MEMOIRS">memoirs</a> of his past <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of his son. These Memoirs were accidentally found in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a> castle in the year 1650, though nobody knew how they came to be deposited there; and were published in folio in 1683. **MEMBERS,** in anatomy, the exterior parts, arising from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUNK">trunk</a> or body of an animal, like the boughs from the trunk of a tree. **Member,** in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>, denotes any part of a building; as a frieze, cornice, or the like. **Member** is sometimes also used for moulding. **Member,** in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a>, is applied to the parts of a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a>. **Member,** is also used to denote some particular order or <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-RANK">rank</a> in a state or <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>: thus we say, "member of a corporation, member of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, member of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>," &c. **MEMBRANE,** Membrana, in anatomy, a similar part of an animal body; being a thin, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FLEXIBLE">flexible</a>, expanded skin, formed of several sorts of fibres interwoven together, and serving to cover or wrap up certain parts of the body. See Anatomy paffim. **MEMEL,** or Memmel; a town of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a>, situated on the northern extremity of the Curische Haf, an inlet of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SEA">sea</a> about 70 miles in length, which is here joined to the Baltic by a narrow strait.—It is an ill-built town, with narrow dirty streets; but remarkable for its extensive <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, being provided with the finest harbour in the Baltic. In 1744, 996 ships, amongst which were 500 English, arrived here. The imports chiefly are, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, iron, and salted herrings; the exports, which greatly exceed the imports, are <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBER">amber</a>, corn, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FLAX">flax</a>, and particularly <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a>. An English <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONSUL">consul</a> resides here. The trade is daily increasing, on account of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> duties which the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COURT">court</a> of Rulfsia has laid on the imports of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGA">Riga</a>. **MEMNON (fab. hist.),** a king of Ethiopia, son of Ithonus and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AURORA">Aurora</a>. He came with a body of 10,000 men to assist his uncle Priam, during the Trojan <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WAR">war</a>. He behaved with great courage, and killed Antilochus, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NESTOR">Nestor</a>'s son. The aged father challenged the Ethiopian monarch; but Memnon refused it on account of the venerable <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> of Nestor, and accepted that of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACHILLES">Achilles</a>. He was killed in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMBAT">combat</a>, in the fight of the Grecian and Trojan armies. Aurora prayed <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> her son such honours as might distinguish him from other mortals. The god consented; and immediately a numerous flight of birds issued from the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> pile on which the body was laid, and dividing themselves into two separate bodies, fought with such fury, that above half of them fell down in the fire as victims to appease the manes of Memnon. These birds were called Memnonides; and it has been observed by some of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, that they never failed to return yearly to the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a> of Memnon in Troas, and repeat the same bloody engagement in honour of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HERO">hero</a> from whom they received their name. The Ethiopians or Egyptians, over whom Memnon reigned, erected a celebrated statue to the honour of their monarch. This statue had the wonderful <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of uttering a melodious <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> at sunrise like that which was heard at the breaking of the string of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARP">harp</a> when it is wound up. This was effected by the rays of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> when they fell upon it. At the setting of the sun, and in the night, the sound was lugubrious. This is supported by the testimony of the geographer Strabo, who confesses himself ignorant whether it proceeded from the basis of the statue, or the people that were then around it. This celebrated statue was dismantled by order of Cambyses when he conquered <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>; and its ruins still astonish <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> travellers by their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a> and beauty. Memnon of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RHODES">Rhodes</a>, one of the generals of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DARIUS">Darius</a> king of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, advised that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> to lay waste the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, in order to deprive Alexander the Great's <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> of support, and afterwards to attack Macedon; but this counsel was disapproved by Darius's other generals. Memnon behaved at the passage of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GRANICUS">Granicus</a> like an experienced general. He afterwards defended the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Miletum with great courage; seized the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CHIO">Chio</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LESBOS">Lesbos</a>; spread terror throughout all <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>; and would have put a stop to the conquests of Alexander, if he had not been prevented by death. Barina, Memnon's widow, was taken prisoner with Darius's wife, and Alexander had a son by her named <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a>.

MEMOIRS

Pages 393-393

in matters of literature, a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, written by persons who had some share in the transactions they relate; answering to what the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> called Commentarii.—The journals of the proceedings of a literary <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> a collection of matters transacted therein, are likewise called Memoirs.

MEMORY

Pages 393-393

a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a> of the mind, which presents to us <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> notions of what is past, accompanied with a persuasion that the things themselves were formerly real and present. What we distinctly remember to have perceived, we as firmly believe to have happened, as what is now present to our senses.

MEMPHIS

Pages 395-397

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CITY">city</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> residence of the kings in the Higher <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>; distant from the Delta to the south 15 miles, according to Pliny. Called also Moph and Noph, in scripture. Though this city is now so completely ruined, that authors greatly disagree concerning its situation; yet Strabo informs that in his <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a> it was the most magnificent in Egypt, next to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a>. It was called the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>; and there was an entire temple of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OSIRIS">Osiris</a>, where the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APIS">Apis</a> <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> sacred ox was kept and worshipped. In the same <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLACE">place</a> was an apartment of the mother of the ox; a very magnificent temple of Vulcan; a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CIRCUS">Circus</a> or space for fighting bulls; and a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> Colossus in the middle of the city, which was thrown <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DOWN">down</a>. There was likewise a temple of Venus, and a Serapium in a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a> place, where the <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> heaps up hills of sand very dangerous to travellers; together with a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of Sphinxes, the heads of some of them only being visible, the others covered up to the middle of their body. The same author likewise informs us, that in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FRONT">front</a> of the city there were many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a>; and that it contained a number of palaces, at that time in ruins. These buildings, he said, formerly stood upon an eminence; they lay along the side of the hill, stretching down to the lakes and groves, 40 stadia from the city. There was likewise a mountain in the neighbourhood, on which were a great number of pyramids, with the sepulchres of the kings, among which were three remarkable, and two of them accounted wonders of the world. From this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a>, Mr Bruce concludes that the celebrated capital of Egypt stood in the place where the villages of Metrahenny are now situated; in opposition to Dr Shaw's <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, who thinks it was situated at Geeza or Gifa. M. Savary has also shown, that Gifa was not the situation of the ancient Memphis. This <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FLOOD">flood</a>, he says, on the western <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NILE">Nile</a>, on the spot where the village of Memphis now stands, which still preserves the name. Large heaps of rubbish are still to be seen there; but the Arabs have transported to <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CAIRO">Cairo</a> the columns and remarkable <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, which they have disposed, without <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> and without order, in their mosques and public buildings. This city extended as far as Saccara; and was almost wholly encompassed by lakes, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">part</a> of which are still subsisting. It was necessary to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> them to convey the dead to the sepulchre of their fathers. The tombs, hewn out of the rock, were closed up with stones of a proportionable size, and covered with sand. These bodies, embalmed with so much care, preserved with so much respect, are torn from the monuments they repose in, and sold without decency to strangers by the inhabitants of Saccara. This place is called the plain of mummers. There too we find the wall of the birds, into which one descends by means of a rope. It leads to subterranean galleries, filled with earthen vases, containing the sacred birds. They are rarely met with entire, because the Arabs <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> them in hopes of finding idols of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>. They do not conduct travellers into the places where they have found more precious <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>. They even <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> them up carefully, reserving to themselves some secret <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> by which they descend. In a journey into Egypt made by the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> de Chaulnes, he advanced very far into these winding labyrinths, sometimes crawling, and sometimes scrambling, on his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNEES">knees</a>. Informed by Mr Edward Worley Montague, who has carefully visited Egypt, he arrived at one of those passages which had an opening shut up from without by branches of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DATE">date</a>-tree interwoven, and covered with sand. He remarked there some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIEROGLYPHICS">hieroglyphics</a> in relief, executed in the highest perfection. But the Arabs refused every offer he made them to permit him to take drawings of them, or to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOLD">mold</a> them, in order to preserve their form. The duke de Chaulnes is of opinion that these hieroglyphics, sculptured with so much art that the objects they represent may be discovered at the first sight, might possibly furnish the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KEY">key</a> of the others, whose contours are simply expressed, and form a sort of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALPHABET">alphabet</a> of this unintelligible <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>. Several pyramids are distinguishable Menage along the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> which bound Saccara on the west, the greatest part of which appear as lofty as those of Giza. See Pyramids. Menage (Fr.), denotes a collection of animals; whence we have derived the word menagery. Menage (Giles), in Latin Egidius, a celebrated French writer, born at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGERS">Angers</a> in 1613. He finished his studies in that city, was made advocate, and pleaded for some time at Angers, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POITIERS">Poitiers</a>; but, becoming at length disgusted with the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BAR">bar</a>, turned ecclesiastic, and gave himself up entirely to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of polite literature. He at length entered into the family of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CARDINAL">cardinal</a> de Retz; but disagreeing with some persons belonging to his Eminence, went to live in the cloister of Notre Dame, where he held an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> of learned men every Wednesday. He read a great <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEAL">deal</a>; had a prodigious <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>; and was incessantly quoting in his conversation verses in Greek, Latin, Italian, French, &c., on which account he was often turned into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIDICULE">ridicule</a> by the wits, especially towards the end of his days. His great memory he retained even in his old <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>; and what is very rare, it returned to him after some interruption. The reputation of his works procured him a place in the academy della Crusca at <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a>. He might have been a member of the French academy at its first <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it had not been for his Registre des Dictionnaires; but when that was forgot, he was proposed in 1684 to fill up a vacant place in that academy, and was excluded only by the superior <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of his competitor Mr Bergent; for there was not one member of all those who gave their votes against them, but owned that he deserved the place. He would not suffer his friends to propose him again. He died at Paris in 1692, aged 79. He wrote a great number of books in prose and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>; the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> of which are, 1. Miscellaneous works. 2. The Origin of the French Language. 3. The Origin of the Italian Tongue; the best edition of which is that of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-GENEVA">Geneva</a>, in 1685, folio. 4. An edition of Malherbe's Poems, with Notes. 5. An edition of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DIOGENES">Diogenes</a> Laertius, with Observations. 6. Remarks on the French Tongue. 7. Greek, Latin, Italian, and French Poems. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MENANDER">Menander</a>, an ancient Greek poet, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a> in the same year with Epicurus, which was the third of the 109th Olympiad. His <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> in introducing the new <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMEDY">comedy</a>, and refining an art which had been so <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GROSS">gross</a> and licentious in former times, quickly spread his name over the world. Pliny informs us, that the kings of Egypt and Macedon gave a noble testimony of his merit, by sending ambassadors to invite him to their courts, and even fleets to bring him over; but that Menander was so much of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, as to prefer the free enjoyment of his studies to the promised favours of the great. Of his works, which amounted to above 100 comedies, we have had a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> loss, the originals being not only vanished, but the greatest part of them, when copied by Terence, having unfortunately perished by shipwreck before they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAW">saw</a> Rome. Yet the four plays which Terence borrowed from him before that accident happened, are still preserved in the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HABIT">habit</a>; and it is chiefly from Terence that most people form their judgment of Menander, the fragments that remain of him not being sufficient to enable them to do it. The <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> have said <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> things of Menander; and we find the old masters of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-RHETORIC">rhetoric</a> recommending his works as the true patterns of every <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> and every <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GRACE">grace</a> of public speaking. Quintilian declares, that a careful <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of Menander only, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WILL">will</a> satisfy all the rules he has laid down in his Institutions. It is in Menander that he would have his orator search for a copiousness of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a>, for a happy elegance of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a>, and especially for that universal genius which is able to accommodate itself to persons, things, and affections.—But Julius Cesar has left the loftiest as well as the justest praise of Menander's works, when he calls Terence only a Half-Menander. For while the virtues of the Latin poet are so deservedly admired, it is impossible we should raise a higher notion of excellency than to conceive the great original still shining with half its lustre unreflected, and preserving an equal part of its graces, above the power of the best copier in the world. Menander died in the 3rd year of the 122nd Olympiad, as we are taught by the same old inscription from which we learn the time of his birth. His <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a>, in Paufanias's age, was to be seen at Athens, in the way from the Piraeus to the city, close by the honorary monument of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EURIPIDES">Euripides</a>. Quintilian, in his judgment of Afranius the Roman comedian, who imitated him, censures Menander's morals as much as he commends his writings; and his character, according to Suidas, is, that he was a very "mad fellow after women." Phaedrus has given him the gait and dress of a most affected fop: "Unguento delibutus, vestitu adfluens, Veniebat gressu delicatulo & languido." Lib. v. fab. 2. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MENANDRIANS">Menandrians</a>, the most ancient branch of Gnostics; thus called from Menander their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a>, said by some, without sufficient foundation, to have been a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of Simon Magus, and himself a reputed magician. He taught, that no person could be saved, unless he were baptized in his name; and he conferred a peculiar sort of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAPTISM">baptism</a>, which would render those who received it immortal in the next world; exhibiting himself to the world, with the phrensy of a lunatic more than the founder of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a>, as a promised favour. For it appears by the testimonies of Irenæus, Justin, and Tertullian, that he pretended to be one of the Æons sent from the pleroma, or <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> regions, to succour the souls that lay groaning under bodily oppression and servitude; and to maintain them against the violence and stratagems of the demons that hold the reins of empire in this sublunary world. As this doctrine was built upon the same foundation with that of Simon Magus, the ancient writers looked upon him as the instructor of Menander. See Simonians. Menasseh (Ben Israel), a celebrated rabbi, born in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a> about the year 1644, was the son of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a> Ben Israel, and followed his father into <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>. Here he was educated by Rabbi <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> Uziel, under whom he in a short time made such progress in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> tongue, that at 18 years of age he succeeded him in the synagogue of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a>. In this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> he <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> several years, and married Rachel of the the family of the Abarbanels, whom the Jews imagine to be descended from <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KING">king</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DAVID">David</a>. He afterwards went to his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> Ephraim, a rich merchant, who had settled at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASIL">Basil</a>; by whose advice he entered into trade. Some time after, the hopes of a more agreeable settlement induced him to come into England, under the protection of Cromwell; who gave him a very favourable reception, and one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> entertained him at his <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TABLE">table</a> with several other learned divines. However, he soon after passed into <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ZEALAND">Zealand</a>; and died at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-MIDDLEBURG">Middleburg</a> about the year 1657. The Jews at Amsterdam obtained his body, and interred it at their expense. He was of the sect of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PHARISEES">Pharisees</a>; had a lively <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WIT">wit</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> judgement, great learning, and all the virtues that can adorn private <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. He wrote many works in Hebrew, Latin, Spanish, and English. The principal of those published in Latin, are, 1. His Conciliator; a learned and curious <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a>, in which he reconciles those passages of Scripture which seem to contradict each other. 2. De refutatione mortuorum. 3. De termino vita. 4. Dissertatio de fragilitate humana, ex lapso Adami, duque Divino in bono opere auxilio. 5. Spes Israel. Dr Thomas Pococke has written his life in English.

MENCKE

Pages 397-397

son to the preceding. After his studies he travelled into England and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>; and upon his return was appointed professor of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> at Leipzig in 1699. He gained <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> reputation by his lectures as well as his writings. He died in 1732, aged 58. He wrote many pieces. His De Charlataneria eruditorum declamationes dua, is an excellent satire, designed to expose the artifices used by false scholars to raise themselves a name. As he named and pointed at certain persons, it exasperated them, and they procured his book to be seized; but it spread, and editions of it were multiplied. He likewise published Méthode pour étudier l'Histoire, avec un catalogue des principaux historiens, &c. He made a great many additions to Mr Lenglet's book, especially with regard to the German historians.

MENDELSON

Pages 397-397

that is, Moses the son of Mendel, a Jew of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BERLIN">Berlin</a>, and one of the most celebrated writers in Germany, died there in the year 1785 at the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 57. His first attempt as an author was in 1755, by a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> intitled <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>; in which, besides other bold and unjustifiable opinions, he maintains, that the Jews have a revealed <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LAW">law</a> but not a revealed <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>; that opinions are not subjects of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-REVELATION">revelation</a>; and that the only religion of the Jewish <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATION">nation</a> is that of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. He acquired <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> by his Phedon, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> "Discourse on the Immateriality and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IMMORTALITY">Immortality</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SOUL">Soul</a>," translated into French in 1773, 8vo; in which he unfolds this important <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, the great foundation of all morality, with the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a> of an enlightened <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> and the charms of an elegant writer. In <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of this excellent work, he was styled the Jewish <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SOCRATES">Socrates</a> by some of the periodical writers; but he wanted the firmness and courage of the Grecian philosopher. His timidity, and even pusillanimity, defects too <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMON">common</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SPECULATIVE">speculative</a> men, prevented him from being of any essential <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> to his nation; of which he might have become the benefactor by being the reformer. The pliancy of his character, his soft, modest, and obliging disposition, gained him the esteem alike of the superstitious and of the incredulous. After all, he could never procure admission to the Berlin <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>, or to the conversation of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a>. At his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEATH">death</a> he received from his nation those honours which are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> paid to their first rabbins. Contrary to an imprudent <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> prevalent among the Jews of burying their dead before funest, his <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-INTERMENT">interment</a> was delayed till 24 hours after he expired. Though Mendelshon was descended from a respectable family, he was very <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-POOR">poor</a>. In early <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> he entered into a counting-<a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of his own nation, wherein he greatly recommended himself by his capacity and integrity in business: but <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> and literature soon became his <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> occupation; and to the famous Lessing he was indebted for counsels which, without diverting his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> from those pursuits that were necessary to his subsistence, accelerated his progress in his literary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAREER">career</a>. Even after the death of his benefactor, Mendelshon retained for him the sincerest regard and the most lively <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GRATITUDE">gratitude</a>. Notwithstanding the very strict regimen which he observed, he survived him only a few years; for his feeble frame and weak <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> were gradually and insensibly undermined by intense application to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a>.

MENDEZ

Pages 398-399

a Chaldean word, which signifies "he has numbered <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> counted;" being one of the three words that was written upon the wall by the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HAND">hand</a> that appeared to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELSHAZZAR">Belshazzar</a>, the last <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BABYLON">Babylon</a>, the night that he was put to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. See BELSHAZZAR.

MENDEZ PINTO

Pages 397-398

was born at Montemor-o-Velho in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>, and was at first <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a> to a Portuguese <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>. In <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EXPECTATION">expectation</a> of making a fortune, he embarked for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-INDIA">India</a> in 1537. His vessel being taken by the Turks on his passage, he was carried to Mocka, and sold to a Greek renegade, and afterwards to a Jew, in whose possession he <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> till he was redeemed by the governor of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORMUS">Ormus</a>, a Portuguese fort. The governor procured him an opportunity of going out to India, agreeable to his first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>. During a residence of twenty-one years in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, he was witness to very important transactions, and experienced many singular adventures. He returned to Portugal in 1558, where he enjoyed the reward of his labours, after having been thirteen times a slave and fifteen times sold. A very curious account of his travels was written by himself, and published at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LISBON">Lisbon</a>, A.D. 1614, in folio. This <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> was translated into French by Bernard Figuier, a Portuguese gentleman, and printed at <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> 1645, in 4to. It is written in a very interesting manner, and in a style more elegant than might have been expected from a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MAN">man</a> whose whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> was spent in the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CAMP">camp</a> and in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SLAVERY">slavery</a>. It elucidates a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> variety of particulars relating to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">geography</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, and manners of the inhabitants of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHINA">China</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JAPAN">Japan</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PEGU">Pegu</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SIAM">Siam</a>, Achien, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JAVA">Java</a>, &c. Many of his facts appeared fabulous, but their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> has been since ascertained. M. de Surgi compiled an interesting history from the most singular facts in Mendez Pinto's relation, which he published in the *Vicissitudes de la Fortune*, Paris, 2 vols, 8vo.

MENDICANTS

Pages 398-398
or **BEGGING FRIARS**, several orders of religious in Popish countries, who having no settled revenues, are supported by the charitable contributions they receive from others. This sort of society began in the 13th century; and the members of it, by the tenor of their institution, were to remain entirely destitute of all fixed revenues and possessions; though in process of time their number became a heavy tax upon the people. Innocent III. was the first of the popes who perceived the necessity of instituting such an order; and accordingly he gave such monastic societies, as made a profession of poverty, the most distinguishing marks of his protection and favour. They were also encouraged and patronized by the succeeding pontiffs, when experience had demonstrated their public and extensive usefulness. But when it became generally known, that they had such a peculiar place in the esteem and protection of the rulers of the church, their number grew to such an enormous and unwieldy multitude, and swarmed so prodigiously in all the European provinces, that they became a burden, not only to the people, but to the church itself. The great inconvenience that arose from the excessive multiplication of the mendicant orders was remedied by Gregory X. in a general council, which he assembled at Lyons in 1272. For here all the religious orders that had sprung up after the council held at Rome in 1215, under the pontificate of Innocent III., were suppressed; and the extravagant multitude of mendicants, as Gregory called them, were reduced to a smaller number, and confined to the four following societies or denominations, viz. the Dominicans, the Franciscans, the Carmelites, and the Augustins or hermits of St. Augustine. As the pontiffs allowed these four mendicant orders the liberty of travelling wherever they thought proper, of conversing with persons of every rank, of instructing the youth and multitude wherever they went; and as those monks exhibited, in their outward appearance and manner of life, more striking marks of gravity and holiness than were observable in the other monastic societies, they arose all at once to the very summit of fame, and were regarded with the utmost esteem and veneration through all the countries of Europe. The enthusiastic attachment to these sanctimonious beggars went so far, that, as we learn from the most authentic records, several cities were divided or cantoned out into four parts, with a view to these four orders; the first part being assigned to the Dominicans, the second to the Franciscans, the third to the Carmelites, and the fourth to the Augustinians. The people were unwilling to receive the sacrament from any other hands than those of the mendicants, to whose churches they crowded to perform their devotions, while living; and were extremely desirous to deposit there also their remains after death; nor did the influence and credit of the mendicants end here; for we find in the history of this and of the succeeding ages, that they were employed, not only in spiritual matters, but also in temporal and political affairs of the greatest consequence, in composing the differences of princes, concluding treaties of peace, concerting alliances, presiding in cabinet councils, governing courts, levying taxes, and other occupations, not only remote from, but absolutely inconsistent with, the monastic character and profession. However the power of the Dominicans and Franciscans greatly surpassed that of the other two orders: insomuch that these two orders were, before the reformation, what the Jesuits have been since that happy and glorious period, the very soul of the hierarchy, the engines of the state, the secret springs of all the motions of the one and the other, and the authors and directors of every great and important event, both in the religious and political world. By very quick progression their pride and confidence arrived at such a pitch, that they had the presumption to declare publicly, that they had a divine impulse and commission to illustrate and maintain the religion of Jesus; they treated with the utmost insolence and contempt all the different orders of the priesthood; they affirmed without a blush, that the true method of obtaining salvation was revealed to them alone; proclaimed, with ostentation, the superior efficacy and virtue of their indulgencies; and vaunted beyond measure their interest at the court of heaven, and their familiar connections with the Supreme Being, the Virgin Mary, and the saints in glory. By these impious wiles, they so deluded and captivated the miserable, and blinded the multitude, that they would not intrust any other but the mendicants with the care of their souls. They retained their credit and influence to such a degree, towards the close of the 14th century, that great numbers of both sexes, some in health, others in a state of infirmity, and others at the point of death, earnestly desired to be admitted into the Mendicant order, which they looked upon as a sure and infallible method of rendering heaven propitious. Many made it an essential part of their last wills, that their bodies after death should be wrapped in old ragged Dominican or Franciscan habits, and interred among the Mendicants. For such was the barbarous superstition and wretched ignorance of this age, that people universally believed they should readily obtain mercy from Christ, at the day of judgment, if they appeared before his tribunal associated with the Mendicant friars. About this time, however, they fell under an universal odium; but being resolutely protected against all opposition, whether open or secret, by the popes, who regarded them as their best friends and most effectual supports, they suffered little or nothing from the efforts of their numerous adversaries. In the 15th century, besides their arrogance, which was excessive, a quarrelsome and litigious spirit prevailed among them, and drew upon them justly the displeasure and indignation of many. By affording refuge at this time to the Beguins in their order, they became offensive to the bishops, and were hereby involved in difficulties and perplexities of various kinds. They lost their credit in the 16th century by their rustic impudence, their ridiculous superstitions, their ignorance, cruelty, and brutish manners. They discovered the most barbarous aversion to the arts and sciences, and expressed a like abhorrence of certain eminent and learned men, who endeavoured to open the paths of science.

MENECHRATES

Pages 399-399

a physician of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SYRACUSE">Syracuse</a>, who flourished about 360 B.C. is famous for his skill in his profession, but much more for his vanity. He would always be followed by some of the patients he had cured, and with whom he previously stipulated that they should follow him wherever he went. One appeared with the attributes of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a>, another with those of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a>, and others again with those of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-MERCURY">Mercury</a> <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> Aesculapius; while he, clad in a purple robe, with a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> on his head, and a sceptre in his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, presented himself, to the admiration of the public, under the name of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>, and travelled through different countries escorted by these counterfeit deities. He once wrote the following <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KING">king</a> of Macedon: Menechrates—Jupiter to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a>, greeting. Thou reignest in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MACEDONIA">Macedonia</a>, and I in medicine; thou givest <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEATH">death</a> to those who are in good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>, I restore <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> to the sick; thy <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> is composed of Macedonians; the gods themselves constitute mine." Philip answered him in a word, that he wished him restored to reason. Learning some <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a> after that he was in Macedon, Philip sent for him, and invited him to an entertainment. Menechrates and his companions were placed on rich and lofty couches; before which was an altar, covered with the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARVEST">harvest</a>; and whilst an excellent repast was served up to the other guests, perfumes and libations only were offered to these new gods, who, unable to endure the affront, hastily left the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, in which they never more made their appearance.

MENEDEMUS

Pages 399-399

a Greek <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, born at Erythreum, was the son of Calithenes, and one of Phedo's followers. He was in greatest esteem, and enjoyed several important posts, in his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. He several times defended Erythreum with <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> bravery, and died of grief when Antigonus became <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of it. A person one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> saying to him, "It is a great <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> to have what we desire," he replied, "It is a much greater to desire nothing but what we have." Menelaus flourished about 300 B.C.

MENELAUS

Pages 399-399

the son of Atreus, and the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> of Agamemnon, reigned at <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SPARTA">Sparta</a>, when <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> deprived him of his wife Helen. This <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-RAPE">rape</a> occasioned the famous <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WAR">war</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TROY">Troy</a>. See HELEN. Menelaus, a mathematician in the reign of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Trajan, wrote three books on the Sphere, which have been published by father Marfene.

MENES

Pages 399-399

born at This, a town of Thebais in Upper <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, was the founder of the Egyptian empire. He had three sons, viz. Athotis, who ruled after him at This and Thebes; Curudes, who in Lower Egypt founded the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HELIOPOLIS">Heliopolis</a>, which afterward was the kingdom of Diospoli; and Necheropes, who reigned at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-MEMPHIS">Memphis</a>. It is thought this Menes reigned 117 years after the birth of Phaleg, son of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HEBER">Heber</a>, which was the very year of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISPERSION">dispersion</a> of the people throughout the whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>. In <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> Memphis, he stopped the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NILE">Nile</a> near it, by the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of a causeway 100 furlongs <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, and caused it to run through the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>.

MENESTRIER

Pages 399-399

a native of Dijon, and one of the most learned and curious French antiquaries of his <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a>, wrote, 1. A Treatise on the Medals, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">Money</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> Monuments, of the Roman Empresses, in folio. 2. The most famous Medals of the Ancient Roman Emperors and Empresses, in quarto. He died in 1634, aged 70. MENGs (Anthony Raphael), first painter to the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, was born at Augsburg in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOHEMIA">Bohemia</a>, A.D. 1728. His father, painter to Augustus III., king of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>, perceiving his superior talents, carried him from Dresden to Rome in 1741. After having there pursued his art for four years, and copied the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> monuments of that <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>, he returned to Dresden, where he executed different works for Augustus with very uncommon success. During his abode in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, he became acquainted with <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DON">Don</a> Carlos king of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>; and when this <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> succeeded to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of Spain in 1761, he was careful to engage Mengs in his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>, by granting him an yearly pension of 2000 doubloons, together with a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> and equipage. He lived, however, chiefly at Rome; where in 1779 he fell a sacrifice to his confidence in a German quack, who pretended to cure him of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a> which he had contracted partly by his intense application, and partly by grief for the loss of his wife. His <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> timidity and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> of the world, the distrust which seemed to be expressed in his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> and manners, and his melancholy <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> of body, by no means lessened the envy of his rivals. Under this rude appearance, he had a heart full of kindness and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a>. On one occasion, when he perceived that he had offended a certain person by his bluntness (excusable only in a great genius), he was not only sorry for his inattention, but he affixed with his advice the painter whom he had offended. He made no mystery of his art any more than of his sentiments. Clement XIV. submitted to his judgment some pictures of no great value, and in excuse told him that he had bought them at the recommendation of an eminent painter. "This <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MAN">man</a> and I (replied Mengs) are two artists, one of whom praises every thing which he cannot equal, and the other blames every thing which he can surpass."

MENIPPEAN

Pages 399-400

a kind of satire consisting of prose and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VERSE">verse</a> intermixed. It is Menippe thus called from Menippus a cynic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> who delighted in composing satirical letters, &c. In <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of him, Varro also wrote satires under the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Satirae Menippae; whence this sort of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> is also denominated Varroonian satire. Among the moderns there is a famous piece under this title first published in 1594, against the chiefs of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a>, called also the Catholicicon of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>. It is esteemed a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MASTER">master</a>-piece for the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a>.

MENISCUS

Pages 400-400

in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OPTICS">optics</a>, a glass <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LENS">lens</a>, concave on one side and convex on the other; sometimes also called lunula. See Optics.

MENISPERMUM

Pages 400-400

moonseed: A genus of the decandra order, belonging to the dioecia class of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 11th order, Sarmentaceae. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MALE">male</a> has four exterior and eight interior petals; there are 16 stamens; the corolla of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> is the same as in the male; there are eight barren stamens, and two monoecious berries. There are three <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, all of them climbing plants, rising 14 feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, and natives of warm climates; but noway remarkable for <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>. The seeds of a kind which grows in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEVANT">Levant</a>, being formed into a paste, are regarded by the inhabitants as specific against <a class="xref" href="../1823/vol0.html#article-LICE">lice</a> and cutaneous eruptions. The same paste is likewise used for the purpose of intoxicating fishes. - See Cocculus Indicus.

MENNITH

Pages 400-402
or Minnith, Judges xi. 33, a town near Hebron (Jerome), in Arabia Petraea; in a district named Ecypolis, or twenty-twos, (Cellarius). There is also a Minnith mentioned Ezekiel xxvii, as being in a good wheat country; but whether the name with the foregoing is uncertain; though some think that the first Minnith lay in the country of Ammon, (Wells). Mennonites, a sect in the United Provinces, in most respects the same with those in other places called Anabaptists. They had their rise in 1536, when Menno Simon, a native of Friesland, who had been a Romanist priest, and a notorious profligate, resigned his rank and office in the Roman church, and publicly embraced the communion of the Anabaptists.
