Menno was born at Witmarsum, a village in the neighbourhood of Boltwerp in Friesland in the year 1505, and died in 1561 in the duchy of Holstein, at the country seat of a certain nobleman not far from the city of Oldeloe, who, moved with compassion by a view of the perils to which Menno was exposed, and the snares that were daily laid for his ruin, took him with certain of his associates into his protection, and gave him an asylum. The writings of Menno, which are almost all composed in the Dutch language, were published in folio at Amsterdam in the year 1651. About the year 1637, Menno was earnestly solicited by many of the sect with which he connected himself, to assume among them the rank and functions of a public teacher; and as he looked upon the persons who made this proposal to be exempt from the fanatical phrenzy of their brethren at Munster (though according to other accounts they were originally of the same stamp, only rendered somewhat wiser by their sufferings), he yielded to their intreates. From this period to the end of his life, he travelled from one country country to another with his wife and children exercising his ministry, under pressures and calamities of various kinds, that succeeded each other without interruption, and constantly exposed to the danger of falling a victim to the severity of the laws. East and West Friesland, together with the province of Groningen, were first visited by this zealous apostle of the Anabaptists; from whence he directed his course into Holland, Gelderland, Brabant, and Westphalia, continued it through the German provinces that lie on the coasts of the Baltic Sea, and penetrated so far as Livonia. In all these places his ministerial labours were attended with remarkable success, and added to his sect a prodigious number of followers. Hence he is deservedly considered as the common chief of almost all the Anabaptists, and the parent of the sect that still subsists under that denomination. Menno was a man of genius, undirected by a very sound judgment; he possessed a natural and persuasive eloquence, and such a degree of learning as made him pass for an oracle in the estimation of the multitude. He appears, moreover, to have been a man of probity, of a meek and tractable spirit, gentle in his manners, plausible and obsequious in his commerce with persons of all ranks and characters, and extremely zealous in promoting practical religion and virtue, which he recommended by his example as well as by his precepts. The plan of doctrine and discipline drawn up by Menno was of a much more mild and moderate nature than that of the furious and fanatical Anabaptists, whose tumultuous proceedings have been recited under that article, but somewhat more severe though more clear and consistent than the doctrine of the wiser branches of that sect, who aimed at nothing more than the restoration of the Christian church to its primitive purity. Accordingly he condemned the plan of ecclesiastical discipline that was founded on the prospect of a new kingdom, to be miraculously established by Jesus Christ on the ruins of civil government and the destruction of human rulers, and which had been the fatal and pernicious source of such dreadful commotions, such execrable rebellions, and such enormous crimes. He declared publicly his dislike of that doctrine, which pointed out the approach of a marvellous reformation in the church by the means of a new and extraordinary effusion of the Holy Spirit. He expressed his abhorrence of the licentious tenets, which several of the Anabaptists had maintained, with respect to the lawfulness of polygamy and divorce; and finally, considered as unworthy of toleration those fanatics who were of opinion that the Holy Ghost continued to descend into the minds of many chosen believers, in as extraordinary a manner as he did at the first establishment of the Christian church, and that he testified this peculiar presence to several of the faithful by miracles, predictions, dreams, and visions of various kinds. He retained indeed the doctrines commonly received among the Anabaptists, in relation to the baptism of infants, the millennium, or 1000 years reign of Christ upon earth, the exclusion of magistrates from the Christian church, the abolition of war, and the prohibition of oaths enjoined by our Saviour, and the vanity as well as the pernicious effects of human science. But while Menno retained these doctrines in a general tenor, he explained and modified them in such a manner as made them resemble the religious tenets that were universally received in the Protestant churches; and this rendered them agreeable to many, and made them appear indifferent even to numbers who had no inclination to embrace them. It however so happened, that the nature of the doctrines considered in themselves, the eloquence, of Menno which set them off to such advantage, and the circumstances of the times, gave a high degree of credit to the religious system of this famous teacher among the Anabaptists, so that it made a rapid progress in that sect. And thus it was in consequence of the ministry at Menno, that the different sorts of Anabaptists agreed together in excluding from their communion the fanatics that dishonoured it, and in renouncing all tenets that were detrimental to the authority of civil government, and by an unexpected coalition formed themselves into one community. Though the Mennonites usually pass for a sect of Anabaptists, yet M. Herman Schyn, a Mennonite minister, who has published their history and apology, maintains, that they are not Anabaptists either in principle or by origin. However, nothing can be more certain than this fact, viz. that the first Mennonite congregations were composed of the different sorts of Anabaptists, of those who had been always inoffensive and upright, and of those who, before their conversion by the ministry of Menno, had been sedulous fanatics: besides it is alleged, that the Mennonites do actually retain, at this day, some of those opinions and doctrines, which led the sedulous and turbulent Anabaptists of old to the commission of so many and such enormous crimes: such particularly is the doctrine concerning the nature of Christ's kingdom, or of the church of the New Testament, though modified in such a manner as to have lost its noxious qualities, and to be no longer pernicious in its influence. The Mennonites are subdivided into several sects; whereof the two principal are the Flemings or Flemingsians, and the Waterlanders. The opinions, says Motheim, that are held in common by the Mennonites, seem to be all derived from this fundamental principle, that the kingdom which Christ established upon earth is a visible church or community, into which the holy and just alone are to be admitted, and which is consequently exempt from all those institutions and rules of discipline that have been invented by human wisdom, for the correction and reformation of the wicked. This principle, indeed, was avowed by the ancient Mennonites, but it is now almost wholly renounced: nevertheless, from this ancient doctrine, many of the religious opinions that distinguish the Mennonites from all other Christian communities, seem to be derived: in consequence of this doctrine, they admit none to the sacrament of baptism but persons that are come to the full use of their reason; they neither admit civil rulers into their communion, nor allow any of their members to perform the functions of magistracy; they deny the lawfulness of repelling force by force, and consider war, in all its shapes, as unchristian and unjust; they entertain the utmost aversion to the execution of justice, and more especially... especially to capital punishments; and they also refuse to confirm their testimony by an oath. The particular sentiments that divided the more considerable societies of the Mennonites are the following: The rigid Mennonites, called the Flemings, maintain, with various degrees of rigour, the opinions of their founder Menno, as to the human nature of Christ, alleging that it was produced in the womb of the Virgin by the creating power of the holy Ghost; the obligation that binds us to wash the feet of strangers, in consequence of our Saviour's command; the necessity of excommunicating and avoiding, as one would do the plague, not only avowed sinners, but also all those who depart, even in some light instances pertaining to dress, &c., from the simplicity of their ancestors; the contempt due to human learning, and other matters of less moment. However this austere system declines, and the rigid Mennonites are gradually approaching towards the opinions and discipline of the more moderate or Waterlanders. The first settlement of the Mennonites, in the United Provinces, was granted them by William prince of Orange, towards the close of the 16th century; but it was not before the following century that their liberty and tranquillity were fixed upon solid foundations, when, by a confession of faith published in the year 1626, they cleared themselves from the imputations of those pernicious and detestable errors that had been laid to their charge. In order to appease their intestine discords, a considerable part of the Anabaptists of Flanders, Germany, and Friesland, concluded their debates in a conference held at Amsterdam, in the year 1630, and entered into the bonds of fraternal communion, each referring to themselves a liberty of retaining certain opinions. This association was renewed and confirmed by new resolutions, in the year 1649; in consequence of which the rigorous laws of Menno and his successors were, in various respects, mitigated and corrected.

MENOCHIUS

Pages 402-402

vulgarly Menochia, (James), a famous lawyer, meanly born at <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PAVIA">Pavia</a>, but who became so skilful in the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LAW">law</a>, that he was called the Balduus and Bartholus of his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>; all the princes of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> soliciting him to their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a>. He read at <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PADUA">Padua</a> 23 years together; and for <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> removed to Pavia, and succeeded Nicholas Gratiani. He hath got an immortal fame by his works, De recuperanda possessione; De adspicienda possessione; De presumptivis; De arbitrariorum Judicum questionibus & causis conciliorum, tom. i. &c. He died in 1607, aged 75.

MENOLOGY

Pages 402-402

Menologium, (from μήν, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MONTH">month</a>, and ἀγγελία, discourse), in much the same as <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MARTYROLOGY">martyrology</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CALENDAR">calendar</a>, in the Latin. The Greek menologium is divided into the several months in the year; and contains an abridgement of the lives of the saints, with a bare commemoration of the names of such whose lives were never written. The Greeks have various menologies; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> tax them with inferring <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> heretics in their menologies as saints.—Baillet treats of them at <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LARGE">large</a>.

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LAW">law</a>-books, a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TERM">term</a> that includes in it all patrimony, and necessaries for livelihood.

MENSALS

Pages 402-402

mensalia, in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, such livings as were formerly united to the tables of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> houses, and hence called mensal benefices. See the Manse article BENEFICE.

MENSES

Pages 402-405

Catamenia, in medicine, the monthly evacuations from the uterus of women not with child <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> not giving suck. They are so called from mensis "<a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MONTH">month</a>," the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> wherein they return. They are also called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, courses, &c. By the Jewish <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LAW">law</a> a woman was unclean while the menstrual blood flowed; and the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MAN">man</a> who touched her, or the moveables she had touched, was declared unclean.—Lev. xv. The menes make one of the most curious and difficult phenomena in the whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> body; for the explanation whereof, many hypotheses have been framed, though the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> is yet scarcely ascertained. It is generally agreed by all, that the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> women are under for some extraordinary supply to compensate the expense, and support them during the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a> of gestation, was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FINAL">final</a> reason why this redundancy at other times was given them, which continues whilst this necessity subsists, and ceases when, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> frame, it is no longer required; but this is all they agree in. Some, not content with this occasion alone, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WILL">will</a> have the menstrual blood offend in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> more than <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a>; which they argue from the pain it gives many women in the evacuation; with many other idle notions. Others ascribe this effect to an imaginary dominion of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MOON">moon</a> over the bodies of women. This was formerly the prevailing <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>; though the smallest reflection would have shown the weakness of it; for, had this purgation been owing to the influence of the moon, all women of the same <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TEMPERAMENT">temperament</a> would have found it at the same periods and revolutions of the moon, i.e., at the same time; which all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> shows to be false. There are two other opinions which carry with them <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a>, and are argued with a great <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of strength and reason; in both which, the quality of the blood is allowed to be innocent, but they still differ about the reason of its issue. The former is that of Dr Bohn and Dr Freind, who maintain this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FLUX">flux</a> to be the result of a plethora or plenitude; and to be evacuated only for relief against the quantity. Dr Freind, who has maintained the cause of a plethora with the greatest strength and clearness, supposes, that this plethora arises from a coagulation in the blood-vessels of a superfluity of aliment, which, he thinks, remains over and above what is expended by the ordinary ways; and that women have this plethora, and not men, because their bodies are more humid, and their vessels, especially the extremities of them, more tender, and their manner of living generally more inactive than that of men; and that these things concurring, are the occasion that women do not perspire sufficiently to carry off the superfluous alimentary parts, till they be accumulated in such quantities as to distend the vessels, and force their way thro' the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CAPILLARY">capillary</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTERIES">arteries</a> of the uterus. It is supposed to happen to women more than the females of other <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, which have the same parts, because of the erect posture of the former, and the the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VAGINA">vagina</a> and other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANALS">canals</a> being perpendicular to the horizon; so that the pressure of the blood is directed towards their orifices; whereas in <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-BRUTES">brutes</a>, they are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> to the horizon, and the pressure wholly is on the sides of those vessels. The discharge, he thinks, happens in this <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">part</a> rather than in any other, as being more favoured by the structure of the vessels; the arteries being very numerous, and the veins finous and winding, and therefore more apt to retard the impetus of the blood; and consequently, in a plethoric <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CASE">case</a>, to occasion the rupture of the extremities of the vessels, which may last till, by a sufficient discharge, the vessels are eased of their overload. This is the substance of Dr Freind's <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-THEORY">theory</a>; from whence he very mechanically and very philosophically accounts for the symptoms. To his argument, why women have menses rather than men, we may add from Boerhaave, that, in the former, the os sacrum is wider, and stands farther out, and the os coccygis farther in; the os innominata wider, and farther apart, and the lowest of them, as well as the lower eminences of the os <a class="xref" href="../1815/vol0.html#article-PUBIS">pubis</a>, farther outwards than in the latter. Hence, in women, the latitude or expansion about these <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BONES">bones</a>, and the capacity of the pelvis, is vastly great in proportion to those of men; and yet, in a woman not pregnant, there is not much to fill this expanse. Again, the foreside of the thorax is smoother in women than in men and the blood-vessels, lymphatics, adipose, and nervous vessels, membranes, and fibres, are much laxer in women than in men: whence all their cavities, cells, vessels, &c. are more easily replenished, and the humours aggregated in them; besides, that they are found to perspire less than men, and to arrive much sooner at their maturity, or state of increase. To which he adds the consideration of the soft pulposus texture of the uterus, and the vast <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of veins and arteries with which it is filled. Hence a healthy maid, being arrived at her growth, begins to prepare more nutriment than is required for the support of the body; which, as there is not to be any farther accretion, must of necessity fill the vessels, and especially those of the uterus and breasts, they being the least compressed. These will be dilated more than the others; whence the lateral vasa evacuating their humour into the cavity of the uterus, it will be filled and extended. Hence a pain, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, and heaviness will be felt about the loins, pubes, &c. the vessels of the uterus, at the same time, will be so dilated as to emit blood into the cavity of the uterus, and its mouth will be lubricated and loosened, and blood issue out. As the quantity of blood is diminished, the vessels will be less pressed, and will <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a> themselves again closer, so as again to retain the blood, and let <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> the groser part of the serum; till at length only the usual serum passes. Again, there are more humours prepared, which are more easily lodged in vessels once dilated; and hence the menses go and return at various periods in various persons. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HYPOTHESIS">hypothesis</a>, however plausible, is opposed by Dr Drake, who maintains, that there is no such repletion, or at least that it is not necessary to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MENSTRUATION">menstruation</a>; arguing, that, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the menses were owing to a plethora so accumulated, the symptoms would arise gradually, and the heaviness, stiffness, and inactivity, necessary symptoms of a plethora, would be felt <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">long</a> before the periods were completed, and women would begin to be heavy and indisposed soon after evacuation, and the symptoms would increase daily; which is contrary to all experience, many women, who have them regularly and easily, having no warning, nor any other rule to prevent an indecent surprize, than the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> of the time; in which, some that have slipped, have been put to confusion and shifts no ways consistent with the notice a plethoric body would give. He adds, that even those who are difficulty purged this way, the symptoms, though very vexatious and tedious, do not make such regular approaches as a gradual accumulation necessarily requires. If we consider what violent symptoms come on in an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>, we shall be extremely puzzled to find the mighty <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACCEPTION">acception</a> of matter, which should, in an hour or a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>'s time, make such great alterations. According to the hypothesis, the last hour contributed no more than the first; and of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a> should not be greater in the one than in the other, setting aside the bare eruption. This is the substance of what is argued against Dr Freind's theory; which, it must be owned, notwithstanding these objections, is still the most rational and consistent that has yet been advanced. Those who oppose it, give into the doctrine of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FERMENTATION">fermentation</a>, and maintain the evacuation of blood in those parts to be an effect of an effervescence or ebullition of the blood. This opinion has been maintained by many, particularly by Dr Charleton, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BALE">Bale</a>, De Graaf, and Drake; the two first of whom suppose a ferment peculiar to the women, which produces this flux, and affects that part only, or at least principally. Dr Graaf, less particular in his notion, only supposes an effervescence of the blood, raised by some ferment, without afflicting how it acts, or what it is. The sudden turgescence of the blood occasioned them all to think, that it arose from something till then extraneous to the blood, and led them to the parts principally affected to seek for an imaginary ferment, which no anatomical inquiry could ever show, or find any receptacle for, nor any reasoning necessarily infer. Again, that heat which frequently accompanies this turgescence, led them to think the case more than a plethora, and that there was some extraordinary intestine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> at that time. Dr Drake improves on the doctrine of a ferment; and contends, not only that it is necessary there should be a ferment, but a receptacle also for this ferment; concluding, from the suddenness and violence of the symptoms, that a great quantity must be conveyed into the blood in a short time, and consequently, that it must have been ready gathered in some receptacle, where, while it was lodged, its <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a> was restrained. But he goes farther still, and pretends to ascertain the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, &c. both of the one and the other, making the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-GALL">gall</a>-bladder to be the receptacle, and the bile the ferment. This liquor he thinks well adapted to raise a fermentation in the blood, when discharged into it in a quantity; and, as it is contained in a receptacle that does not admit of a continual issue, it may be there reserved, till in a certain period of time... the bladder becoming turgid and full, through the compression of the incumbent viscera, it emits the gall; which, by the way of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LACTEALS">lacteals</a>, insinuating itself into the blood, may raise that effervescence which occasions the aperture of the uterine arteries. To confirm this, he alleges, that persons of a bilious constitution have the menses either more plentifully, or more frequently, than others; and that distempers manifestly bilious, are attended with symptoms resembling those of women labouring under difficult menstruation. If it be objected, that on this principle men should have menses as well as women, he answers, that men do not abound in bile so much as women, the pores of the former being more open, and carrying off more of the serum part of the blood, which is the vehicle of all the other humours, and consequently a greater part of each is discharged through them than in women, wherein the superfluity must either continue to circulate with the blood, or be gathered into proper receptacles, which is the case in the bile. The same reason he gives why menstruation should not be in brutes: the pores of these being manifestly more open than those of women, as appears from the quantity of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> which they bear, for the vegetation whereof a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LARGE">large</a> cavity, and a wider aperture of the glands, is necessary, than where no such thing is produced: yet there is some <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between the males and females even among these, some of the latter having their menses, though not so often, nor in the same form and quantity, as women. He adds, that the several phenomena of the menses, whether in a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a>, a regular, or diseased case, flow naturally and readily from this hypothesis; and that whatever may be accounted for from a plethora, or from any particular ferment, may without any straining be applied to this. Females generally begin to menstruate about the age of fourteen or fifteen, and cease about fifty; though instances have occurred of their commencing sooner and continuing longer. There are, therefore, two critical periods in the lives of females which require their particular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>. In order to escape the chlorosis, and other similar diseases, incident to that period of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> when the menses commence, they should avoid indolence and inactivity, and accustom themselves to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> in the open <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> as much as possible. Unwholesome food, dainties of disposition, and frail cloaths, are very injurious to females at this season. The discharge in the beginning is seldom so instantaneous as to surprise them unawares. The eruption is generally preceded by symptoms that indicate its approach; such as a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of heat, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>, and dull pain in the loins; distention and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HARDNESS">hardness</a> of the breasts, headache, loss of appetite, languor, paleness of the countenance, and sometimes a slight <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of fever. When these symptoms occur, everything should be carefully avoided which may obstruct the menstrual flux, and all means used to promote it; as sitting frequently over <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHS">baths</a> of warm <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WATER">water</a>, drinking warm diluting liquors, &c. When the menses have begun to flow, great care should be taken to avoid every thing that tends to obstruct them; such as fish, and all kinds of food that are hard of digestion, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COLD">cold</a> acid liquors. Cold is likewise hurtful at this period; as also <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANGER">anger</a>, fear, grief, and other affections of the mind. From whatever cause this flux is obstructed, except in the state of pregnancy, proper means should be used to restore it; and if exercise in a dry, open, and rather cool air, wholesome diet, generous liquors in a weak and languid state of the body, cheerful <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>, and amusement fail, recourse must be had to medicine. When obstructions proceed from a weak relaxed state of the solids, such medicines as tend to promote digestion, to brace the solids, and assist the body in preparing good blood, ought to be used. See Medicine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. When the menstrual flux is too great, the patient becomes weak, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a>, the appetite and digestion are bad, and oedematous swellings of the feet, dropsies, and consumptions, often ensue. This frequently happens to women about the age of forty-five or fifty, and is very difficult of cure. It may proceed from a sedentary life; a full diet, consisting chiefly of salted, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> seasoned, or acrid food; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of spirituous liquors; excessive fatigue; relaxation; a dissolved state of the blood; violent passions of the mind, &c. In order to restrain the flux, the patient should be kept easy both in body and mind. If it be very violent, she ought to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a> with her head low; to live upon a cool and slender diet, as veal or chicken-broths with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>, and to drink decoctions of nettle-roots or the greater comfrey. If these fail, recourse must be had to stronger astringents, &c. See Medicine No. 246. The discharge of the menses is interrupted naturally during pregnancy; but this is not always the case, because some have them three months, some six months, and some during the whole time of gestation, though in less quantity than at other times. The menses are mostly interrupted during the time of giving suck, though many women have a return about the third or fourth month after delivery, and almost all have them again in the ninth or tenth month. In <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CASES">cases</a> of obstruction, the menstrual blood hath discharged itself by other outlets. It usually happens that this periodical discharge ceases between the age of forty and fifty; and the season in which this takes place is critical to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SEX">sex</a>. However, those who survive this period without contracting any chronic <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>, become more healthy and vigorous than they were before. About this time, some are afflicted with the well known symptoms of plethora, heat, flushings, restless nights, troublesome <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DREAMS">dreams</a>, and unequal spirits; others are attacked with inflammations of the bowels, or other internal parts; spasmodic affections of various parts, stiffness in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMBS">limbs</a>, swelled ankles, with pain and inflammation, the piles, and other effects of plenitude. Those of full plethoric habits, accustomed to copious evacuations, will find great relief by bleeding frequently in moderate quantities, keeping the bowels lax, moderating their diet, and using sufficient exercise that is not too heating. If an immoderate flux of the menses happens at this period, it should be restrained by gentle laxatives, cooling medicines, rest, anodynes, a most sparing not too liquid diet, rather than by very copious bleedings and astringents of any kind. Dr Fostergill observes, that various purgations of aloes, the tinctura sacra, pil. Ruffi, elixir proprietatis, and other compositions of this kind, are recommended as proper purgatives. purgatives to be used on the cessation of the menes. But many inconveniences have arisen from these heating medicines, as the piles, strangury, immoderate discharges of the menes, racking pains in the loins, and other similar complaints. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RHUBARB">Rhubarb</a>, senna, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MAGNESIA">magnesia</a>, sulphur medicines, small doses of jalap, and various <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBINATIONS">combinations</a> of these, may be substituted in the room of the others, and will supply sufficient variety to the prescriber and patient. When the menes are about to go off, they appear for the most part irregularly both in time and quantity; once in a fortnight, three, five, or six weeks; sometimes very sparingly, at other times in immoderate quantities. Great losses of this kind are often prevented by taking away four or five ounces of blood a few days after the first menstrual suppression. If a patient has in early life been subject to cutaneous eruptions, sore eyes, glandular swellings, or other obvious marks of morbid humours subsisting in the constitution, and all which may have disappeared about the time the menes became regular, an inflow is an advisable drain, and may prevent many inconveniences. If at this time ulcerous sores <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> out about the ankles, or in other parts of the body, they ought to be <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> open, or <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DRAINS">drains</a> substituted in their stead; for those who will have them dried up are soon after carried off by acute diseases, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> into those of a chronic <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>.

MENSORES

Pages 405-405

among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, were harbingers, whose business it was to go before the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>, and fix upon lodgings for him when he travelled into any of the provinces. They also marked out encampments, and assigned every regiment its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a>. Menores were also <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LAND">land</a>-surveyors, architects, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> appraisers of houses and public buildings. The distributors of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> were called menores frumentarii. And menores was also an appellation given to servants who waited at <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TABLE">table</a>.

MENSTRUAL

Pages 405-405
or MENSTRUOUS, a term in medicine, applied to the blood which flows from women in their ordinary monthly purgations. See MENSES.

MENSTRUUM

Pages 405-405

in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHEMISTRY">chemistry</a>, any body which in a fluid <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> subtilized state is capable of interposing its small parts betwixt the small parts of other bodies, so as to divide them subtilly, and form a new uniform <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> of the two.

MENSURATION

Pages 405-405

in general, denotes the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> art of measuring <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>, surfaces, or solids. See <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-GEOMETRY">GEOMETRY</a>.

MENTHA

Pages 405-405

MINT, in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a>: A genus of the gymnospemaria order, belonging to the didynamia class of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 42d order Verticillate. The corolla is nearly equal, and quadrifid, with one segment broader than the rest, and emarginated; the stamens are erect, standing a-funder. There are many <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>; but not more than three are cultivated for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>, namely, the viridis <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMON">common</a> spearmint, the piperita or peppermint, and the pulegium or pennyroyal. All these are so well known as to need no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a>; and all of them are very easily propagated by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTINGS">cuttings</a>, parting the roots, or by offsets. Uses. For culinary purposes, the spearmint is preferable to the other two; but for medicine, the peppermint and pennyroyal have in some places almost entirely superseded it. A conserve of the leaves is very grateful, and the distilled waters both simple and spirituous are universally thought pleasant. The leaves are used in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> salads; and the juice of them boiled up with <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a> is formed into tablets. It has been imagined that cataplasm and fomentations of mint, would dissolve coagulations of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MILK">milk</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>; but Dr <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LEWIS">Lewis</a> says, that the curd of milk, digested in a strong infusion of mint, could not be perceived to be any otherwise affected than by common <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WATER">water</a>; however, milk, in which mint-leaves were set to macerate, did not coagulate near so soon as an equal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of the same milk kept by itself. Dr Lewis says, that dry mint digested in rectified spirits of wine, gives out a tincture, which appears by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> of a fine dark green, but by <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CANDLE">candle</a>-light of a bright <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RED">red</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>. The fact is, that a small quantity of this tincture is green either by day-light or by candle-light, but a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LARGE">large</a> quantity of it seems impervious to common day-light; however, when held betwixt the eye and a candle, or betwixt the eye and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, it appears red. The virtues of mint are those of a warm stomachic and carminative: in loss of appetite, nausea, and continual retching to vomit, there are few simples of equal efficacy. In colicky pains, the gripes to which children are subject, lientery, and other immoderate fluxes, this plant frequently does good <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>. It likewise proves beneficial in many hysterical <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, and affords an useful cordial in languors and other weaknesses consequent upon delivery. The best <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a> in these cases is a strong infusion of the dried <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HERB">herb</a> in water (which is much superior to the green), or rather a tincture or extract prepared with rectified spirit. These possess the whole virtues of the mint; the essential <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OIL">oil</a> and distilled water contain only the aromatic <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">part</a>; the expressed juice only the astringency and bitterness, together with the mucilaginous substance common to all vegetables. The peppermint is much more pungent than the others. Pennyroyal has the same general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> with the mint, but is more acid and less agreeable when taken into the stomach. It has <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">long</a> been held in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> esteem, and not undeservedly, as an aperient and deobstruent, particularly in hysteric complaints and suppressions of the menes. For these purposes the diluted water is generally made use of, or, what is of equal efficacy, an infusion of the leaves. It is observable, that both water and rectified spirit extract the virtues of this herb by infusion, and likewise elevate the greatest part of them by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISTILLATION">distillation</a>. The expressed juice, with a little sugar, is not a bad medicine in the cough.

MENTOR

Pages 405-405

a faithful friend of Ulysses; a son of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a>; a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KING">king</a> of Sidonia, who revolted against <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTAXERXES">Artaxerxes</a> Ochus, and afterwards was restored to favour by his treachery to his allies, &c. Diod. 16. An excellent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a> in polishing cups and engraving <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> on them. Plin. 33. c. 11.—Mart. 9. ep. 6c. v. 16.

MENTZ

Pages 405-408

an archbishopric and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-ELECTORATE">electorate</a> in Germany. It lies on the banks of the river Mayne, between the electorate of Triers on the west, the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PALATINATE">Palatinate</a> on the south, Franconia on the east, and the Wetterau. on the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NORTH">north</a>. It is about 60 miles in length from north-east to south-west, and about 50 in breadth. A considerable <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELECTOR">elector</a>'s revenue arises from the toll on the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a> and the Mayne, and from the tax on the excellent wines produced in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> of any trade are, Mentz; (see the next article.) In its neighbourhood is Hockheim, so celebrated for good wines, that the best Rhenish is from thence called old hock. It is a pretty village, containing about 300 families; and belongs to the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a> of Mentz, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEAN">dean</a> of which enjoys the revenue of it: in a good year he makes from twelve to fifteen thousand guilders of his wine. He and the Augustines of Mentz and Francfort have the exclusive enjoyment of the best Hockheimer wine, of which, in good years, a piece, consisting of 100 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a>, sells for from 900 to 1000 guilders from the press. "This (says the Baron Riesbeck) is certainly one of the dearest wines in the world. Having a desire to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> it on the spot, we were obliged to pay a rix-dollar; it was, however, of the best vintage in this century, viz. that of 1766. Nor should we have had it, but for an advocate of Mentz, to whom the hostels meant to show favour. This was the first German wine I had met with which was entirely without any fine taste: it was quite a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PERFUME">perfume</a> to the tongue; whereas the other wine of Hockheim, let it be as good as it may, is not quite clear of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-VINEGAR">vinegar</a>; though for this also, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it has any <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, you are forced to pay a guilder and a half." 2. Bingen is a pleasant town, which stands in the district called Rhinegau. This town, which, together with the toll on the Rhine, is worth about 30,000 guilders, belongs to the chapter of Mentz, is extremely beautiful, and contains about 4500 inhabitants. A <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> part of the corn which is carried into the Rhinegau from the neighbouring Palatinate, comes through this <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, which, on the other <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, supplies the Palatinate with drugs, and various foreign commodities. This traffic alone would make the place very lively; but besides this, it has very fruitful vineyards. The hill, at the foot of which it lies, and one side of which is made by the gullet, through which the Nahe runs into the Rhine, forms another steep rock behind this gullet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> to the Rhine and the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> Rudesheimer mountain; it therefore enjoys the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> as this does, which makes the Rudesheimer wine that grows on it little inferior to the Rudesheimer. See Rudesheim. The rising grounds about it produce wines that are esteemed preferable to those of Baccharac, so much in vogue heretofore.—3. Elfeld, five miles west from Mentz, is a strong fortified town, on the north-side of the Rhine, and the chief of the Rhinegau.—Here is Rudesheim, a place noted for the growth of the best wines in these parts. 4. Weisbaden lies between six and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> leagues from Francfort, and about five <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> six miles north of Mentz: it is the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a> of a country belonging to the branch of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NASSAU">Nassau</a>-Saarbruck, and is famous for its mineral waters. After the pope, there is no doubt but the archbishop of this place is the most considerable and richest prelate in the Christian world. According to Baron Riesbeck, the see is indebted for its increase of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-RICHES">riches</a> to St Boniface, who may be called, with great <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APOSTLE">apostle</a> of the Germans. It was this <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MAN">man</a>, an Englishman by birth, who in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLEMAGNE">Charlemagne</a> baptized Witikind and the other brave Saxons who had so <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">long</a> resisted <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAPTISM">baptism</a> with their swords, and spread the empire of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-VICAR">vicar</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ as far as the northern and eastern seas. He it was who introduced the Roman liturgy into Germany, and made the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a> inhabitants abstain from eating <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>. He raised the papal power to a higher pitch than it had been raised in any other country in Christendom; and, in recompense of his services, the pope made all the new-founded bishoprics in the north of Germany subject to the see of Mentz, which Boniface had chosen for his residence. The provinces, the most considerable in the whole papal dominions, all Swabia, Franconia, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOHEMIA">Bohemia</a>, and almost all <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a>, with a part of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAVARIA">Bavaria</a>, and the upper Rhine, belong to this <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a>. Though the reformation, and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a> of the kings of Bohemia, have lessened it one third, it still contains the archbishopric of Sprengel and eleven bishoprics, most of which are the most considerable of Germany, as <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WURZBURG">Wurzburg</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PADERBORN">Paderborn</a>, Hildesheim, Augsburg, &c. When the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> of the papal <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MONARCHY">monarchy</a> was completed by Gregory VII., the archbishops of Mentz became powerful enough to be at the head of the empire. In the 13th and 14th centuries, they were so eminent as to be able to make emperors without any foreign <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a>; and it was to one of them that the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of Hapsburg was indebted for its first elevation. Since the boundaries of the two powers have been more accurately ascertained, and the temporal has so much got the better of the spiritual, the power and influence of the archbishops of this place have of course been much reduced; still, however, they are possessed of very important prerogatives, which they might exert with much more efficacy than they do, were it not that various circumstances have rendered them too dependent on the emperors. They are still the speakers in the Electoral <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COLLEGE">College</a>, have the appointment of the diets under the emperors, and may order a re-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a> of the proceedings of the imperial courts. These <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> privileges are, however, too much subject to the control of the house of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>; nor are their spiritual powers any longer what they once were. Their suffragan <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> have taken it into their heads that all bishops are alike as to power, and that the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of archbishop only intitles its possessor to the first place amongst brothers who are equal. The temporals, however, which are still annexed to this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a>, make him who sits in it rich amends for the diminution of his spiritual and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> splendor. Though he does not absolutely possess the largest, yet he certainly has the richest and most peopled domain of any <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> potentate in Germany. The country, it is true, does not contain more than 125 German miles <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, whereas the archbishopric of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SALZBURG">Salzburg</a> contains 240; but then Salzburg has only 250,000 inhabitants, whereas Mentz has 320,000. The <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> riches of the territory of Mentz, and its advantageous situation, make a subject of Mentz much richer than one of Salzburg, the greatest part of which is only inhabited by herdsmen. In the territory of Mentz there are 40 cities; in that of Salzburg only seven. The tax on vessels which go <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the Rhine of itself produces 60,000 guilders, or 6000l. a year, which is nearly MEN nearly as much as all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> of Salzburg put together, excepting only the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-SALT">salt</a> mine at <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HALLE">Halle</a>. The tax on wine, here and in the country round, produces the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COURT">court</a> above 100,000 guilders, or 10,000l. a-year, in which sum we do not reckon the customs of the countries which <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> at a greater distance. Upon the whole, the income of the present archbishop may be valued at 1,700,000 guilders, or 170,000l. If the lands of the elector lay all together, they would produce a sufficiency of corn and all the prime necessaries of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>; but as several parts of them lie wide afar, the people are compelled to purchase a great <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> from foreigners. The <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> itself, as well as the adjacent Rhinegau, depends on the Palatinate for its corn, notwithstanding the great abundance of that and every other <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of grain in its own possessions in Wetterau. The noblest production of the elector's territory on the Rhine is the wine, which is almost the only true Rhenish. Connoisseurs, indeed, allow the wines of Neirfein, Bacharach, and a very few other places out of this country, to be true Rhenish: but they do not give this name to the wines of the Palatinate, of Barden, and of Allatia. There is a great deal of wine made in the countries which lie on the south and west of the Rhine, at Laubenheim, Bodenheim, Budeleheim, and Bingen; but the true Rhenish, that which inspires so many who are and so many who are not poets, comes only from the Rhinegau, which lies on the northern banks of the Rhine. The civil <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LIST">list</a> of the archbishop (according to Baron Riebeck), is by much too immoderate and expensive. "He has his ministers, his counsellors of state, and eighty or ninety privy counsellors of various denominations. The expense of this establishment is very disproportionate to the revenue of the state. This is owing to the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-POOR">poor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>, who can only accept of employments of this kind. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IGNORANCE">Ignorance</a> of the true principles of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> are the causes of this evil. The consequences are, that a great number of persons, who might be usefully employed, live in idleness. Even the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> establishment of the country appears to me more calculated for the purpose of feeding a hungry nobility than for real <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>. At the accession of the present elector, though the whole <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> only consisted of 2,200 men, there were six generals. The regular establishment paid for and supported by the country is 800 men; but though there are only 2,000 men kept up, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> expended for their support, particularly that given to numberless useless officers, might be made use of more for the benefit of the country. The army of the archbishop consists of a German <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> of 50 men and 25 horses, a Swiss guard, a squadron of hussars of 130 men (the most useful troops, as they purge the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LAND">land</a> of robbers and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MURDERERS">murderers</a>), a corps of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTILLERY">artillery</a> of 104 men, three regiments of infantry of 600 men each, and some companies belonging to the armies of Franconia and the Upper Palatinate. Of the fortifications of the capital we may say much the same as of the army. Were they, indeed, improved and kept up as they ought to be, they would vie with Luxemburg, and be the most powerful of all the barriers against France. It is true, that the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the ground does not allow of a regular <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLAN">plan</a>; but for single parts, I have seen no place of the same capabilities, where greater advantages have been taken of the ground for the erection of the several works. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>, as well as size of them, is indeed an object of great wonder; but though the circle of the Upper Rhine, and even the empire in general, has laid out great sums on the building these fortifications, parts of them are not finished, and parts of them are ready to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> to pieces. Their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, indeed, would require a great army to man them. But this, as well as the maintaining and keeping them up, is evidently beyond the power of this court, or indeed of the whole circle of the Upper Rhine united. They are, therefore, also to be looked upon as one of the things which serve more for magnificence than real use." Mentz, a considerable town of Germany, in the circle of the Lower Rhine, and capital of the electorate of the same name, is situated on the Rhine near its confluence with the Mayne, 20 miles north-west of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-WORMS">Worms</a>, 15 west of Francfort, and 75 east of Triers, in E. Long. 8. 20 N. Lat. 49. 51. This <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CITY">city</a> claims a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of the art of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PRINTING">printing</a>; (see <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of Printing). Here is a very beautiful quay along the river, defended by several works well fortified with cannon. That part of the city which extends towards the river is most populous. The best vineyards for Rhenish wine being in this neighbourhood, Mentz has a flourishing trade in that commodity more particularly; and its <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> is the brisker, by reason that all the merchandize which passes up and down the Rhine stops in its harbour to change bottoms. The northern part of the city, in which the archbishop resides, is full of very regular buildings. Here are three regular streets, called the Bleichen, which run parallel to each other from the banks of the Rhine to 600 yards within the city, and are cut almost regularly by very pretty <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> streets. The archbishop's <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> has a most commanding view of these streets, the Rhine, and the Rhinegau. There are also some good buildings in the old part of the city. The market of beasts is extremely well worth seeing; and you here and there meet with other agreeable spots. The market in the middle of the town, though not regular, is one of the prettiest places in Germany. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> is well worth notice. It is an immense large old Gothic building, the spire of which was struck with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LIGHTNING">lightning</a> about 20 years ago, and entirely laid in ashes. As it was made of a forest of wood, it burned 14 hours before it was entirely consumed. To prevent these accidents for the future, the chapter had the present one built to the same height in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, an undertaking which cost them 40,000 guilders or L. 4,000. It is a great pity (Baron Riebeck observes) that it is overloaded with small ornaments; and a still greater, that this wonderful edifice is so choked up with shops and houses as to be hardly more than half visible. As, however, houses and shops are very dear in this part of the town, one cannot be very angry with the chapter for choosing rather to make the most of its ground, than to show off the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> to the best advantage. The rent of a shop and a single room to live in is 150 guilders or L. 15 per annum in this part of the town. There is hardly another church in Germany of the height and length of this cathedral; and the inside of it is decorated with several magnificent monuments of princes and other great personages. Besides the cathedral, the city of Mentz contains several other churches in the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> style, very well worth seeing. St <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PETER">Peter</a>'s, and the Jesuits church, though both too much loaded with ornament, are among this number. The church of the Augustines, of which the inhabitants of Mentz are so proud, is a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>-piece of bad taste; but that of Ignatius, though little is said about it, would be a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MODEL">model</a> of the antique, if here likewise there had not been too much ornament lavished. Upon the whole, the palaces of the noblest want that noble simplicity which alone constitutes true beauty and magnificence. In another century the externals of the city <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WILL">will</a> be quite changed. The late <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> built a great deal, and the present has a taste for the same sort of expense. The monks and governors of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOSPITALS">hospitals</a> also have been forced to rebuild their houses; so that when a few more streets are made broader and straighter, the whole will have no bad appearance. The inhabitants, who together with the garrison amount to 30,000, are a good kind of people, and, like all the catholics of Germany, make great account of a good <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TABLE">table</a>. Their faces are interesting, and they are not deficient either in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WIT">wit</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a>. There are few cities in Germany besides <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-VIENNA">Vienna</a> which contain so rich and numerous a nobility as this does: there are some houses here which have estates of 100,000 guilders, or L. 10,000 a-year. The counts of Bassenheim, Schonborn, Stadion, Ingelheim, Elz, Ostein, and Walderdorf, and the lords of Dahlberg, Breitenbach, with some others, have incomes of from 30,000 to 100,000 guilders. Sixteen or eighteen houses have from 15,000 to 30,000 guilders annual revenue.—The nobility of this place are said to be some of the oldest and most untainted in Germany. There are amongst them many persons of extraordinary merit, who join uncommon knowledge to all the duties of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> life. Upon the whole, they are far superior to the greater part of the German nobility. Their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>, however, is still too stiff. The first minister of the court was refused admittance into their assemblies for not being sufficiently noble; and they think they degrade themselves by keeping <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> with bourgeois. The clergy of this place are the richest in Germany. A canonry brings in 3500 Rhenish guilders in a moderate year. The canonry of the provost brings him in 40,000 guilders a-year; and each of the deaneries is worth 2600 guilders. The income of the chapter altogether amounts to 300,000 guilders. Though it is forbidden by the canons of the church for any one to have more than a single prebend, there is not an ecclesiastic in this place but what has three or four; so that there is hardly a man amongst them who has not at least 8000 guilders a-year. The last provost, a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COUNT">count</a> of Eltz, had prebends enough to procure him an income of 75,000 guilders. Exclusive of the cathedral, there are several other choirs in which the canonries bring in from 1200 to 1500 guilders a-year. To give an idea of the riches of the monasteries of this place, Baron Riesbeck informs us, that at the destruction of the Jesuits, their wine, which was reckoned to sell extremely cheap, produced 120,000 rixdollars. A Mentz, little while ago the elector abolished one Carthusian Mentzel convent and two nunneries, in the holy cellars of which there was found wine for at least 500,000 rixdollars. "Notwithstanding this great wealth (continues our author), there is not a more regular clergy in all Germany. There is no diocese in which the regulations made by the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TRENT">Trent</a> have been more strictly adhered to than they have here; the archbishops having made a particular point of it both at the time of the reformation and ever since. One thing which greatly contributes to keep up <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a> is the not suffering any <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> to remain in the country who has not fixed and stated duties, and a revenue annexed to them. Most of the irregularities in Bavaria, Austria, and other countries, arise from abbés who are obliged to subsist by their daily industry and any masses which they can pick up. These creatures are entirely unknown here. The theological tenets of this court are also much purer than those of any other ecclesiastical prince in Germany. I was pleased to see the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BIBLE">Bible</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of so many <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMON">common</a> people, especially in the country. I was told that the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-READING">reading</a> of it was not forbidden in any part of the diocese; only persons were enjoined not to read it through, without the advice of their confessors. For a long time <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a> has been hunted through its utmost recesses; and though it is not quite possible to get entirely clear of pilgrimages and wonder-working images, you will meet with no priest bold enough to exorcise or to preach such nonsense as we hear in the pulpits of other German churches." Though the trade of this place has been constantly on the increase for these 18 or 20 years past, yet it is by no means what it ought to be from the situation and other advantages. The persons here who call themselves <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a>, and who make any considerable <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, are in fact only brokers, who procure their livelihood at the expense of the country or territory round, or who <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> for the merchants of Frankfort. A few toy-shops, five or six druggists, and four or five manufacturers of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a>, are all that can possibly be called traders. There is not a banker in the whole town; and yet this country enjoys the staple privilege, and commands by means of the Mayne, Neckar, and Rhine, all the exports and imports of Alsatia, the Palatinate, Franconia, and a part of Swabia and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HESSE">Hesse</a>, as far as the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a>. The port too is constantly filled with ships, but few of them contain any merchandise belonging to the inhabitants of the place.

MENTZEL

Pages 408-408

born at Furttenwalde in the Mittel-mark, is celebrated for his skill in medicine and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a>, in pursuit of which he travelled through many countries. He had correspondents in the most distant parts of the world. He died A.D. 1701, about the 79th year of his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>. He was a member of the academy des Curieux de la <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURE">Nature</a>. His works are, 1. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a> nominum plantarum, printed at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BERLIN">Berlin</a> in folio, 1696; and reprinted with additions in 1715, under the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Lexicon plantarum polyglotton universale. 2. A <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHRONOLOGY">Chronology</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHINA">China</a>, in German, printed at Berlin 1696 in 4to. The following <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUSCRIPTS">manuscripts</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> are preserved in the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> library at Berlin: 1. Sur l'Histoire Naturelle du Brésil, in four volumes folio.

MENUS

Pages 408-409

a river of Germany; now the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAINE">Maine</a>, rising in Franconia, and running from east to west into the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-MENTZ">Mentz</a>.

MENUTHIAS

Pages 409-409

an <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> adjoining to the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east of the promontory Prafum of Ethiopia beyond <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>. Some take it to be Madagascar, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> the island St Laurence. <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> Vossius <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WILL">will</a> have it to be Zanzibar; Madagascar being at a greater distance from the continent than the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> ever failed to, whereas Menuthias was nearer; yet though Zanzibar be nearer the continent, it is however nearer the equator than Ptokmy's Menuthias, placed in south latitude 12½ degrees.

MENYANTHES

Pages 409-409

MARSH-TREFOL, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> Buckbean: A genus of the monogyne order, belonging to the pentandria clas of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 21st order, Preciae. The corolla is hairy; the stigma bifid; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPSULE">capsule</a> unilocular. This plant grows wild in moist marshy places in many parts of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>. It has three oval leaves standing together upon one pedicle, which issues from the root; their <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> is very bitter, and somewhat nauseous. According to Mr Lightfoot, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> of this plant are so extremely beautiful, that nothing but their native <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> could exclude it from a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in every garden. They grow in an elegant spike; are <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, dashed with pink, and fringed internally with hairs. The Highlanders esteem an infusion or <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TEA">tea</a> of the leaves as good to strengthen the stomach. According to Dr Withering, an infusion of the leaves is prescribed in rheumatisms and dropsies; a dram of them in powder purges and vomits, and is sometimes given to destroy <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-WORMS">worms</a>. In a scarcity of hops, the plant is used in the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> to bitter the ale. The powdered roots are sometimes used in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LAPLAND">Lapland</a> instead of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>, but they are unpalatable. Some people say, that sheep <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WILL">will</a> eat it, and that it cures them of the rot; but from the Upsal Experiments it appears, that though goats eat it, sheep sometimes will not. Cows, horses, and swine, refuse it.—Dr <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LEWIS">Lewis</a> informs us, that it is an efficacious aperient and deobstruent; promotes the fluid secretions; and, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> liberally taken, gently loosens the belly. It has of late gained <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> reputation in scurbutic and scrophulous disorders; and its good effects in those <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CASES">cases</a> have been warranted by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>. Inveterate cutaneous diseases have been removed by an infusion of the leaves, drank to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of a pint a-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, at proper intervals, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> for some weeks. Boerhaave relates, that he was relieved of the gout by drinking the juice mixed with whey.

MENZIKOFF

Pages 409-410

was originally an apprentice to a palfry-cook near the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MOSCOW">Moscow</a>; but by a fortunate circumstance was drawn from that situation in early <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, and placed in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">Great</a>. Having made himself <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of several languages, and being formed for <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WAR">war</a> and for business, he first rendered himself agreeable, and afterwards became necessary, to his master. He assisted Peter in all his projects; and was rewarded for his services with the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of Ingria, the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MAJOR">major</a>-general. He signalized himself in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a> in 1708 and 1709; but in 1713 he was accused of embezzling the public <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, and Menzikoff fined in 300,000 crowns. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CZAR">Czar</a> remitted the fine; and having restored him to favour, gave him the command of an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> in the Ukraine in 1719, and sent him as his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a> into Poland in 1722. Constantly employed about the means of preserving his influence after the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of his master, who was then evidently on the decline, Menzikoff discovered the person to whom the Czar intended to leave the succession. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> was highly offended, and his penetration cost him the principality of Plescoff. Under the Czarina Katharine, however, he was higher in favour than ever; because, on the death of the Czar in 1725, he was <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> in bringing different parties in Russia to agree to her succession. This princess was not ungrateful. In appointing her son-in-<a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LAW">law</a> Peter II. to be her successor, she commanded him to marry the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Menzikoff, and gave the Czar's sister to his son. The parties were actually betrothed; and Menzikoff was made <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Cozel and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GRAND">grand</a>-teward to the Czar. But this summit of elevation was the prelude to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a>. The Dolgorouki favourites of the Czar, had influence enough to procure his banishment, together with that of his family, to one of his own estates at the distance of 250 leagues from Moscow. He had the imprudence to leave the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> with the splendor and magnificence of a governor going to take possession of his <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>. His enemies took advantage of this circumstance to inflame the indignation of the Czar. At some distance from Moscow he was overtaken by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DETACHMENT">detachment</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>. The officer who commanded them made him alight from his chariot, which he sent back to Moscow; and placed him and his whole family in covered waggons, to be conducted into <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SIBERIA">Siberia</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> of peasants. When he arrived at the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of his destination, he was presented with cows and sheep big with young, and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-POULTRY">poultry</a>, without knowing from whom he received the favour. His <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> was a simple cottage; and his employment was to cultivate the ground, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> to superintend its cultivation. New causes of sorrow were added to the severities of exile. His wife died in the journey; he had the misfortune to lose one of his daughters by the small-pox; and his other two children were seized with the same <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>, but recovered. He sunk under his misfortunes, November 2, 1729; and was buried beside his daughter, in a little chapel which he had built.
