His misfortunes had inspired him with sentiments of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a>, which, amid the splendor of his former situation, he had altogether neglected. His two surviving children enjoyed greater <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> after the death of their father. The officer permitted them to attend public worship on Sundays by turns. One <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> when his daughter was returning from the village, she heard herself accosted by a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PEASANT">peasant</a> from the widow of a cottage, and, to her great surprize, recognized in this peasant the persecutor of her family, Dolgorouki; who, in his turn, had fallen a sacrifice to the intrigues of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COURT">court</a>. She communicated this intelligence to her <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>, who could not behold, without <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EMOTION">emotion</a>, this new instance of the vanity and instability of honours and power. Young Menzikoff and his sister were soon after recalled to Moscow by the Czarina Ann; and left Dolgorouki in possession of their cottage. He was made Menzini made <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a> of the guards, and received the fifth <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">part</a> of his father's possessions. His sister was appointed maid of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> to the Empress, and afterwards married to great advantage.

MENZINI

Pages 410-410

a celebrated Italian poet, born at <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a>, was professor of eloquence at the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> Della Sapienza at Rome, where he died in 1704. He wrote, 1. The art of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>. 2. Satires, elegies, hymns, and the Lamentations of Jeremiah. 3. Academia Tusculana, a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VERSE">verse</a> and prose, which passes for his masterpiece.

MEOPOTAMIA

Pages 422-422

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> name of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Diarbeck, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>. It is situated between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EUPHRATES">Euphrates</a> and Tigris; having <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSYRIA">Assyria</a> on the east, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMENIA">Armenia</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a> on the west, and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a> Deferta with <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BABYLONIA">Babylonia</a> on the south. The Hebrews called it Padan-aram (Gen. xxviii. 2. &c.), and Aram Naharaim (<a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Pfal. lx.) <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> Aram of the two rivers, because it was first peopled by Aram father of the Syrians, and is situated between the two rivers already mentioned. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> is much celebrated in scripture, as being the first dwelling of men both before and after the deluge; and because it gave birth to Phaleg, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HEBER">Heber</a>, Terah, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABRAHAM">Abraham</a>, Nahor, Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel, Leah, and to the sons of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JACOB">Jacob</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BABYLON">Babylon</a> was in the ancient Mefopotamia, till, by vast labour and industry, the two rivers of the Tigris and Euphrates were united into one channel. The plains of Shinar were in the same country. Often they gave it the name of Mefopotamia (Deut. xxiii. 4. &c.) and sometimes that of Syria, (Hosea xii. 2.) Bilaam son of Beor was of Mefopotamia, Deut. xxiii. 4. Chushan-rishathaim <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KING">king</a> of Mefopotamia kept the Hebrews in subjection some <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a> after the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Joshua, Judg. iii. 8.

MEOTIS

Pages 410-410
or PALUS MEOTIS, a sea of Turkey, which divides Europe from Asia; extending from Erim Tartary to the mouth of the river Don or Tanais.

MEPHITIC

Pages 410-410

a name expressing any kind of noxious vapour; but generally applied to that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of vapour called fixed <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a>. See AIR, FIXED AIR, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAS">GAS</a>, &c.

MEPHITIS FANUM

Pages 410-410

a temple erected to the god Mephitis, near Lacus Amiancti; who was worshipped also at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CREMONA">Cremona</a>. Figuratively, Mephitis denotes a noisome <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> pestilential exhalation, (<a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>.)

MEQUINEZ

Pages 410-410
or MIQUINEZ, the northern capital of the Morocco empire, stands at the extremity of the province of Beni-Hassen, 80 leagues north from the city of Morocco (which is the southern imperial city), and 20 to the east of Salee and the ocean. Maknaffa, its founder, built it first at the bottom of a valley; but Muley Ismael extended it considerably over the plain that lies to the west of the valley. It is surrounded with well cultivated fields and hills, adorned with gardens and olive plantations, and abundantly watered with rivulets. Accordingly, fruits and kitchen stuffs thrive here exceedingly, and even the superior urbanity of the inhabitants announces the temperature of the climate. The winter indeed is very inconvenient, on account of the dirtiness of the town, the streets not being paved, and the soil being flinty. Mequinez is surrounded with walls; the palace itself is fortified with two bastions, on which formerly some small guns were mounted. Muley Ismael, and Muley Abdallah, often in this city resisted the efforts of the Brebes, the sworn enemies of their tyranny. To the west are seen some walls of circumvallation, six feet in height, which were probably mere intrenchments for the infantry; the attacks of the Brebes being only sudden and momentary inroads, which did not require long defence. There is at Mequinez, as well as at Morocco, a walled and guarded suburb for the Jews. The houses are neater here than at Morocco. The Jews here are more numerous; and they can turn their industry to greater account, because the Moors in this city are more polished, and (being nearer to Europe) more visited, than those in the southern parts. Near the Jewry, there is another inclosed and separate quarter, called the Negro-town. It was built by Muley Ismael, for the accommodation of those black families which composed his soldiery. This town is now uninhabited, as are all those destined for the same use through the rest of the empire. At the fourth-east extremity of the city stands the palace of the emperor, which was built by Muley Ismael. The space occupied by this palace is very great; it includes several gardens, elegantly disposed, and well watered. There is a large garden in the centre, surrounded by a vast and pretty regular gallery, resting on columns, which communicates with the apartments. Those of the women are very spacious, and have a communication with a large chamber which looks into the garden. As you pass from one apartment to another, you find at intervals regular courts paved with square pieces of black and white marble; in the middle of these courts is a marble basin, from the centre of which rises a jet-d'eau, and the water falls down into this basin. These fountains are numerous in the palace; they are useful for domestic purposes, and they serve for the ablutions, which the scruples of the Mahometans have exceedingly multiplied. The palaces of the Moorish kings are large, because they are composed only of one range of apartments; these are long and narrow, from 18 to 20 feet high; they have few ornaments, and receive the light by two large folding doors, which are opened more or less as occasion requires. The rooms are always lighted from a square court in the centre, which is generally encompassed with a colonade. The Moors here are more courteous than those in the southern parts; they are civil to strangers, and invite them into their gardens, which are very neat. The women in this part of the empire are beautiful; they have a fair complexion, with fine black eyes, and white teeth. I have sometimes seen them taking the air on the terraces; they do not hide themselves from Europeans, but retire very quickly on the appearance of a Moor.

MERCATOR

Pages 410-410

one of the most celebrated geographers of his <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a>, was born at Ruremonde in 1512. He applied himself with such industry to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">geography</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>, that he is said to have frequently forgot to eat and drink. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> V. had a particular esteem for him, and the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Juliers made him his cosmographer. He composed a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHRONOLOGY">chronology</a>, some geographical tables, an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATLAS">Atlas</a>, &c. engraving and colouring the maps himself. He died in 1594. His method of laying <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DOWN">down</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARTS">charts</a> is still used, and bears the name of Mercator's charts. Mercator (Nicholas), an eminent mathematician in the 17th century, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HOLSTEIN">Holstein</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a>; and came to England about the time of the restoration, where he lived many years. He was fellow of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a>; and endeavoured to reduce astrology to rational principles, as appeared from a MS. of his in the possession of William Jones, Esq. He published several works, particularly Cosmographia. He gave the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUADRATURE">quadrature</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-HYPERBOLA">hyperbola</a> by an infinite <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERIES">series</a>; which was the first appearance in the learned world of a series of this sort drawn from the particular <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the curve, and that in a manner very new and abstracted. Mercator's Sailing, that performed by Mercator's chart. See <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NAVIGATION">Navigation</a>.

MERCATORUM FESTUM

Pages 410-411

was a festival kept by the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> on the 15th of May in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-MERCURY">Mercury</a>, who presided over merchandise. A sow was sacrificed on the occasion, and the people present sprinkled themselves with <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WATER">water</a> fetched from the fountain called <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AQUA">aqua</a> Mercurii; the whole concluding with prayers to the god for the prosperity of trade.

MERCHANT

Pages 411-411

a person who buys and sells commodities in grofs, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> deals in exchanges; or that traffic in the way of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, either by importation or <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EXPORTATION">exportation</a>. Formerly every one who was a buyer or seller in the retail way was called a merchant, as they still are both in France and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>; but here shopkeepers, or those who attend <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARKETS">markets</a>, have lost that appellation. Previous to a person's engaging in a general trade, and becoming an universal dealer, he ought to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a> up such a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FUND">fund</a> of useful knowledge as <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WILL">will</a> enable him to carry it on with ease to himself, and without risking such losses as <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> ill-concerted undertakings would naturally expose him to. A merchant should therefore be acquainted with the following parts of commercial learning: 1. He should write properly and correctly. 2. Understand all the rules of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARITHMETIC">arithmetic</a> that have any relation to commerce. 3. Know how to keep books of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> and single entry, as journals, a leger, &c. 4. Be expert in the forms of invoices, accounts of sales, policies of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INSURANCE">insurance</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a>-parties, bills of lading, and bills of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a>. 5. Know the agreement between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, weights, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> of all parts. 6. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> he deals in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, woollen, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>, he ought to know the places where the different sorts of merchandizes are manufactured, in what manner they are made, what are the materials of which they are composed, and from whence they come, the preparations of these materials before working up, and the places to which they are sent after their fabrication. 7. He ought to know the lengths and breadths which silk, woollen, or hair-stuffs, linen, cottons, fustians, &c. ought to have according to the several statutes and regulations of the places where they are manufactured, with their different prices, according to the times and seasons; and if he can add to his knowledge the different dyes and ingredients which form the various colours, it will not be useless. 8. If he confines his trade to that of oils, wines, &c., he ought to inform himself particularly of the appearances of the succeeding crops, in order to regulate his disposing of what he has on <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HAND">hand</a>; and to learn as exactly as he can what they have produced when got in, for his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> in making the necessary purchases and engagements. 9. He ought to be acquainted with the sorts of merchandize found more in one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> than another, those which are scarce, their different <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> and qualities, and the properest method for bringing them to a good market either by <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LAND">land</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. 10. To know which are the merchandizes permitted or prohibited, as well on entering as going out of the kingdoms or states where they are made. 11. To be acquainted with the price of exchange, according to the course of different places, and what is the cause of its rise and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a>. 12. To know the customs due on importation or exportation of merchandizes, according to the usage, the tariffs, and regulations, of the places to which he trades. 13. To know the best manner of folding up, embaling, or tunning, the merchandizes for their preservation. 14. To understand the price and condition of freighting and insuring ships and merchandize. 15. To be acquainted with the goodness and value of all necessaries for the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> and repairs of shipping, the different manner of their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>; what the wood, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASTS">masts</a>, cordage, cannons, sails, and all requisites, may cost. 16. To know the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WAGES">wages</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> given to the captains, officers, and sailors, and the manner of engaging with them. 17. He ought to understand the foreign languages, or at least as many of them as he can attain to; these may be reduced to four, viz. the Spanish, which is used not only in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> but on the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CANARIES">Canaries</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> of Good Hope; the Italian, which is understood on all the coasts of the Mediterranean, and in many parts of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEVANT">Levant</a>; the German, which is understood in almost all the northern countries; and the French, which is now become almost universally current. 18. He ought to be acquainted with the consular jurisdiction, with the laws, customs, and usages of the different countries he does or may trade to; and in general all the ordinances and regulations both at home and abroad that have any relation to commerce. 19. Though it is not necessary for a merchant to be very learned, it is proper that he should know something of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, particularly that of his own country; <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">geography</a>; hydrography, or the science of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>; and that he be acquainted with the discoveries of the countries in which trade is established, in what manner it is settled, of the companies formed to support those establishments, and of the colonies they have sent out. All these branches of knowledge are of great <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> to a merchant who carries on an extensive commerce; but if his trade and his views are more limited, his learning and knowledge may be so too; but a material requisite for forming a merchant is, his having on all occasions a strict regard to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, and his avoiding fraud and deceit as corroding cankers that must inevitably destroy his reputation and fortune. Trade is a thing of so universal a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, that it is impossible for the laws of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, or of any other <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, to determine all the affairs relating to it; therefore all nations, as well as Great Britain, show a particular regard to the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LAW">law</a>-merchant, which is a law made by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> among themselves; however, merchants and other strangers are subject to the laws of the country in which they reside. Foreign merchants are to sell their merchandize at the port where they land, in grofs, and not by retail; and they are allowed to be paid in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> or silver <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BULLION">bullion</a>, in foreign <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a> or jewels, which may be exported. If a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> arises between the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KING">king</a> and any foreign state, the merchants of that state are allowed six months' <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a> to sell their effects and leave the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>; during which time they are to remain free and unmolested in their persons and goods. See the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> Commerce, and Mercantile Law.

MERCHET

Pages 411-412

a fine <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> paid by inferior tenants to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LORD">lord</a>, for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> to dispose of their daughters in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>. No baron, or <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> tenant, could marry his sole <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> and heir, without such leave purchased from the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KING">king</a>, pro maritanda. And many of our servile tenants could neither send their sons to school, nor give their daughters in marriage, without express leave from the superior lord. See Kennet's Glossary in Mariagium. See also Marchet.

MERCIA

Pages 412-412

the name of one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> kingdoms founded in England by the Saxons. Though the latest formed; it was the largest of them all, and grew by degrees to be by far the most powerful. On the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NORTH">north</a> it was bounded by the Humber and the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-MERSEY">Mersey</a>, which separated it from the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NORTHUMBERLAND">Northumberland</a>; on the east by the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, and the territories of the East-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLES">Angles</a> and Saxons; on the south by the river <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a>; and on the west by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SEVERN">Severn</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEE">Dee</a>. It comprehended well nigh 17 of our <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> counties, being equal in size to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LANGUEDOC">Languedoc</a> in France; very little, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> at all, less than the kingdom of Arragon in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>; and superior in size to that of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOHEMIA">Bohemia</a> in Germany. Penda is regarded as its first monarch; and the kingdom is thought to derive its name from the Saxon word *merc*, which signifies "a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MARCH">march</a>, bound, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> limit," because the other kingdoms bordered upon it on every side; and not from the river Mersey, as some would persuade us. Penda assumed the regal <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TITLE">title</a> A.D. 626, and was of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 50 at the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a> of his accession; after which he reigned near 30 years. He was of a most furious and turbulent temper, breaking at different times with almost all his neighbours, calling in the Britons to his assistance, and shedding more Saxon blood than had been hitherto spilled in all their intestine quarrels. He killed two kings of Northumberland, three of the East-Angles, and compelled Kenwall <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KING">king</a> of the West-Saxons to quit his dominions. He was at length slain, with most of the princes of his family, and a multitude of his subjects, in a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> fought not far from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEEDS">Leeds</a>, by Offa king of Northumberland. This battle, which the Saxon <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHRONICLE">chronicle</a> tells us was fought at Winwidfield, A.D. 655, made a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> change in the Saxon affairs, which the unbridled fury of Penda had thrown into great confusion. He had the year before killed <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANNA">Anna</a> king of the East-Angles in battle, whose <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol4.html#article-ETHELRED">Ethelred</a> notwithstanding took <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">part</a> with Penda. On the other <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, Penda the eldest son of Penda, to whom his father had given the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> kingdom of the Mid-Angles, had two years before married the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of King Offa, and had been baptized at his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COURT">court</a>. At that time it should seem that Offa and Penda were upon good terms; but after the latter had conquered the East-Angles, he resolved to turn his arms against the kingdom of Northumberland. Offa by no means had provoked this rupture; on the contrary, Bede tells us that he offered <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LARGE">large</a> sums of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, and jewels of great value, to purchase peace; these offers being rejected, he was reduced to the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of deciding the quarrel by the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>. The river near which the battle was fought overflowing, there were more drowned than killed. Amongst these, as the Saxon chronicle says, there were 30 princes of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> line, some of whom bore the title of kings; and also Ethelred king of the East-Angles, who fought on the side of Penda against his family and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. His son Penda, who married the daughter of that conqueror, became a Christian, and was not <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">long</a> after murdered, as is said, by the malice of his mother. His brother Wolfher becoming king of Mercia, embraced in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of time the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> of the Gospel, and proved a very victorious and potent monarch; and is, with no fewer than seven of his immediate successors, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> styled king of the Anglo-Saxons, though none of them are owned in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> by the Saxon chronicle. But though possibly none of them might enjoy this <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>, they were undoubtedly very illustrious princes, maintaining great wars, and obtaining many advantages over the sovereigns of other Saxon states, and especially the East-Angles, whom they reduced. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of the Mercian territories was so ample as to admit, and so situated as to require, the constituting subordinate rulers in several provinces; to whom, especially if they were of the royal line, they gave the title of kings; which occasions some confusion in their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>. Besides the establishing episcopal sees and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONVENTS">convents</a>, the Saxon monarchs took other methods for improving and adorning their dominions; and as Mercia was the largest, so these methods were most conspicuous therein. <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COVENTRY">Coventry</a>, as being situated in the centre, was usually, but not always, the royal residence. Penda, who was almost continually in a state of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WAR">war</a>, lived as his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> operations directed, in some great town on the frontiers. Wolfher built a castle or fortified <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> for his own residence, which bore his name.—Offa kept his court at Sutton Walls near <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HEREFORD">Hereford</a>. In each of the provinces there resided a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a>; and if he was of the royal blood, had usually the title of king. Penda, at the time he married Offa's daughter, had the title of king of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEICESTER">Leicester</a>.—Ethelred made his brother Merowald king of Hereford; who, dying without issue, bequeathed it to his younger brother Mercelm. The like honours were sometimes conferred upon the princesses; and hence, in Mercia especially, we occasionally read of *vice-queens*. By these means the laws were better executed, the obedience of the subjects more effectually secured, and the splendor of these residences constantly kept up and augmented. At length, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> devolving sometimes on minors and sometimes on weak princes, intestine factions also prevailing, the force of this hitherto mighty kingdom began sensibly to decline. This falling out in the days of Egbert, the most prudent as well as the most potent monarch of the West-Saxons, he took advantage of these circumstances; and having encouraged the East-Angles to make an attempt for the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-RECOVERY">recovery</a> of their independence, he, in a conjuncture every way favourable to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>, broke with the Mercians, and after a short war obliged them to submit. But this was not an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> conquest; the kings of Mercia being allowed by him and his successors to retain their titles and dominions, till the invasion of the Danes put an end to their rule, when this kingdom had subsisted above 250 years; and when the Danes were afterwards expelled by the West-Saxons, it sunk into a province, or rather was divided into many.

MERCURIALIS

Pages 413-413
Mercury, in botany: A genus of the enneandra order, belonging to the dioica class of plants; and in the natural method ranking under the 38th order, Tricocae. The calyx of the male is tripartite; there is no corolla, but nine or twelve stamens; the anthers globular and twin. The female calyx is tripartite; there is no corolla, but two styles; the capsule biconcave, bilocular, and monospermous. There are three species. 1. The annua, or French mercury, with spiked flowers, male and female. This is an annual plant, with a branching stalk about a foot high, garnished with spear-shaped leaves of a pale or yellowish green colour. The male plants have spikes of hermaphrodite flowers growing on the top of the stalks; these fall off soon; but the female plants, which have teficated flowers proceeding from the side of the stalks, are succeeded by seeds, which, if permitted to scatter, will produce plenty of plants of both sexes. 2. The perennis mountain, or dog's mercury, with spiked and teficated flowers, grows under hedges and in woods in many parts of Britain. This has a perennial root, which creeps in the ground; the stalks are single, and without branches, rising 10 or 12 inches high, garnished with rough leaves, placed by pairs at each joint, of a dark green colour, indented on their edges; these have their male flowers growing in spikes, upon different plants from those which produce seeds. 3. The tomentosa, or shrubby hairy mercury, is a native of the south of France, Spain, and Italy. It has a shrubby branching stalk, growing a foot and an half high, garnished with oval leaves placed by pairs, and covered with a white down on both sides. The male flowers grow in short spikes from the side of the stalks upon different plants from the first. All the species are easily propagated by seeds, and are apt to become troublesome weeds where they have once got a footing. Properties. The perennis, according to Mr Lightfoot, is of a soporific deleterious nature, noxious both to man and beast. There are instances of those who have eaten it by mistake instead of chenopodium, bonus Henricus, or English mercury, and have thereby slept their last. In the isle of Skye, it is called hu-glen-bracadale; and an infusion of it is sometimes taken to bring on a salivation; but our author knows not how the experiment answers. Tournefort informs us, that the French make a syrup of the juice of the annua, two ounces of which is given as a purge; and that they use it in pellacies and clysters, mixing one quantity of honey to one and a half of the juice. Mr Withering differs greatly from Lightfoot concerning the qualities of the perennis. "This plant (says he), drenched like spinach, is very good eating early in the spring, and is frequently gathered for that purpose; but it is said to be hurtful to sheep. Mr Ray relates the case of a man, his wife, and three children, who experienced highly deleterious effects from eating it fried with bacon; but this was probably when the spring was more advanced, and the plant became acrimonious. Steeped in water, it affords a fine deep blue colour. Sheep and goats eat it; cows and horses refuse it.

MERCURIFICATION

Pages 413-413

in metallurgic <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHEMISTRY">chemistry</a>, the obtaining the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-MERCURY">mercury</a> from metallic minerals in its fluid form. For the effecting this, those who have been engaged in these researches have proposed three methods. The first is by means of a certain mercury, so prepared as to have a dissolving power, by which it could take up the mercuries of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-METALS">metals</a> in the same manner as <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WATER">water</a> dissolves <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-SALT">salt</a> from ashes. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SECOND">second</a> is by means of certain regenerating salts, such as sal ammoniac, which are to detain the more earthy parts of metals, and leave their mercuries separate <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> separable from them by sublimation or otherwise; and the third method is by means of a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LENS">lens</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BURNING">burning</a>-glass, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FOCUS">focus</a> whereof, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> any metal be applied, its mercurial <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">part</a> is said to separate and go off in fume, which when collected and condensed, appears to be running mercury. The first of these methods would be very easy if the proper mercury were to be readily produced; the second is extremely laborious, and requires much <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PATIENCE">patience</a> and reiteration. But the third seems easy enough, and practicable to advantage, when a glass of three or four feet in diameter is at <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, the sky serene, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> shines strong. For other processes, the reader may consult Junker's Conspicetus Chemicus. But these mercurified metals, or their mercurial principle rendered sensible, are a kind of philosophical mercury, which, although they resemble ordinary mercury, are nevertheless said by persons exercised in such studies, to differ from it considerably, by having a greater specific gravity, by more effectually penetrating and dissolving metals, by a stronger <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADHESION">adhesion</a> to these, and by a less volatility.

MERCURY

Pages 413-416

in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol12.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. See also <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-METALLURGY">Metallurgy</a>, and Quicksilver. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of mercury in medicine seems to have been little known before the 17th century. The <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> looked upon it as a corrosive <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-POISON">poison</a>, tho' of itself perfectly void of acrimony, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, and smell: there are examples of its having been lodged for years in cavities both in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BONES">bones</a> and fleshly parts, without its having injured <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> affected them. Taken into the body in its crude state, and undivided, it passes through the intestines unchanged, and has not been found to produce any considerable effect. It has indeed been recommended in asthmas and disorders of the lungs; but the virtues attributed to it in these <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CASES">cases</a> have not been warranted by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>. Notwithstanding the mildness and inactivity of crude quicksilver undivided; yet, when resolved by fire into the form of fume, or otherwise divided into very minute particles, and prevented from re-uniting by the interpolation of proper substances, or combined with mineral <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ACIDS">acids</a>, it has very powerful effects; affording the most violent poisons, and the most excellent remedies with which we are acquainted. The mercurial preparations, either given internally or introduced into a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> application, Mercury seem to forward circulation through even the minutest and most remote vessels of the body; and may be so managed as to promote excretion through all the emunctories. Hence their <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMON">common</a> use in inveterate chronic disorders, and obstrucive obstructions of the excretory glands; in scrophulous and cutaneous diseases; and in the venereal lues. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> their power be not restrained to certain emunctories, they tend chiefly to affect the mouth; and occasion a plentiful evacuation from the salivary glands. The salutary effects of mercurials do not depend on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of sensible evacuation. This medicine may be gradually introduced into the habit, so as, without occasioning any remarkable discharge, to be productive of very happy effects. To answer this purpose, it should be given in very small doses, in conjunction with such substances as determine its <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a> to the kidneys or the pores of the skin. By this method, inveterate cutaneous and venereal distempers have been cured, without any other sensible excretion than a gentle increase of perspiration or urine. Where there are ulcers in any <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">part</a>, they discharge for some <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a> a very fetid <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, the quantity of which becomes gradually less, and at length the ulcer kindly heals. If the mercury should at any time, from <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, or the like, affect the mouth, it may be restrained by omitting a dose, and by warmth, or suitable medicines promoting the perspiration. Cooling purgatives are also often employed with advantage; but perhaps the most effectual means of giving with safety a sudden check to a mercurial salivation, is by the application of a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LARGE">large</a> blister to the back. Mercury, as used in medicine, has been employed in a vast variety of different forms. But there is reason to believe, that every useful purpose to be answered by mercury may be obtained from a very few. The mercurial preparations in general, with a view to their use both externally and internally, may be divided into two <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> classes, the mild and the acrid. Almost every purpose to be answered by the former, may be accomplished by the unguentum hydrargyri and pilulae ex hydrargyro of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONDON">London</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a> pharmacies; while most of the effects to be obtained from the latter may be derived from the proper use of those preparations, hitherto generally known under the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CALOMEL">calomel</a>, and corrosive sublimate mercury. The marks of pure mercury are, its globules not losing their spherical <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> when poured on wood; its not communicating a tinge to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WATER">water</a>, or sweetness to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-VINEGAR">vinegar</a>, when rubbed with them; its evaporating entirely in an <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-IRON">iron</a> spoon over the fire; and its having a shining appearance without any pellicle on its surface. Mercury is best purified by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISTILLATION">distillation</a> in an iron pot, with a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">long</a> neck bent and immersed in vinegar. Quicksilver has sometimes been used in its pure metallic state, with the view of removing obstructions in the alimentary canal, from an idea that it would operate by its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>. But it is seldom attended with a good effect, and sometimes it must do harm. Whole volumes have been written respecting its operation and use in different diseases, and particularly in venereal affections. Some refer its operation to an evacuant power, others to its operating as a peculiar stimulus, and a third set to its possessing a power of Mercury, destroying or neutralizing the venereal virus. Of these opinions, the latter is the most generally received, and perhaps the best founded. But for a more full view of the controversy, we may refer our readers to late publications on the venereal <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>, and on mercury, by Mr John Hunter, Dr Schwedauer, and Dr Duncan. In virulent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GONORRHEA">gonorrhea</a>, it is doubted whether mercury be necessary. This disease is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> treated like any similar inflammation; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> things attended to are cleanliness of the parts, a regular belly, and an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSTINENCE">abstinence</a> from every thing stimulant in food, drink, &c. An <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INJECTION">injection</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OIL">oil</a> with calomel, or <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WHITE">white</a> precipitate, is much used, and some prefer a watery solution of opium. The more <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> injections have sometimes very disagreeable consequences. When the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> is affected, which is known by ulcers on the glands, buboes, ulcers in the mouth or throat, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>-coloured spots and ulcers on the surface, nodes, &c., mercury is thrown into the body either by friction or by the mouth. The general rule is, to keep up a slight soreness of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GUMS">gums</a> for some short time after the symptoms disappear; at the same time it is to be remembered, that mercury sometimes continues gleets, and induces ulcers, that are difficultly distinguished from venereal ones; and that these last only yield to warm <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHING">bathing</a>, diaphoretic diluents, opiates, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MILK">milk</a> diet. Corrosive sublimate is sometimes used, as more speedily arresting disagreeable, spreading, or dangerous ulcers; but the completion of the cure should always be trusted to the mild preparations alone. Mercury is also used in rabies canina, in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-WORMS">worms</a>, in hydrocephalus internus, in tetanus, and is by some considered as an antidote to the various matter. Mercury, in the heathen <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">mythology</a>. See Hermes. Most of the actions and inventions of the Egyptian Mercury have likewise been ascribed to the Grecian, who was said to be the son of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAIA">Maia</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATLAS">Atlas</a>. No one of all the heathen divinities had so many functions allotted to him as this god; he had constant employment both <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> and night, having been the common minister and messenger of the whole Pantheon; particularly of his father Jupiter, whom he served with indefatigable labour, and sometimes indeed in a capacity of no very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> kind. Lucian is very pleasant upon the multitude of his avocations; and, according to the confession of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Julian, Mercury was no <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HERO">hero</a>, but rather one who inspired mankind with <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WIT">wit</a>, learning, and the ornamental arts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, than with courage. The pious emperor, however, omits some of his attributes; for this god was not only the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> of trade, but also of theft and fraud. Amphion is said, by Pausanias, to have been the first that erected an altar to this god; who, in return, invested him with such extraordinary powers of music (and masonry), as to enable him to fortify the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Thebes in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BOEOTIA">Boeotia</a>, by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> of his lyre. Horace gives us the best part of his character. Thou god of wit, from Atlas sprung, Who by persuasive pow'r of tongue, And And graceful <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a>, refin'd The <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-RACE">race</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> kind, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HAIL">Hail</a>! winged messenger of Jove, And all th' immortal pow'rs above. Sweet <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PARENT">parent</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BENDING">bending</a> lyre, Thy praise shall all its sounds inspire. Artful and cunning to conceal Whate'er in sportive theft you steal, When from the god who gilds the pole, E'en yet a boy, his herds you stole; With angry <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> the threat'ning pow'r Bade thee thy fraudulent prey restore; But of his quiver too beguil'd, Pleas'd with the theft, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a> smil'd. You were the wealthy Priam's guide, When safe from Agamemnon's <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PRIDE">pride</a>, Through hostile <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CAMPS">camps</a>, which round him spread Their watchful fires, his way he sped. Unspotted spirits you confine To blissful seats and joys divine; And, pow'rful, with thy <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> wand, The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, unbodied crowd command; Thus grateful does thy office prove To gods below, and gods above. Francis. This ode contains the substance of a very long <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-HYMN">hymn</a> to Mercury, attributed to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>. Almost all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> poets relate the manner in which the Grecian Mercury discovered the lyre; and tell us that it was an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> strings; a circumstance which makes it essentially different from that said to have been invented by the Egyptian Mercury, which had but three. However, there have been many claimants besides Mercury to the seven-stringed lyre. See Lyre. His most magnificent temple was on mount <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CYRENE">Cyrene</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCADIA">Arcadia</a>. He is described by the poets as a fair beardless youth, with flaxen <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>, lively blue eyes, and a smiling countenance. He has wings fixed to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a> and sandals, and holds the caduceus (or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STAFF">staff</a> surrounded with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERPENTS">serpents</a> with two wings on the top) in his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HAND">hand</a>; and is frequently represented with a purse, to show that he was the god of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-GAIN">gain</a>. The animals sacred to him, were the dog, the goat, and the cock. In all the sacrifices offered to him, the tongues of the victims were burnt; and those who escaped imminent danger sacrificed to him a calf with milk and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>. Mercury, § in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a>. See Astronomy, Index. This planet is brightest between his elongations and superior conjunction, very near to which last he can generally be seen. He becomes invisible soon after he has found his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-ELONGATION">elongation</a>, going towards his inferior conjunction; and becomes visible again a few days before his next elongation. The brightness of this planet alters sometimes very considerably in 24 hours. It has been observed when less than three degrees distant from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, and may, perhaps, sometimes be seen even in conjunction with it. Mercury and Venus appear brightest and most beautiful in the opposite parts of their orbits: the first, between his elongations and superior conjunction; and the other, between her elongations and inferior conjunction. Therefore, Venus is seen in great perfection as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CRESCENT">crescent</a>, particularly in her inferior conjunction, whilst Mercury is seldom seen in such perfect phases. Mercury should be always observed on or near the meridian. When farther from the sun, he always appears with a very faint light; and when he has a great south declination, or the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a> is not perfectly clear, he seldom can be seen in those parts of his orbit, where he only begins to recover his brightness, or where it is much diminished. He has frequently been seen on the meridian even with a small <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TELESCOPE">telescope</a> and small power; and it appears from the above statement that he may be obscured in a clear day rather more than half his orbit, or near one hundred and four score days in the year. Mercury, in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HERALDRY">heraldry</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TERM">term</a> used in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLAZONING">blazoning</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANETS">planets</a>, for the purple <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> used in the arms of sovereign princes. Mercy, a virtue that inspires us with compassion for our brethren, and which inclines us to give them assistance in their necessities. Mercy is also taken for those favours and benefits that we receive either from God or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MAN">man</a>, particularly in the way of forgiveness of injuries or of debts. Nothing can be more beautiful than the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of mercy given us by Shakespear, in the pleading between Portia and the Jew: Por. Then must the Jew be merciful. Shy. On what compulsion must I? tell me that. Por. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of mercy is not strain'd; It droppeth as the gentle <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-RAIN">rain</a> from heav'n Upon the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLACE">place</a> beneath. It is twice blest: It blestest him that gives, and him that takes. 'Tis mightiest in the mightiest; it becomes The throned monarch better than his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>: The sceptre shows the force of temporal power, The <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATTRIBUTE">attribute</a> to awe and majesty, Wherein doth sit the dread and fear of kings; But mercy is above this scepter'd sway, It is enthroned in the hearts of kings; It is an attribute to God himself, And earthly power doth then show likest God's, When mercy seasons <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>. Therefore, Jews, Though justice be thy <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PLEA">plea</a>, consider this, That in the course of justice none of us Should see <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-SALVATION">salvation</a>. We do pray for mercy; And that same <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a> doth teach us all to render The deeds of mercy. Merchant of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> iv. Mercy-seat, or Propitiatory, in Jewish antiquity, the covering of the ark of the covenant.—The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> name of this cover, which we translate mercy-seat, is Kapporeth (Exod. xxv. 17, 22.), from Kappor, which signifies to cover, to shut up, to expiate, to pay. This cover was of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, and at its two ends were fixed the two cherubims of the same metal, which by their wings extended forwards, seemed to form a throne for the majesty of God, who in scripture is represented to us as sitting between the cherubims, and the ark itself was as it were his footstool. It was from hence that God gave his <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-ORACLES">oracles</a> to Moses, or to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> that consulted him, (Exod. xxv. 22. Numb. vii. 89.) Meretrix, among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, differed from the profligata. The profligata were common courtezans, with bills over their doors, signifying their profession, Merganser, and were ready at all times to entertain customers; whereas the meretrices entertained none but at night. The meretrices differed in their dress from the matrons; the former wore the toga and short tunic, like those of the men; the latter wore the pallia and the folla of such a length as to reach to their feet. MERGANSER. See MERGUS.

MERGUS

Pages 416-416

in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">ornithology</a>, a genus of birds of the order of anseres; distinguished by having the beak of a cylindrical <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, and hooked at the extremities, and its denticulations of a tubulated form. 1. The cucullatus, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> crested diver of Catesby, has a globular crest, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WHITE">white</a> on each side; and the body is <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> above and white below. This elegant <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> inhabits <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>. It appears at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HUDSON_S_BAY">Hudson's <a </a>class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">Bay</a> the end of May, and builds <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a>. The nest is composed of grass, lined with feathers from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>; the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of eggs from four to six. The young are <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>, and are fit to fly in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a>. They all depart from thence in autumn. They appear at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEW_YORK">New <a c</a>lass="xref" href="vol0.html#article-YORK">York</a>, and other parts as low as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VIRGINIA">Virginia</a> and Carolina, in November, where they frequent fresh waters. They return to the north in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MARCH">March</a>; and are called at Hudson's Bay Omifka fiber. 2. The merganser, or goosander, weighs four pounds; its length is two feet four inches; the breadth three feet four. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BILL">bill</a> is three inches <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">long</a>, narrow, and finely toothed or ferrated; the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> of that and of the irides is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RED">red</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DUN">dun</a>-diver, or <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FEMALE">female</a>, is less than the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MALE">male</a>; the head and upper <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">part</a> of the neck is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FERRUGINOUS">ferruginous</a>; the throat white; the feathers on the hind part are long, and form a pendent crest; the back, the coverts of the wings, and the tail, are of a deep ash-colour; the greater quill-feathers are <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, the lesser white; the breast and middle of the belly are white, tinged with yellow. The goosander seems to prefer the more northern situations to those of the south, not being seen in the last except in very severe seasons. It continues the whole year in the Orkneys; and has been <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HEBRIDES">Hebrides</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>. It is <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMON">common</a> on the continent of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, but most so towards the north. It is found also in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ICELAND">Iceland</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREENLAND">Greenland</a>, and breeds there, retiring southward in winter, at which <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a> it is found about the lake <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BAIKAL">Baikal</a>. It is frequent in America; inhabits the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of New York in winter; retires from thence in April, probably to Hudson's Bay; and, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it be the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BIRD">bird</a> called a Fisherman-duck, found also in Carolina. 3. The ferrator, or red-breasted merganser, weighs about two pounds; the length is one foot <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NINE">nine</a> inches, the breadth two feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a>; the bill is three inches long; the lower mandible red; the upper dusky; the irides a purplish red; head and throat a fine changeable black and green; on the former a long pendent crest of the same colour; the tail short and brown; the legs <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-ORANGE">orange</a>-coloured. The head and upper part of the female are of a deep rufous-colour, and the tail ash-coloured. These birds are most frequent in the northern parts of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>. They are observed to breed on Loch Mari, in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Ross, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> of Islay. The species is common in most parts of the north of Europe, on the continent; and as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> as Iceland, where it is called Vatus-and; also in the Russian dominions, about the great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SIBERIA">Siberia</a>, and the lake Baikal. It is likewise frequent in Greenland in the summer, where it breeds on the shores. The eggs are like those of a wild duck, but smaller and whiter. It dives well, and is very <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WATER">water</a>; but the Greenlanders often take it by darts thrown at it, especially in August, being the time when it is in moult. It is frequent in Newfoundland, and often appears at Hudson's Bay in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LARGE">large</a> flocks, but is observed to be of a larger size there than in Europe. They generally come in pairs the beginning of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JUNE">June</a>, as soon as the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ICE">ice</a> breaks up; make the nest soon after their arrival, chiefly on dry spots of ground in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, and lay from eight to thirteen white eggs, the size of those of a duck; the nest made of withered grass, and lined with the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DOWN">down</a> of the breast. The young are of a dirty brown, like young goslings. They all depart south in October to the lakes, where they may have open water. They are known at Hudson's Bay by the name of As-fisk. 4. The albellus, or smew, weighs about 34 ounces; the length 18 inches, the breadth 26; the bill is near two inches long, and of a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> colour; the head is adorned with a long crest, white above and black beneath; the head, neck, and whole under part of the body, are of a pure white; the tail is of a deep ash-colour, the legs a bluish grey. The female, or lough diver, is less than the male; the back, the scapulars, and the tail, are dusky; the belly is white. The smew is seen in England only in winter, at which season it <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WILL">will</a> sometimes be met with at the southern parts of it; as also in France, in the neighbourhood of Picardy, where it is called la Piette; similar to this, we have heard it called in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KENT">Kent</a> by the name of Magpie-diver. On the continent we find it as far south as <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CARNIOLA">Carniola</a>; frequents also Iceland, at which <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, or some other arctic region, it passes the summer; and where it in course breeds, probably along with the other Mergansers; as it has been observed to migrate, in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> with those birds, several kinds of ducks, &c., in their course up the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-VOLGA">Volga</a>, in February. It also inhabits America, having been sent from New-York, where it is probably a migratory species, as in Europe. 5. The minutus, or redheaded smew, weighs about 15 ounces; the length one foot four inches, the breadth one foot eleven; the bill is of a lead colour; the head slightly crested, and of a rust colour; the hind part of the neck is of a deep grey, the forepart clouded with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHTER">lighter</a> colour of the same kind; the back and tail are of a dusky ash-colour, the legs of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> ash-colour.—It is a native of Europe. Birds of this genus (Mr <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LATHAM">Latham</a> observes) "are in general not so well flavoured as those of the duck kind; yet we have often met with the last species in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONDON">London</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARKETS">markets</a>, and by some they are thought to be very little inferior to the wild duck; which last now and then partakes of the fishy haut goût, a flavour not disagreeable to the palates of the connoisseurs in good eating."

MERIAN

Pages 416-417

a celebrated painter, born at Frankfort in 1647, was the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Matthias Merian, a noted engraver and geographer. As she showed a very early fondness for <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>, she was instructed by <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABRAHAM">Abraham</a> Mignon; from whom she learned <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> neatness of handling and delicacy of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>. Meida lour. Her genius particularly led her to paint reptiles, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, and insects, which she designed after <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, and studied every object with a most curious and inquisitive observation; so that her works rose every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> more and more into reputation. Frequently the painted her subjects in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WATER">water</a>-colours on <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-VELLUM">vellum</a>, and finished an astonishing <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of designs, as she was equally indefatigable in her <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> and in her inquiries into the curiosities of nature. She drew the flies and caterpillars in all the variety of changes and forms in which they successively appear from their quiescent state till they become butterflies; and also drew frogs, toads, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERPENTS">serpents</a>, ants, and spiders, after nature, with extraordinary exactness and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>. She even undertook a voyage to Surinam, to paint those insects and reptiles which were peculiar to that <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a>; and at her return to her own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> published two volumes of engravings after her designs, which are well known to the curious. She died in 1717. Her daughter Dorothea Henrietta Graff, who painted in the same style, and had accompanied her mother to Surinam, published a third volume collected from the designs of Sibylla; which complete work has been always admired by the learned, as well as by the professors of painting.

MERIDA

Pages 417-417

a town of South <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of New <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GRANADA">Granada</a>, seated in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> abounding with all kinds of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, 130 miles N. E. of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-PAMPLONA">Pamplona</a>. W. Lon. 71° 0. N. Lat. 8° 30'.

MERIDEN

Pages 417-417
or Mireden, a town of Warwickshire, 97 miles from London, in the London road, near Coventry. It is pleasantly situated, though in a wet clayey situation, and is not ill built. The church stands on an elevated spot, and contains some good monuments. There is an inn here, about half way from St Clement's forest to Coventry, one of the finest in this part of England, being built like a nobleman's seat.

MERIDIAN

Pages 417-417

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">geography</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> circle supposed to be drawn through any <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">part</a> on the surface of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, and the two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLES">poles</a>; and to which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> is always perpendicular at noon. See Geography. In <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a>, this circle is supposed to be in the heavens, and exactly perpendicular to the terrestrial one. See Astronomy.

MERIDIANS

Pages 417-417

in antiquity, a name which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> gave to a kind of gladiators who entered the arena about noon after the bellaria (who fought in the morning against beasts) had finished. They were thus called from meridies, i.e., noon, the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a> when they exhibited their shows. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERIDIANI">meridiani</a> were a sort of artless combatants, who fought <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MAN">man</a> with man, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HAND">hand</a>. Hence Seneca takes occasion to observe, that the combats of the morning were full of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a> compared with those which followed.

MERIDIONAL DISTANCE

Pages 417-417

in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>, the same with departure, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> easting and westing; being the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a> between the meridian, under which the ship now is, and any other meridian which she was under before. MERIDIONAL parts, miles, or minutes, in navigation, are the parts by which the meridians in a Mercator's chart do increase, as the parallels of latitude decrease.

MERIONETHSHIRE

Pages 417-417

a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, is bounded on the north by <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CAERNARVONSHIRE">Caernarvonshire</a> and Denbighshire; on the east by <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MONTGOMERYSHIRE">Montgomeryshire</a>; on the west by St George's channel, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> the Irish <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SEA">sea</a>; and on the south by the river Dyfi, which parts it from Cardiganshire; extending 40 miles in length and 36 in breadth. It is divided into six <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HUNDREDS">hundreds</a>, in which are four market-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, 37 parishes, about 2500 houses, and 17,100 inhabitants. It lies in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BANGOR">Bangor</a>, and sends one member to <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> is very sharp in winter, on account of its many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> barren <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>; and the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> is as bad as any in Wales, it being very rocky and mountainous. However, this county feeds <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LARGE">large</a> flocks of sheep, many goats, and large herds of horned cattle, which find pretty good pasture in the valleys. Besides these, among their other commodities may be reckoned Welch cotton, deer, fowl, fish, and especially herrings, which are taken on this <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COAST">coast</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> plenty.

MERIT

Pages 417-417

signifies <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESERT">desert</a>. This <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TERM">term</a> is more particularly applied to signify the moral goodness of the actions of men, and the rewards to which those actions entitle them.

MERLIN

Pages 417-417

a famous English poet and reputed prophet, flourished at the end of the 5th century. Many surprising and ridiculous things are related of him. Several English authors have represented him as the son of an incubus, and as transported from <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a> to England the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-STONES">stones</a> which form <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONEHENGE">Stonehenge</a> on <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-SALISBURY">Salisbury</a> plain. Extravagant prophecies and other works are also attributed to him, on which some authors have written commentaries. Merlin, in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">ornithology</a>. See Falco.

MERLON

Pages 417-417

in fortification, is that <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">part</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARAPET">parapet</a> which is terminated by two embrasures of a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTERY">battery</a>.

MERMAID

Pages 417-419
or Merman, a sea-creature frequently talked of, supposed half human and half a fish. However naturalists may doubt of the reality of mermen or mermaids, we have testimony enough to establish it; though, how far these testimonies may be authentic, we cannot take upon us to say. In the year 1187, as Laray informs us, such a monster was shipped in the county of Suffolk, and kept by the governor for six months. It bore so near a conformity with man, that nothing seemed wanting to it but speech. One day it took the opportunity of making its escape; and plunging into the sea, was never more heard of. Hist. de Anglterre, P. I. p. 403. In the year 1430, after a huge tempest, which broke down the dikes in Holland, and made way for Mermaid, the sea into the meadows, &c. Some girls of the town of Edam in West-Frieseland, going in a boat to milk their cows, perceived a mermaid embarrassed in the mud, with a very little water. They took it into their boat, and brought it with them to Edam, dressed it in women's apparel, and taught it to spin. It fed like one of them, but could never be brought to offer at speech. Some time afterwards it was brought to Haerlem, where it lived for some years, though still showing an inclination to the water. Parival relates, that they had given it some notion of a Deity, and that it made its reverences very devoutly whenever it passed by a crucifix. Delices de Hollande. In the year 1560, near the island of Manar, on the western coast of the island of Ceylon, some fishermen brought up, at one draught of a net, seven mermen and mermaids; of which several Jesuits, and among the rest F. Hen. Henriques and Dimas Bolquez, physicians to the viceroy of Goa, were witnesses. The physician, who examined them with a great deal of care, and made dissection thereof, asserts, that all the parts both internal and external were found perfectly conformable to those of men. See the Hist. de la compagnie de Jésus, P. II. T. IV. n° 276, where the relation is given at length. We have another account of a merman, seen near the great rock called Diamond, on the coast of Martinico. The persons who saw it, gave in a precise description of it before a notary. They affirmed that they saw it wipe its hand over its face, and even heard it blow its nose. Another creature of the same species was caught in the Baltic in the year 1531, and sent as a present to Sigismund king of Poland, with whom it lived three days, and was seen by all the court. Another very young one was taken near Rocca de Sintra, as related by Damian Goes. The king of Portugal and the grand master of the order of St James, are said to have had a suit at law to determine which party these monsters belong to. In Pontopidan's href="vol12.html#article-NATURAL">Natural History of Norway, also, we have accounts of mermaids; but not more remarkable or any way better attested than the above. Merns, or Kincardineshire, a county of Scotland, stretching 27 miles in length and 20 in breadth, is bounded on the east by the German ocean, on the south by the river of North Esk, on the west by Angus, and on the north by the river Dee and Aberdeenshire.
