The country is pretty plain and level, fruitful in corn and pasturage, producing an infinite number of fir-trees, besides a great number of agreeable plantations; and along the sea-coasts there are many convenient creeks and harbours.—The people are Lowlanders, civil, hospitable, and industrious.—The name Merns is by some derived from that of a valiant nobleman, who, subduing the country, received it in reward from Kenneth II. Camden supposes it to retain part of the ancient name of Vernicenses. The other name is derived from Kincardin, its ancient capital, now an inconsiderable village. The stocking-trade employs the natives from the banks of the Dee to Stone-hive; from thence to the North Esk they are wholly employed in weaving. Merodach was an ancient king of Babylon, who was placed among the gods, and worshipped by the Babylonians. Jeremiah (chap. I. 2.), speaking of the ruin of Babylon, says, "Babylon is taken, Bel is confounded; Merodach is broken in pieces, her idols are confounded, her images are broken in pieces." We find certain kings of Babylon, in whose names that of Merodach is contained; for example, Evilmerodach and Merodach-baladan. Evilmerodach was the son of Nebuchadnezzar the Great, and had for his successor the wicked Belhazzar. Merodach-baladan, son of Baladan king of Babylon, having heard that Hezekiah had been cured miraculously (Isa. xxxix.), and that the sun had gone backwards to give him an assurance of his recovery, sent him presents, and made him compliments upon the recovery of his health. Ptolemy calls him Marsocampus; and says, that he began to reign at Babylon 26 years after the beginning of the era of Nabonassar, that is, in the year of the world 2283. Meroe (anc. geog.), an island of Ethiopia beyond Egypt, in the Nile; with a cognominal town, the metropolis of the Ethiopians. The Jesuits have endeavoured to prove, that the province of Gojam in Abyssinia is the Meroë of the ancients; but this is strongly contested by Mr Bruce, who is of opinion that it must be looked for somewhere between the source of the Nile and its union with the Atbara. The latter, he thinks, is very plainly the Attaboras of the ancients; and Pliny says that this stream incloses the left side of Meroë as the Nile does the right; in which case we must suppose him looking southward from Alexandria, otherwise the words would not apply. We are told by Diodorus Siculus, that Meroë had its name from a sister of Cambyses king of Persia, who died there in the expedition undertaken by that prince against the Ethiopians. His army perished with hunger and thirst in the deserts beyond Meroë; which could not have happened if they had reached Gojam, the latter being one of the most plentiful countries in the world. A further proof that Gojam cannot be the ancient Meroë is, that the latter was inclosed between the rivers Nile and Attaboras, while Gojam is almost entirely surrounded by the Nile. If the ancients were acquainted with Gojam, they must also have been acquainted with the fountains of the Nile, which we certainly know they were not. Pliny says that Meroë, the most considerable of all the islands of the Nile, was called Attaboras, from the name of its left channel, which cannot be supposed any other than the junction of the Nile and Atbara. He informs us moreover, that the sun was vertical twice in the year, viz. when proceeding northward he entered the 18th degree of Taurus, and when returning he came to the 14th degree of Leo; but this could never be the case with Gojam, which lies in about 10 degrees north latitude. Again the poet Lucan describes Meroë by two circumstances which cannot apply to any other than the peninsula of Atbara. One is, that the inhabitants were black; which was the case with the Gymnocephals and first inhabitants, and which has been the case with all the rest down to the Saracen conquest; but the inhabitants of Gojam, as well as the other Abyssinians, are fair, at least greatly different in complexion from the blacks; they are also long haired, and and nobody imagined that they ever had philosophers or science among them, which was eminently the case with the ancient inhabitants of Meroë. The other circumstance is, that the ebony tree grew in the island of Meroc, which at this day grows plentifully in the peninsula of Athara, and part of the province of Kuara, but not in Gojam, where the tree could not subsist on account of the violent rains which take place during six months of the year. Mr Bruce mentions another circumstance quoted from the poet Lucan, which likewise tends to prove the identity of Meroë and Athara; viz. that though there are many trees in it, they afford no shade. This our traveller found by experience, when returning from Abyssinia through Athara. "The country (says he) is flat, and has very little water. The forest, though thick, afforded no fort of shade, the hunters for the sake of their sport, and the Arabs for destroying the flies, having set fire to all the dry grass and shrubs; which passing with great rapidity in the direction of the wood from east to west, though it had not time to destroy the trees, did yet wither, and occasion every leaf that was upon them to fall, unless in those spaces where villages had been and where water was. In such spots a number of large spreading trees remained full of foliage; which from their great height and being cleared of underwood, continued in full verdure, loaded with large, projecting, and exuberant branches. But even here the pleasure that their shade afforded was very temporary, so as to allow us no time for enjoyment. The sun, so near the zenith, changed his azimuth so rapidly, that every few minutes I was obliged to change the carpet on which I lay, round the trunk of the tree to which I had fled for shelter; and though I lay down to sleep perfectly screened by the trunk or branches, I was presently awakened by the violent rays of the scorching sun, the shade having passed beyond me. In all other places, though we had travelled constantly in a forest, we never met with a tree that could shade us for a moment, the fire having deprived them of all their leaves." The heat of Athara is excessive, the thermometer having been observed at 119°: two of Mr Bruce's company died of thirst, or at least of the consequences of drinking after extreme thirst. The inhabitants live in the greatest misery, and are continually in danger from the neighbouring Arabs, who, by destroying and burning their corn, are able to reduce them to a starving condition. Notwithstanding all their disadvantages, however, they have a manufacture of coarse cotton towels, of a size just sufficient to go round the waist, which pass current as silver money throughout the whole country.

MEROM

Pages 419-419

(anc. geog.) The waters of Merom, at which <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLACE">place</a> Jabin and the other confederate kings met to fight Joshua (xi. 5.), are generally supposed by the learned to be the lake Semechon, which lies between the head of the river Jordan and the lake Genesareth; since it is agreed on all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, that the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CITY">city</a> Hazor, where Jabin reigned, was situated upon this lake. But others think, that the waters of Merom, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> Merome were somewhere about the brook Kishon, since there is a place of that name mentioned in the account of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> against Sifera (Judg. v. 21.). And it is more rational to think, that the confederate kings advanced as far as the brook Kishon, and to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> which led into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, to hinder Joshua from penetrating it, or even to attack him in the country where he himself lay encamped, than to imagine that they waited for him in the midst of their own country; leaving all Galilee at his mercy, and the whole tract from the brook Kishon to the lake Semechon. MEROPE (fab. hist.) one of the Atlantides. She married <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SISYPHUS">Sisyphus</a> the son of Æolus, and like her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SISTERS">sisters</a> was changed into a constellation after <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. It is said that in the constellation of the Pleiades the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-STAR">star</a> of Merope appears more dim and obscure than the rest, because she, as the poets observe, married a mortal, while her sisters married some of the gods or their descendants. MEROPS (fab. hist.) a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KING">king</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Cos, who married Clymene, one of the Oceanides. He was changed into an eagle, and placed among the <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-CONSTELLATIONS">constellations</a>. Also a celebrated footsinger of Perceus in Troas, who foretold the death of his sons Adrastus and Amphius, who were engaged in the Trojan <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WAR">war</a>. They flighted their father's advice, and were killed by <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DIOMEDES">Diomedes</a>.

MEROPS

Pages 419-420

in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">ornithology</a>, a genus belonging to the order of picae. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BILL">bill</a> is crooked, flat, and carinated; the tongue is jagged at the point; and the feet are of the walking kind. 1. The apiafter, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEE">bee</a>-eater, has an <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-IRON">iron</a>-coloured back; the belly and tail are of a bluish green; and the throat is <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>. This <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BIRD">bird</a> inhabits various parts of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, on the continent, though not in England; yet is said to have been seen in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, and flocks of them have been met with at Anspach in Germany in the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JUNE">June</a>. They are now and then seen in Lorraine, though only in pairs; and are not unfrequent in other parts, since Kramer talks of their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> the nest in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a> crags of the Danube. They are met with in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> and the south of France; and in Candia and other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> of the Mediterranean, they are in plenty, as well as in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PALESTINE">Palestine</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a>, being very <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMON">common</a> in the woods about Yemen, where they are called Schagghaga. It takes the name of bee-eater from its being very fond of those insects; but, besides these, it <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WILL">will</a> catch gnats, flies, cicadas, and other insects, on the wing, like the swallow. Willoughby tells us, from <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELON">Belon</a>, "that its singular elegance invites the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANDY">Candy</a> boys to hunt for it with cicadae, as they do for those greater swallows called swaffes, after this manner:—<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BENDING">Bending</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PIN">pin</a> like a hook, and tying it by the head to the end of a thread, they thrust it through a cicada (as boys bait a hook with a fly), holding the other end of the thread in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>; the cicada, fo fattened, flies nevertheless in the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a>; which the Merops spying, flies after it with all her force; and catching it, swallows pin and all, where-with she is caught."—This bird is said to be in most plenty in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> of Candia; and, in defect of insects, to eat seeds of many kinds; and Ray supposes, from its similarity to the kingfisher, it may possibly feed on fish. Most probably some think it good to eat, as Willoughby <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAW">saw</a> many of them exposed for <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-SALE">sale</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARKETS">markets</a> of Rome. These birds make their nests in deep holes in the banks of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, like the sand martin and kingfisher, at the end of which the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> lays from five to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WHITE">white</a> eggs, rather less than those... The nest itself is composed of moss. 2. The viridis, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> bee-eater, is green, with a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> belt on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>; and the throat and tail are black. It inhabits <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENGAL">Bengal</a>. 3. The congener is yellowish, with a green rump. It inhabits the south of Europe. 4. The superciliosus is green, with a white line both above and below the eyes, and a yellow throat. It is found in Madagascar, where the natives give it the name of Patriksh Tirich. 5. The cinereus is variegated with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RED">red</a> and yellow, with the two longest quill-feathers of the tail red. It is a native of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-MEXICO">Mexico</a>. 6. The erythropterus, or red-winged bee-eater, is in length six inches; the bill is one inch, and black; the upper parts of the head, body, wings, and tail coverts, are green <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BROWN">brown</a>, deepest on the head and back, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHTER">lighter</a> on the rump and tail coverts; behind the eye is a spot of the same, but of a very deep <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>; the quills and tail are red, tipped with black; the last two inches in length; the throat is yellow; the under parts of the body are a dirty white; and the legs black.—This inhabits <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SENEGAL">Senegal</a>, from which <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLACE">place</a> a well-preserved skin was brought by M. Adanson. (See fig. A.) 7. The wattle bee-eater (fig. B.) is the size of a cuckow, in length about 14½ inches. The feathers on the upper <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">part</a> of the head, being longer than the rest, give the appearance of a crest; those of the under part are smooth; the plumage for the most part is brown; the feathers are <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">long</a> and pointed, and each feather has a streak of white <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the middle; under the eye, on each side, is a kind of wattle, of an <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-ORANGE">orange</a> colour; the middle of the belly is yellow; the tail is wedge-shaped, similar to that of the magpie, and the feathers are tipped with white; the bill and legs are brown.—This bird is supposed to be peculiar to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-NEW_HOLLAND">New <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>. There are 14 or 15 other <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>.

MEROVINGIAN CHARACTER

Pages 420-420

derives its name from Merouée, the first <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KING">king</a> of France of that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-RACE">race</a>, which reigned 333 years, from Pharamond to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES_MARTEL"><a class="xref</a>" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> Martel. This race is said by some to have terminated in Childeric III. A.D. 751. There are many MSS. in the French <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol13.html#article-LIBRARIES">libraries</a> still extant in this character.

MEROZ

Pages 420-420

(anc. geog.), a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in the neighbourhood of the brook Kishon, whose inhabitants refusing to come to the assistance of their brethren when they fought with Sifera, were put under an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANATHEMA">anathema</a> (Judges v. 23). “Curse ye Meroz, says the angel of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>; curse ye bitterly the inhabitants thereof: because, &c.” Some have thought that Meroz is the same as Merus <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> Merom; and this F. Calmet thinks the most probable <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> in this <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>. Others <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WILL">will</a> have it, that Meroz was a mighty <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MAN">man</a>, who dwelt near the Kishon, and not caring to come to the assistance of Barak and Deborah, was excommunicated by the angel of the Lord by the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> of 400 trumpets. The angel of the Lord, according to some, was Barak, the general of the Lord’s <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>; but according to others he was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> for the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a> being, or a prophet.

MERSA

Pages 420-420

a town of Barbary, pleasantly situated about 11 miles from the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TUNIS">Tunis</a>, and two from Melcha the site of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CARTHAGE">Carthage</a>. The Bey has here two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>-houses, one of them very costly <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a>, built by Hassan Bey surnamed the Good. From these are <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-ORANGE">orange</a> gardens reaching almost to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-shore; on the edge of which is a famous well of sweet <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WATER">water</a>, esteemed the best and lightest in the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CLOSE">Close</a> to this is a coffee-<a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, whether numbers of people from the neighbouring places <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESORT">resort</a> to drink coffee, and a glass of this <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUXURY">luxury</a> so peculiarly enjoyed in the eastern countries. In the middle of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COURT">court</a> is a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LARGE">large</a> mulberry-tree, under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a> of which they sit and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a> and play at <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHESS">chess</a>; inhaling the comfortable sea-breeze that refreshes this delightful spot. The water is drawn up by a camel with the Persian wheel. Here are the remains of an ancient port, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> cothon, (supposed to be an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> one), built by the Carthaginians after Scipio had blocked up the old port, nothing but the turret or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>-house being left. MERS or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERSE">MERSE</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Scotland, called also <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol4.html#article-BERWICKSHIRE">Berwickshire</a>. This last name it derives from the town of Berwick, which was the head of the shire before it fell into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the English, and obtained the appellation of Mers or Mareb, because it was one of the borders towards England. It is washed on the south and east by the river Tweed and the German Ocean, bounded on the west by Tweedale, and on the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOTHIAN">Lothian</a>. It extends 24 miles from east to west, and the breadth amounts to 16. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FACE">face</a> of the country is rough and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a>, exhibiting hills, moors, and mosses, with intermediate valleys, which are pleasant and fruitful. It is watered by many streams; and particularly by the famous Tweed, which, rising from the same hills that give birth to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CLYDE">Clyde</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANNAN">Annan</a>, runs with a rapid course through Tweedale forest and Teviotdale, and after a course of 50 miles discharges itself into the German Ocean. Notwithstanding the length of its course, it is not navigable above Berwick, where there is a noble <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> over it, consisting of 15 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a>. There is another fine one, called the Union Bridge, at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COLDSTREAM">Coldstream</a>. There is a third at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-MELROSE">Melrose</a>, a fourth at <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PEEBLES">Peebles</a>, and a fifth at <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KELSO">Kelso</a>. The shire of Berwick is generally distinguished into the three divisions of Mers, Lammermuir, and Lauderdale. The Mers is low, pleasant, and tolerably fruitful in corn. Lammermuir is a hilly country, abounding with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAME">game</a>, and yielding good pasture for sheep and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> cattle. Lauderdale is a tract of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LAND">land</a> lying on each side of the river Lauder, agreeably varied with hill, dale, and forest, producing good store of corn and pasturage, and giving the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-EARL">earl</a> to the family of Maitland: but the most fruitful and populous parts of Berwickshire, are those that <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> along the Tweed, and on both sides of the lesser <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WHITE">White</a> Water, Black Water, and Eye. The seats of noblemen and gentlemen abound in this county.

MERSENNE

Pages 420-421

in Latin Mercennius, a learned French author, born at Oyé, in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAINE">Maine</a>, anno 1588. He studied at La Flèche at the same <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a> with Des Cartes; with whom he contracted a strict friendship, which lasted till <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. He afterwards went to <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, and studied at the Sorbonne; and in 1611 entered himself among the minimi. He became well skilled in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>. He was of a tranquil, sincere, and engaging temper; and was universally esteemed by persons illustrious for their birth, their <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>, and their learning. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-MERCURY">Mercury</a> learning. He taught philosophy and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a> in the convent of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEVERS">Nevers</a>, and at length became superior of that convent; but being willing to apply himself to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> with more freedom, he resigned all the posts he enjoyed in his order, and travelled into Germany, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a>. He wrote a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of excellent works; the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> of which are, 1. Questiones celeberrima in Genesim. 2. Harmonicorum libri. 3. De sonorum natura, causis, & effectibus. 4. Cogitata physico-mathematica. 5. La verité des Sciences. 6. Les questions inouies. He died at Paris in 1648. He had the reputation of being one of the best men of his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>. No person was more curious in penetrating into the secrets of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, and carrying all the arts and sciences to their utmost perfection. He was in a manner the centre of all the men of learning, by the mutual correspondence which he managed between them. He omitted no means to engage them to publish their works; and the world is obliged to him for several excellent discoveries, which, had it not been for him, would perhaps have been lost.

MERSER

Pages 421-421

an <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-ESSEX">Essex</a>, at the mouth of the Colne, south of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COLCHESTER">Colchester</a>. It was seized by the Danes in the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KING">King</a> Alfred, for their winter-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a>. It had eight parishes, now reduced to two, viz. east and west <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-MERSEY">Mersey</a>. The island had a blockhouse; and, in the Dutch <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WAR">war</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> put 1000 men in it.

MERSEY

Pages 421-421

a river of England, that runs through the counties of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LANCASTER">Lancaster</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-YORK">York</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHESTER">Chester</a>, and empties itself into the Irish <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SEA">sea</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIVERPOOL">Liverpool</a>. By the late inland <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>, it has <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEE">Dee</a>, Ribble, Ouse, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TRENT">Trent</a>, Darwent, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SEVERN">Severn</a>, Humber, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a>, Avon, &c.; which navigation, including its windings, extends above 500 miles, in the counties of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LINCOLN">Lincoln</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NOTTINGHAM">Nottingham</a>, York, Lancaster, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WESTMORELAND">Westmoreland</a>, Chester, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STAFFORD">Stafford</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WARWICK">Warwick</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEICESTER">Leicester</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WORCESTER">Worcester</a>, &c.

MERULA

Pages 421-421

born at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DORT">Dort</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, a famous lawyer, historian, and linguist, was professor of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> in the university of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a> after Lipsius. He wrote, 1. Commentaries on Ennius; 2. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of Erasmus and Junius; 3. A cosmography; 4. A treatise of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LAW">law</a>; and died in 1607.

MERUS

Pages 421-421

(anc. geog.), a mountain of the Hither <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, hanging over the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CITY">city</a> Nysa, built by <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BACCHUS">Bacchus</a>, and situated between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Cophen and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-INDUS">Indus</a>. The name, denoting the thigh, gave rise to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FABLE">fable</a> of Bacchus being inserted into <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>'s thigh, and being born twice; because in this mountain he and his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> are said to have been preserved, when <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a> and pestilence raged in the plains below.

MESARAIC-VESSELS

Pages 421-421

in the general <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, are the same with Mesenteric. In <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>, mesaraic is more frequently applied to the veins, and mesenteric to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTERIES">arteries</a>, of the mesentery. See Anatomy.

MESCHED

Pages 421-421

a considerable town of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Khorasan; fortified with several towers, and famous for the magnificent sepulchre of Iman Rifat, of the family of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALI">Ali</a>, to whom the Persians pay <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a>. It is seated on a mountain near this town, in which are fine torquife-<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-STONES">stones</a>; in E. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 56° 25'. N. Lat. 37° 0'.

MESEMBRYANTHEMUM

Pages 421-421

Fig. marigold, in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a>: A genus of the pentagynia order, belonging to the icofandra clas of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 3rd order, Succulente. The calyx is quinquefied; the petals are numerous and linear; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPSULE">capsule</a> is fleshy, inferior, and monoecious. There are between 40 and 50 <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>; all African plants, from the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> of Good Hope; near 40 of which are retained in our gardens for variety. Of these only one is annual, and the most remarkable of them all. It is called the cryphallium, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIAMOND">diamond</a>, ficoides, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ICE">ice</a>-plant. It rises with a short, thick, succulent stalk, dividing low into many trailing, very spreading, succulent branches, bespangled all over with icy pimples; very pellucid and glittering; oval, undulate, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALTERNATE">alternate</a>, papulose or pimply, glittering leaves; and from the sides of the branches, numerous, almost clove fitting, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, tinged with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RED">red</a> or crimson; succeeded by plenty of seed in autumn. This singular and curious plant, being closely covered with <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LARGE">large</a> pellucid pimples, full of moisture shining brilliantly like diamonds, is in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> esteem. It is a very tender plant while young; and is raised annually from seed by means of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HOT_BEDS">hot-beds</a>. In <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JUNE">June</a> it <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WILL">will</a> endure the open <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> till October, when it perishes; but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> placed in a hot-<a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> in autumn, it will often live all winter. It is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> planted in pots for the convenience of removing from <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLACE">place</a> to place; but if planted in the full ground, it grows considerably stronger, even to luxuriance; however, when confined in pots, it flowers more abundantly. The other species are most durable in stem and foliage. Some are shrubby; others pendulous, with loose straggling stems, and branches inclining to the ground; while others have no stalks at all; their leaves are universally very thick, succulent, fleshy; and of many various shapes, situations, and directions; while some are curiously punctured, or dotted with transparent <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-POINTS">points</a>, and some have pellucid pimples, as already mentioned: they afford a very agreeable variety at all times in the year, and merit a place in every collection. They are greenhouse plants, and are propagated by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTINGS">cuttings</a> of their stalks and branches.

MESENTERIC

Pages 421-421
or Mesaraic, an epithet given to two arteries arising from the descending aorta, and proceeding to the mesentery. See Mesentery.

MESN

Pages 422-422
or MESNE, a term in law, signifying him who is lord of a manor, and so hath tenants holding of him; yet he himself holds of a superior lord. The word is properly derived from meifne, quasi minor natu; because his tenure is derived from another, from whom he holds.

MESN ALSO

Pages 422-422

n also denotes a writ, which lieth where there is <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LORD">lord</a> mesn and tenant; and the tenant is distrained for services due from the mesn to the superior lord. This is in the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of a writ of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>; and in this <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CASE">case</a> the tenant shall have judgment to be acquitted <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> indemnified by the mesne lord; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he makes default therein, or does not appear originally to the tenant's writ, he shall be forejudged of his meifnalty, and the tenant shall hold immediately of the lord paramount himself.

MESOCHRI

Pages 422-422

were musicians among the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> who presided in concerts, and by <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEATING">beating</a> a wooden desk regularly with their feet, directed the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> of the music. For the purpose of beating <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a>, they wore wooden clogs, called by the ancients crupezia, which occasioned the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> to be better heard.

MESOCOLON

Pages 422-422

in anatomy, that <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">part</a> of the mesentery, which, having reached the extremity of the ileum, contracts and changes its name. See ANATOMY, n° 94.

MESOLOGARITHMS

Pages 422-422

according to Kepler, are the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LOGARITHMS">logarithms</a> of the co-sines and co-tangents; the former of which were called by Baron Napier anti-logarithms, and the latter differentials.

MESOPORPHYRON

Pages 432-432

a name given by the Greeks to the Roman laiclaque; because that garment, being edged on each side, where it opened before, with purple, appeared when closed with two purple stripes <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the middle. The same <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TERM">term</a> was also applied to the angusticlava.

MESOPTERYGIUS

Pages 422-422

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">ichthyology</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TERM">term</a> applied to such fishes as have only one back-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIN">fin</a>, and that situated in the middle of the back.

MESPILUS

Pages 422-423

the Medlar, in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a>: A genus of the pentagynia order, belonging to the icofandraia Mespilus class of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 36th order, Pomaceae. The calyx is quinquifid; the petals are five; the berry is inferior and pentaspermous. There are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, viz: 1. The Germanica, German medlar, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMON">common</a> medlar, rises with a deformed tree-stem, branching irregularly 15 or 20 feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>; spear-shaped leaves, downy underneath; and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CLOSE">close</a>-fitting, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, flingy from the sides of the branches; succeeded by large roundish <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> fruit, the size of middling apples, which <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-RIPEN">ripen</a> in October, but are not eatable till beginning to decay. The varieties are, common <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> German medlar—smaller <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NOTTINGHAM">Nottingham</a> medlar—spur-shaped Italian medlar. This species and varieties are all cultivated in the English gardens for the fruit; but the German or Dutch medlar, and the Nottingham kind, are the most common; and the latter of which two, though a smaller fruit, is rather preferable for richness and piquancy of flavour. These kinds of fruit are never eatable until they begin to rot; for when firm and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SOUND">sound</a>, they are of a singularly austere disagreeable <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>; yet having lain some <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a> after being gathered, till they begin to assume a state of decay and become soft, they acquire a delicious flavour, extremely agreeable to many, though to others altogether unpalatable.—All these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> ripen in the latter end of October, or beginning of November; when being gathered, some should be laid in moist straw, in several layers, to forward their decay; others on straw in the fruiteries; those in the barn <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WILL">will</a> begin to be ready for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> in about a fortnight, and those laid on straw will come gradually forward in succession. 2. The arbustifolia, arbutus-leaved medlar, hath a shrubby stem, branching erectly five or six feet high; lanceolate, crenated, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALTERNATE">alternate</a> leaves, downy underneath; and from the sides and ends of the branches, small white flowers in clusters; succeeded by small roundish, purple fruit, like haws. 3. The amelanchier, or shrubby medlar, with <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> fruit, rises with several shrubby, slender, hairy stems, branching moderately about four feet high, having purplish branches; oval, ferrated leaves, downy underneath; and small white flowers, in clusters at the ends of the branches; succeeded by small black fruit. 4. The chamae-mespilus, or <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DWARF">dwarf</a> medlar, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BASTARD">bastard</a> quince, hath a shrubby, slender, smooth stem, branching weakly four or five feet high, having purplish branches; oval, ferrated, smooth leaves, on <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">long</a> footstalks; and from the axillae, purple flowers, collected into round heads, with narrow, purplish, deciduous bracteae; succeeded by small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RED">red</a> fruit. 5. The cotoneaster, commonly called dwarf quince, rises with a shrubby, smooth stem, branching four or five feet high, the branches slender and reddish; oval entire leaves on short footstalks; and from the axillae, small close-fitting purple flowers, two or three together; succeeded by small roundish, bright-red fruit. 6. The Canadenis, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CANADA">Canada</a> snowy medlar, hath a shrubby, smooth stem, branching four or five feet high, with smooth, purplish branches; oval-<a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a>, ferrated, smooth leaves, on long footstalks; and all the Mespilus the branches terminated by clusters of snowy-white flowers; succeeded by small, purplish fruit, like haws. 7. The pyracantha, or ever-green <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-THORN">thorn</a>, rises with a shrubby, spinous stem, branching diffusely 12 or 14 feet high, the branches slender and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FLEXIBLE">flexible</a>, with a dark greenish bark, armed with long sharp spines; spear-shaped-oval, crenated, ever-green leaves; and all the shoots terminated by numerous clutters of whitish flowers; succeeded by large bunches of beautiful red berries, remaining all winter, and exhibiting a very ornamental appearance. All these seven species of mespilus are of the tree and shrub kind; the first five sorts are deciduous, the seventh an ever-green; the leaves are universally simple; those of the mespilus Germanica very large, the others mostly of moderate size, and which in most of the sorts grow upon short footstalks. They all flower abundantly every <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>, the flowers universally hermaphrodite, and consisting each of five large roundish petals, 20 stamina, and five styles. They are all very hardy, and succeed in any common <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> and situation, and their propagation and culture is very easy. The first sort and varieties are cultivated as fruit-trees, principally as standards, sometimes also as espaliers for variety. The other species are very proper furniture for any ornamental plantation, where they will make an agreeable variety with their different foliage; and their flowers make a fine appearance, as also their fruit in autumn and winter, which, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> not devoured by birds, remain long on the branches, and afford a fine variety in those seasons. The pyracantha, being rather of flexible growth, is most commonly trained against walls or the fronts of houses, both for the support of its flexible branches, and that it may exhibit its berries more ornamentally. When it is designed to have any of the common medlars as fruit-trees, they may be trained either as dwarfs, for dwarf standards, or for espaliers, or trained as half or full standards, and managed in either of those modes of training nearly as other fruit-trees, particularly the apple and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEAR">pear</a>; and are raised either by seed, by <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GRAFTING">grafting</a>, or by budding; but either of the two latter methods are the most certain for continuing the sorts without <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VARIATION">variation</a>; observing, after shortening their first shoots from the graft or bud, where it shall seem necessary to force out a proper supply of wood to form a head, to train the branches afterwards principally at full length, and let the standards branch out in their own way.

MESSALINA

Pages 423-423

a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Messala Barbatus. She married the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Claudius, and disgraced herself by her cruelties and incontinence. Her husband's <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> was not the only seat of her licentiousness, but she prostituted herself in the public streets, and few men there were at Rome who could not boast of having enjoyed the favours of the impure Messalina. Her extravagancies at last irritated her husband, who commanded her to appear and answer all the accusations which were brought against her; upon which she attempted to destroy herself; and when her courage failed, one of the tribunes who had been sent to her dispatched her with his <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>. It is in speaking of her debaucheries and lewdness that Juvenal says, *It laffata viris, nequam satiata, recessit.* Her name has become a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMON">common</a> appellation to denote a woman of shameless and inordinate lust.

MESSANA

Pages 423-423

(anc. geog.), the first town of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a> on crossing over from <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, situated on the strait now called the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FARO">Faro</a>, (Italicus). Anciently called Zanicle, according to Diodorus Siculus, from <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KING">king</a> Zanclus; <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a>, according to others, from the Sicilian <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TERM">term</a> Zanclon, denoting a fickle, alluding to the curvity of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COAST">coast</a>: a name appropriated by the poets; and hence Zanclaei, the people, (<a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HERODOTUS">Herodotus</a>, Paufanias). The other name Messana is from the Messenii of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PELOPONNESUS">Peloponnesus</a>, (Strabo). <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-THUCYDIDES">Thucydides</a> ascribes its origin to Anaxilaus the Messenian, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TYRANT">tyrant</a> of Rhegium, who received all comers, calling the town after the name of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. The Greeks always call it Messene; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-MESSENA">Messena</a> constantly, to distinguish it from Messene of Peloponnesus. Now Messina, lately ruined by earthquakes.

MESSENA

Pages 423-423
or Messene, an inland town, and the capital of Messenia, a country of Peloponnesus; erroneously placed by Ptolemy on the coast. It was built by Epaminondas, who recalled all the Messenian exiles, and gave the town the name of Messene. A place varying in point of strength and situation with Corinth, according to Strabo; and therefore Demetrius Phalerius advised Philip, father of Perseus, that if he wanted to have Peloponnesus in his power, he should make himself master of these two towns, as thus he would have the ox by both horns.

MESSENGERS

Pages 423-424

in Scotland. See <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">Part</a> III., p. 651, par. 16. MESSENGERS of the Exchequer, are four officers who attend the exchequer, in the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of pursuivants, and carry the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LORD">lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURER">treasurer</a>'s letters, precepts, &c. MESSANGER of the Press, a person who, by order of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COURT">court</a>, searches <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PRINTING">printing</a>-houses, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOOKSELLERS">booksellers</a> shops, &c. in order to discover the printers <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> publishers of seditious books, pamphlets, &c.

MESSENIA

Pages 424-427

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> in the south of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PELOPONNESUS">Peloponnesus</a>, mostly <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a>, situated between <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-ELEA">Elea</a> to the west, and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LACONIA">Laconia</a> to the east. Anciently a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">part</a> of Laconia under Menelaus, and called Messene by <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>; interpreted by the scholiast, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-MESSENA">Messena</a> Regia. Messenians, the people, reduced to a state of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SLAVERY">slavery</a> and subjection by the Spartans; Messenius, the epithet. This country is famous in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, on account of the resistance made by the Messenians against the Spartans, and the exploits of their <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HERO">hero</a> Aristomenes. The first hostilities commenced about the year 652 B.C. on what occasion is uncertain. Though the Messenians were inferior in the knowledge of the art of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WAR">war</a> to the Spartans; yet, by keeping for some <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a> on the defensive, they improved so much, that in three years time they found themselves in a capacity of giving <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> to their enemies in the open field; nor did they appear to be in any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> inferior either in courage <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> conduct: the war was therefore protracted, with various success, on both sides. At last, both consulted the oracle at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DELPHI">Delphi</a>; and received for answer, "that whoever should first dedicate 100 tripods in the temple of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> at Ithome, a stronghold of the Messenians, should be masters of the country." The inhabitants of Messenia, on hearing this, having no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> to make the tripods of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BRASS">brass</a>, fell to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> them out in wood; but before this could be accomplished, a Spartan having got into the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CITY">city</a> by stratagem, dedicated 100 little tripods of clay; which threw the Messenians into such despair, that they at last submitted to the Spartans. The new subjects of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SPARTA">Sparta</a> were treated with the utmost barbarity by these cruel tyrants; so that a new war commenced under Aristomenes, a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MAN">man</a> of unconquerable valour, and enthusiastically fond of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>. He perceived that the Argives and Arcadians, who were called the allies of the Lacedemonians, adhered to them only through fear of their power; but that in reality they hated them, and wished to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a> the injuries they had done them. To these Aristomenes applied; and receiving an answer conformable to his wishes, he engaged his countrymen unanimously to take up arms. About a year after the revolt began, and before either party had received any auxiliaries, the Spartans and Messenians met at a village called Deres, where an obstinate engagement ensued. Aristomenes was conceived to have performed more than mortal achievements: in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GRATITUDE">gratitude</a> therefore, respect being also had to his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a>, his countrymen unanimously saluted him <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KING">king</a>; which <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TITLE">title</a> he modestly waved, alleging, that he took up arms to set them free, and not to make himself <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a>: he consented, however, to accept the title of general, with a power of doing whatsoever he thought requisite for the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of the public. Knowing well the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> in which he lived, he resolved to intimidate the Spartans, by showing them what he was sure they would take for an ill <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OMEN">omen</a>. Disguising himself therefore, he went privately to the city, where, in the night, he hung up a shield on the wall of the temple of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MINERVA">Minerva</a>, with this inscription: Aristomenes dedicates this, out of the spoils of the Spartans, to the god. It was easily perceived that this war would be both <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">long</a> and bloody; the Lacedemonians therefore sent deputies to Delphi, to inquire of the oracle concerning its event: the answer they received was, That it behoved the Spartans to seek a leader from <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>. The Athenians, naturally envious of the Spartans, granted their request indeed, but in such a manner as manifested their spite; for they sent them for a general Tyrtaeus, a schoolmaster and poet, lame of one foot, and who was suspected to be a little out of his wits. But here their skill failed them; for this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a>, notwithstanding his despicable appearance, proved of great <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> to Sparta, teaching them how to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> good, and how to bear up under evil fortune. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> time, Aristomenes had drawn together a mighty <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, the Eleans, Argives, Sicyonians, and Arcadians, having sent troops to his assistance; the Spartans in this, as in the former war, having no ally but Corinth. The Spartan kings, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of their city, no sooner took the field, than, notwithstanding their inferiority in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, they offered the enemy battle, which Aristomenes readily accepted.—It was long, obstinate, and bloody; but in the end the Messenians were victorious, and the Lacedemonians put to flight with a great slaughter. It is scarce to be conceived how much the Spartans were struck with this defeat: they grew weary of the war, dissatisfied with their kings, disdained of their own power, and in a word sunk into a state of general uneasiness and want of spirit. It was now that the Athenian general convinced them, that he was capable of fulfilling all the promises of the oracle; he encouraged them by his poems, directed them by his councils, and recruited their broken armies with chosen men from among the Helotes. Aristomenes, on the other <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, acted with no less <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a> and vigour. He thought it not enough to restore the reputation of the Messenians, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he did not also restore their wealth and power: he therefore taught them to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> offensively against their enemies; and, entering the territories of Sparta, he took and plundered Phara, a considerable borough in Laconia, putting all such as made any resistance to the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>, carrying off at the same time an immense booty. This, however, was an injury which the Spartans could not brook with <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PATIENCE">patience</a>; they therefore sent immediately a body of forces to overtake the Messenians, which accordingly they did: but Aristomenes routed these pursuers, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to make a mighty slaughter of them, till <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUEL">fuel</a> time as he was disabled by having a spear thrust in his side, which occasioned his being carried out of the battle. His cure, which took up some time, being finished, he resolved to carry the war even to the gates of Sparta; and to that purpose raised a very great army: but, whether he found his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> impracticable, or was really diverted by some dream, he gave out, that <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CASTOR">Castor</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLLUX">Pollux</a>, with their sister Helena, had appeared to him, and commanded him to desist. A short time after this retreat, going with a small party to make an incursion, and attempting to take prisoners some women who were celebrating <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITES">rites</a> near Egila, a village in Laconia, those zealous matrons fell upon him and his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> with such fury, that they put them to flight, and took him prisoner; prisoner; however, he soon afterwards made his escape, and rejoined his forces. In the third year of the war, the Spartans with a great force entered Messenia, whither Arilochares king of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCADIA">Arcadia</a> was come, with a great body of troops, to the assistance of his allies: Arilochares therefore made no difficulty of fighting when the Spartans approached; but they entering privately into a negociation with Arilochares, engaged him with bribes and promises to betray his confederates. When the battle began, the deceitful Arcadian represented to the forces under his command the mighty danger they were in, and the great difficulty there would be of retreating into their own country, in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CASE">case</a> the battle should be lost: he then pretended, that the sacrifices were ominous; and, having terrified his Arcadians into the disposition of mind fitted to serve his purpose, he not only drew them off from both wings, but, in his flight, forced through the Messenian ranks, and put them too in confusion. Arilochares and his troops, however, drew themselves into <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> order, that they might defend themselves the best they could; and indeed they had need of all their valour and skill; for the Lacedemonians, who expected this event, immediately attacked and surrounded them on all sides. Fortune was, on this occasion, too powerful either for the courage or the conduct of the Messenians; so that, notwithstanding their utmost efforts, most of their army were cut to pieces, and amongst them the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>. Arilochares, with the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-POOR">poor</a> remains of his shattered forces, retired as well as he could; and, perceiving that it was now impossible to maintain the war against the Lacedemonians upon equal terms, he exhorted his countrymen to fortify mount Era, and to make the best dispositions possible for a long <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>. He likewise placed garrisons in Pylos and Methone on the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-coasts; and to these three places he gathered all the inhabitants, leaving the rest of Messenia to the mercy of the Spartans. They, on the other hand, looked on the war as now in a manner finished; for which reason they divided the lands among their citizens, and caused them to be carefully cultivated, while they besieged Era. But Arilochares quickly convinced them that the war was far from being over: he chose out of all the Messenians 300 men, with whom he ravaged all the adjacent country; carried off a prodigious booty; and, when Messenia could no longer supply the wants of his garrison, penetrated into Laconia, and bore away corn, wine, cattle, and whatever else was necessary to the subsistence of his countrymen shut up in Era: so that at last the Spartans were constrained to issue a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PROCLAMATION">proclamation</a>, forbidding the cultivation, not only of the Messenian territory in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, but also of Laconia in its vicinity; whereby they distressed themselves more than their enemies, inducing at last a famine in Sparta itself, which brought with it its usual attendant, sedition. Here again all things had gone wrong, if the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a> of the poet Tyrtæus had not supported the Spartan courage; nor was it without much difficulty that he influenced them to continue the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLOCKADE">blockade</a> of Era, and to maintain a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLYING">flying</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CAMP">camp</a> for the security of the country. Arilochares, in spite of all these precautions, committed terrible depredations with his small corps of 300 men. Amongst other places which he plundered, the city of Amyclæ was one; from whence he carried not only a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-RICHES">riches</a>, but also many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARRIAGES">carriages</a> laden with <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>. The kings of Sparta lying with their troops in its neighbourhood, as soon as they heard of this expedition, marched after Arilochares with the utmost diligence; and, as the Messenians were encumbered with their booty, came up with them before they could reach Era. In this situation of things, Arilochares, prompted rather by despair than prudence, disposed his troops in order of battle; and, notwithstanding they were so few, made a long and vigorous resistance against the whole Lacedemonian army. At length, however, numbers prevailed: the greatest part of the Messenians were slain on the spot; and Arilochares, with about 50 of his men who survived the slaughter, were taken prisoners; that chief having received so many wounds, that he was senseless when they carried him away. The Lacedemonians expressed the loudest joy at the sight of this illustrious captive; who for so many years, by his single abilities, had enabled his exhausted country to defend itself against the whole force of Sparta. When he was recovered of his wounds, they decreed him and all his fellow-prisoners to be thrown together into a deep cavern, which was the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> of the lowest kind of offenders. This judgment was executed with the utmost severity, excepting that Arilochares had leave to put on his armour. Three days he continued in this dismal <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, lying upon and covered over with dead bodies. The third <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, he was almost famished through want of food, and almost poisoned with the stench of corrupted carcases, when he heard a fox gnawing a body near him. Upon this he uncovered his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FACE">face</a>, and perceiving the fox <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> by him, he with one hand seized one of its hind-legs, and with the other defended his face, by catching hold of its jaw when it attempted to bite him. Following as well as he could his straggling guide, the fox at last thrust his head into a little hole; and Arilochares then letting go his leg, he soon forced his way through, and opened a passage to the welcome rays of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, from which the noble Messenian had been so long debarred. Feeble as he was, Arilochares wrought himself an outlet with his nails; and travelling by night with all the expedition he could, at length arrived safe at Era, to the great joy and amazement of his countrymen. When this news was first blazed abroad, the Spartans would have had it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> for a fiction; but Arilochares soon put the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of it out of doubt, by falling on the polls of the Corinthians, who, as allies of the Spartans, had a considerable body of troops before Era. Most of their officers, with a multitude of private men, he flew; pillaged their camp; and, in short, did so much mischief, that the Spartans, under the pretence of an approaching festival, agreed to a cessation of arms for 40 days, that they might have time to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BURY">bury</a> their dead. On this occasion, Arilochares for the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SECOND">second</a> time celebrated the hecatomphonia, or the sacrifice appointed for those who had killed 100 of the enemy with their own hands. He had performed the same before and after his second battle; and he lived to do it a third time: which must appear wonderful to the reader, when he is informed, that notwithstanding this truce, certain Cretan archers in the service of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SPAR">Spar</a>- Messenian tans seized Aristomenes as he was walking without the walls, and carried him away a prifoner. There were <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NINE">nine</a> of them in all; two of them immediately flew with the news to Sparta, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> remained to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> their <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PRIZE">prize</a>, whom they bound, and conducted to a lone cottage inhabited only by a widow and her <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a>. It fell out, that the young woman dreamt the night before, that she <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAW">saw</a> a lion without claws, bound, and dragged along by wolves; and that she having loosed his bonds, and given him claws, he immediately tore the wolves to pieces. As soon as Aristomenes came into the cottage, and her mother, who knew him, had told her who he was, she instantly concluded that her dream was fulfilled; and therefore plied the Cretans with drink, and, when they were asleep, took a poinard from one of them, cut the thongs with which Aristomenes was bound, and then put it into his hands. He presently verified her vision, by putting all his guards to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEATH">death</a>; and then carried her and her mother to Era, where, as a reward for her service, he married the young woman to his son Gorgus, then about 18 years of age. When Era had held out near eleven years, it fell into the hands of Sparta by an accident: the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a> of one Empiramus, a Spartan commander, driving his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MASTER">master</a>'s cattle to drink at the river Neda, met frequently with the wife of a Messenian, whom he engaged in an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMOUR">amour</a>. This woman gave him notice, that her husband's <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> was without the wall; so that he could come to it without danger, when the good man was abroad; and she likewise gave him intelligence when her husband was upon duty in the garrison. The Spartan failed not to come at the time appointed; but they had not been long in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a> before the husband returned, which put the house into great confusion: the woman, however, secured her gallant; and then let in her husband, whom she received in appearance with great joy, inquiring again and again by what excess of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOOD_FORTUNE">good fortune</a> she was blessed with his return. The innocent Messenian told her, that Aristomenes being detained in his bed by a wound, the soldiers knowing that he could not walk the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-ROUNDS">rounds</a>, had a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> to retire to their houses, to avoid the inclemency of the season. The Spartan no sooner heard this, than he crept softly out of doors, and hastened away to carry the news to his master. It happened, that the kings were at this time absent from the camp, and Empiramus had the chief command of the army. As soon as he received this information, he ordered his army to begin its <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MARCH">march</a>, though it rained excessively, and there was no <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MOON">moon</a>-light. The fellow guided them to the ford, and managed matters so well that they feigned all the Messenian posts: yet, after all, they were afraid to engage; darkness, an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>, heavy <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-RAIN">rain</a>, together with the dread of Aristomenes, keeping them quiet in the places they had seized. As soon as it was light, the attack began; and Era had been quickly taken, if only the men had defended it; but the women fought with such fury, and by their mingling in the fray, brought such an accretion of numbers, as made the event doubtful. Three days and two nights this desperate engagement lasted: at last, all hopes of preserving the city being lost, Aristomenes drew off his wearied troops. Early the fourth morning, he disposed the women and children in the centre, the Messenian youth in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FRONT">front</a> and rear, the less able men in the main body: himself commanded the van; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-REAR_GUARD">rear-guard</a> was brought up by Gorgus and Manticlus, the former the son of Aristomenes, the latter of Theocles, a Messenian of great merit, who fell with much <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> in this attack, fighting valiantly in the cause of his country. When all things were ready, Aristomenes caused the last <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARRIER">barrier</a> to be thrown open; and, brandishing his spear, marched directly towards the Spartan troops, in order to force a passage. Empiramus, perceiving his intent, ordered his men to open to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> and left, and fairly gave them a passage; so that Aristomenes marched off in triumph, as it were, to Arcadia. The Arcadians, when they heard that Era was taken, were very desirous of succouring their old confederates in this deep distress: they therefore invited their king Aristocrates to <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> them into Messenia. But he, corrupted by the Lacedemonians, persuaded them that it was too late; that the Messenians were all cut off; and that such a step would only expose them to the fury of the conquerors. When the thing appeared to be otherwise, and it was known that Aristomenes was on the frontiers of Arcadia, they went in crowds to carry him provisions, and to testify their readiness to afford him and those under his command all the assistance in their power. Aristomenes desired to be heard before a general <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a>; which being accordingly convoked, he there opened one of the boldest and best laid schemes recorded in history: he said, that he had yet 500 undaunted soldiers, who, at his command, would undertake any thing; that it was very probable most of the Spartans were employed in pillaging Era, and that therefore he determined to march and surprize Sparta; which appeared so sensible, that all the assembly loudly commended his great capacity and unshaken courage. Aristocrates, however, took care to betray him; having, by various pretences, retarded the execution of the project. The Arcadians, who began to suspect him, waited for and surprized the messengers as they came back. They took the letters from him, and read them openly in the assembly. The purport of them was, that they acknowledged his great kindness both now and in the battle; and promised, that the Lacedemonians would be grateful. As soon as the letters were read, the Arcadians fell to stoning their king, frequently calling upon the Messenians to assist them; which, however, they did not, waiting for Aristomenes's orders; who, far from triumphing in this spectacle, stood still, with his eyes fixed on the ground, which he wet with his tears, his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> pierced with sorrow to see a crowned head so shamefully and so deservedly put to death. The Arcadians afterwards erected a monument over him, with an inscription to perpetuate his infamy. As for the Messenians under the command of Gorgus and Manticlus, they passed over into <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>; where they founded the city of Messene, one of the most famous in the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>. Aristomenes remained, however, in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>; where he married all his daughters, except the youngest, to persons of great <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-RANK">rank</a>. A <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RHODES">Rhodes</a>, inquiring of the oracle at Delphi whom he should espouse, that his subjects might be happy under his posterity, was directed directed to marry the daughter of the most worthy of the Greeks; which answer was immediately understood to point at the virgin daughter of Aristomenes. Her therefore he demanded, and received; Aristomenes accompanying him back to his dominions, where he formed a scheme of uniting the Lydians and Medes against the Spartans, resolving with this view to go into Media, and to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-SARDIS">Sardis</a>; but while he meditated these great things, death surprised him, and thereby freed Lacedaemon from the most formidable enemy she ever had.

MESSIAH

Pages 427-427

a word signifying one anointed, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> installed into an office by anointing. It was usual among the Jews to anoint kings, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>-priests, and sometimes prophets, at the consecration or installment of them, to signify emblematically the mental qualifications necessary for discharging these offices. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAUL">Saul</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DAVID">David</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SOLOMON">Solomon</a>, and Joab, kings of Judah, received the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> anointing. <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AARON">Aaron</a> and his sons received the sacerdotal, and Eliash the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of Elijah received the prophetic anointing.—The name MESSIAH, Anointed, or Christ (Χριστός), was given to the kings and high-priests of the Jews. The patriarchs and prophets are also called by the name of Messiah, or the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>'s anointed. See 1 Sam. xii. 3, 5. 1 Chron. xvi. 22. Ps. cv. 15. But this name Messiah was principally and by way of eminence given by the Jews to their expected <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> Deliverer, whose coming they still vainly wait; and is a name the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> apply to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ, in whom the prophecies relating to the Messiah were accomplished. The sum of these prophecies is, That there should be a glorious person named Messiah, descended from <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABRAHAM">Abraham</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JACOB">Jacob</a>, who should be born at Bethlehem, of a virgin of the family of David, then in its decline, before the Jews ceased to be a people, while the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SECOND">second</a> temple was standing, and about 500 years after <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EZRA">Ezra</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a>; who, though appearing in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> circumstances, should be introduced by a remarkable forerunner, whose birth it should be to awaken the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EXPECTATION">expectation</a> of the people.
