That this illustrious person called Messiah should himself be eminent for the piety, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a>, and benevolence of his character, and the miraculous works he should perform: yet that, notwithstanding all this, he should be rejected and put to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEATH">death</a> by the Jews; but should afterwards be raised from the dead, and exalted to a glorious throne, on which he should through all generations continue to rule, at the same time making intercession for sinners. That great calamities should for the present be brought on the Jews for rejecting him: whereas the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of God should by his means be erected among the Gentiles, and diffuse itself even unto the ends of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>; wherever it came, destroying idolatry, and establishing true <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> and righteousness. In a word, That this glorious person should be regarded by all who believed in him as a divine teacher, an atoning sacrifice, and a royal governor: by means of whom God would make a covenant with his people, very different from that made with Israel of old; in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of which they should be restored to, and established in, the divine favour, and fixed in a state of perpetual <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a>. See Jesus Christ, and Christianity. The Jews, as was already observed, still wait for the coming of the Messiah, being infatuated with the notion of a temporal Messiah, who is to be a mighty conqueror, and to subdue all the world. Most of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> rabbins, according to Buxtorf, believe that the Messiah is already come, but that he keeps himself concealed, and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WILL">will</a> not manifest himself because of the sins of the Jews. Some of the Jews, however, in order to reconcile those prophecies that seem to contradict each other as to the character and condition of the Messiah, have had recourse to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HYPOTHESIS">hypothesis</a> of two Messiahs, who are yet to succeed each other; one in a state of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HUMILIATION">humiliation</a> and suffering; the other of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-GLORY">glory</a>, splendor, and power. The first, they say, is to proceed from the tribe of Ephraim, who is to fight against Gog, and to be slain by Annihilus, Zech. xii. 10. The second is to be of the tribe of Judah, and lineage of David, who is to conquer and kill Annihilus, and restore the kingdom of Israel, reigning over it in the highest glory and felicity. Jesus Christ asserts himself the Messiah. In St John iv. 25, the Samaritan woman says to Jesus, I know that when Messiah comes, who is called the Christ, he will tell us all things. Jesus answered her, I that speak to thee am he. There are several impostors, who have endeavoured to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> for Messiah, as Christ himself predicted. J. <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LENT">Lent</a>, a Dutchman, has written a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> De Pseudomessias, "Of False Messiahs." The first he mentions was one Barcochab, who appeared under the empire of Adrian. The last was rabbi Mordecai, who began to be talked of in 1682. A little before him, viz. in 1666, appeared Sabbethai Sebi, who was taken by the Turks, and turned Mahometan.

MESSINA

Pages 427-432

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, handsome, and strong <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>, and in the Val-di-Demona, with a citadel, several forts, a fine spacious harbour, and an archbishop's see. It is seated on the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-side, 110 miles east of Palermo, 200 south by east of Rome, and 180 south-east of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1° 50'. N. Lat. 38° 10'. The public buildings and the monasteries were numerous and magnificent, and it contained about 60,000 inhabitants; the harbour is one of the safest in the Mediterranean, and extremely deep; the viceroy of Sicily resides here six months in the year; and it was a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> trade in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, fruit, corn, and excellent wine, especially since it was declared a free port. This city in the beginning of the year 1783 suffered most dreadfully by the earthquakes, which shook great <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CALABRIA">Calabria</a> and Sicily to their foundations, overturned many rich and populous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, and buried thousands in their ruins: (see Calabria and Earthquake.)—The following account of Messina, as it stood before the above <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, is extracted from Mr Swinburne's Travels in Sicily. A large chain of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> presses upon the shore, and part of the city stands upon elevated ground. The mountains are many of them nobly wooded; the hills before them finely chequered with groves and fields. As the town runs in a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SWEEP">sweep</a> along the edge of a declivity, every <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> is seen to advantage, while the less noble parts are hidden by the Palazzata. This is a regular ornamental range of lofty houses, with 19 gates, answering to as many streets; it follows the semicircular <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BEND">bend</a> of the port for one <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MILE">mile</a> and five <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLES">poles</a>, and would have been the handsomest line of buildings in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> had the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> been completed; but a considerable part of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> is not finished, except merely in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FRONT">front</a> wall, and that seems to be in a very ruinous condition. Philibert Emmanuel of Savoy, viceroy of Sicily, in 1622 began this princely <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a>. Before it is a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> quay, decorated with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a> and fountains; ships of any burden can moor <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARAPET">parapet</a> in great depth of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WATER">water</a>. At the west extremity is a small fort and a gate; the other end is closed by the governor's <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> and the citadel, a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> pentagonal fortress, built on the point where the isthmus <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> braccio di San Raniero flows from the main <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LAND">land</a>. On this slip of low ground, which with the Palazzato forms the circular harbour of Messina, are placed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>-house (faroetto), and on the point the old castle of St Salvatore. The circumference of the port is four miles: it probably owes its formation to an earthquake, which opened an immense chasm, and then filled it with water. Near the light-house is a kind of whirlpool in the sea, known as the Charybdis of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>. The inner part of Messina is dirty, though it contains a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of neat churches and large substantial dwellings. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> is Gothic, enriched with Saracenic mosaics on the altars and shrines; the front of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> altar is particularly splendid: Gagini has embellished the pulpit and some tombs with excellent specimens of his art.—In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURY">treasury</a> of this <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> is preserved the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PALLADIUM">palladium</a> of Messina, a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> from the Virgin <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> to its citizens (a). This is the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TITLE">title</a> upon which the Messinese build their pretensions to pre-eminence over the whole <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, nay over the whole world; to its virtues and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PATRONAGE">patronage</a> they <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATTRIBUTE">attribute</a> every piece of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOOD_FORTUNE">good fortune</a>, and to their own unworthiness all sinister events that have befallen them. The authenticity of this epistle has been seriously impugned, and of course vigorously defended by many Sicilian divines and disputators. No 211. There is another church in this city that deserves particular notice, not so much on account of its <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a> or ornaments, as for its being the last refuge of the Greek liturgy, which was once the predominant <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of the island, but gradually abolished by different conquerors. It is dedicated to the Virgin Mary de Graphico, or of the Letter, which denomination may perhaps have furnished Lafcaris with the idea of his letter. It is known at present by the name of la Cattolica. According to the Greek canons, the entrance of monastic churches was reciprocally forbidden to each <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SEX">sex</a>, and the cathedrals were the only places of worship where a daily sacrifice was offered up by the bishop and clergy, and where both men and women were present at the same <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a>, but in different parts of the church. From this general admittance the building acquired the title of Catholic or universal. Messina is all paved with <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LAVA">lava</a>, cut into large flags of two feet <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>; a material which the vicinity of lavas render it easy to procure, and which being very hard resists friction better than any other. During a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of ages, notwithstanding the various revolutions and calamities to which it has been exposed, this city has still maintained its original situation; while most other cities have shifted their ground more or less from the place where they were first founded. But its situation enjoys advantages which have still tempted such of its inhabitants as escaped from the ravages of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WAR">war</a> and the desolation of earthquakes, to prefer it to every other spot, however delightful or secure. It is of very ancient origin; it has been under many different races of monarchs; and its name has been repeatedly changed: It has been at different times called Zancle, Naxarina, Messina. Its first name Zancle, which in the old <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> of Sicily meant "a fickle," alluding, as some authors suppose, to the form of the port; or, according to others, to (a) The story is as follows: After St Paul had made some stay at Messina (a circumstance of his travels unnoticed by St Luke), the Messinese prevailed upon him to return to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a> with an embassy of four persons sent by the city to the Virgin Mary. Their excellencies were graciously received by her, and brought back a letter written with her own <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HAND">hand</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> tongue, which St Paul translated into Greek. By the irruption of the Saracens this invaluable <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a> was lost, and utterly forgotten till the year 1467, when Constantine Lafcaris, a refugee Greek, found a copy of it, and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> it into Latin, made it known to the citizens, and then to all the Catholic world. Its authenticity is now so well established at Messina, that Regna the historian candidly acknowledges, that whoever was to confess even a doubt on the subject in that city would be treated as an <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-INFIDEL">infidel</a>. This curious epistle is conceived in these terms:—<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MARIA">Maria</a> Virgo Joachim filia, Dei humillima Christi Jesu crucifixi Mater, ex tribu Iuda filiae <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DAVID">David</a>, Messinensibus omnibus salutem, et Dei patris omnipotentis benedictionem. Vos omnes fide magna legatos ac nuncios per publicum documentum <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AD">ad</a> nos missae confest. Filium nostrum Dei genitum Deum et hominem esse fatemini, et in coelum <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> suam resurrectionem ascendisse, Pauli apostoli electi praedicatione mediante viam veritatis agnoscentes. Ob quod vos et ipsam civitatem bene-dicimus cujus perpetuum protecitricem nos esse volumnus. Anno filii nostri XLII. Indict. I. III. Nonas Junii, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LUNA">Luna</a> XXVII. feria V. ex Hyerofolymis. Thus translated:—"The Virgin Mary, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Joachim, most humble mother of God, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ crucified, of the tribe of Juda and the family of David, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> and the blessing of God the Father Almighty to all the people of Messina. Out of the abundance of your <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>, you have, in consequence of a public deliberation, sent a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEPUTATION">deputation</a> to me; and since you acknowledge that my Son is both God and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MAN">man</a>, and that he ascended into heaven after his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-RESURRECTION">resurrection</a>, as you have learned from the preaching of St Paul the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APOSTLE">apostle</a>, I give my blessing to you and all your city, and agree to become your protectress. In the 42nd year of my Son, the 1st of the Indiction, the 3rd <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JUNE">June</a>, and the 27th of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MOON">moon</a>, at Jerusalem." Not to dwell upon the astronomical blunders in these dates, let it suffice to observe, that Lafcaris was not aware that Denis the Little, a Syrian monk in the 6th century, was the first who made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the era that commences at our Saviour's birth. the fertility of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. Allured by the advantages of its situation, the Cumæans, a commercial and enterprising people, invaded the island and drove the Siculi from this settlement; they were in their turn overpowered by a band of Samian adventurers, who made way for a colony of citizens of Messene, and under these masters it changed its name to Messina. Their <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> was of short <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DURATION">duration</a>; for in the 286th year before Christ it was destroyed by the Mamertines, a warlike unprincipled <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATION">nation</a> inhabiting the south part of Brutium. These <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> being received into Messina on their return to <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SYRACUSE">Syracuse</a>, where they had served as mercenaries in the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> of Agathocles, took an opportunity of massacring the inhabitants and usurping their possessions. The city was now called Mamertina: and, in order to support themselves against the resentment of the Sicilian powers, the Mamertines implored the protection of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, who, eager to extend their dominion beyond the limits of Italy, and jealous of the growing power of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CARTHAGE">Carthage</a>, made no scruple to succour these afflatus with a consular army. This step brought on the first Punic war. The Mamertines reaped no other fruit from the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a> but a more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SLAVERY">slavery</a>; for such was the real <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of their connection with Rome, whatever name it might be disguised under. Messina was, however, always distinguished by particular attentions and favours from the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SENATE">senate</a>; and, excepting a short period during the wars of the triumvirate, appears to have tasted all the sweets of Roman prosperity, without partaking of the bitter draughts of adversity. Its fate, in the ruin of the empire, was similar to that of the rest of Sicily. In 829 Messina fell into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the Saracens, but obtained very honourable terms of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CAPITULATION">capitulation</a>; for half the city was left to the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>, where they were to be governed by their own laws, and profess their own <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> undisturbed. In the other resided the bey of one of the five provinces into which the Arabian conquerors had divided the island. Notwithstanding this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDULGENCE">indulgence</a>, Messina was the first to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> off the yoke in 1037, when George Maniaces landed an army of Greeks and Normans on the shore of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FARO">Faro</a>. It afterwards held out against the whole Muslim force, till the feeble state of a distracted empire shut out all hopes of assistance from Constantinople. This unfortunate city then opened its gates to the army of the caliph, and felt very severely the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of his resentment, but it did not long groan under the yoke; for in less than 20 years Roger the Norman took it by surprise and delivered it from Mahometan oppression. During the crusade our Richard Cœur de Lion and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> Augustus <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KING">king</a> of France wintered here in their way to <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PALESTINE">Palestine</a>; a sojourn marked by continual quarrels, conflagration, and bloodshed. The Messinians were particularly tardy in entering into the national <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSPIRACY">conspiracy</a> of 1282, but afterwards exceeded the rest of the insurgents in deeds of cruelty: This and the importance of their situation singled them out for the first objects of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a>’s vengeance. He invested their city very closely, and declared so openly his determination to refuse all terms whatever to the besieged, that they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAW">saw</a> no hopes of safety but in an obstinate <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>. Their courage, perseverance, and sufferings, were excessive; at length their strength and resources began to fail rapidly, and every circumstance seemed to denounce their speedy destruction, when Roger Lauria appeared off the harbour with the Aragonian fleet, forced the king to retire with precipitation across the straits, and in his flight defeated and destroyed his naval armament. Robert, grandson of Charles I., also made a fruitless attack; but in the disturbed reign of Frederick III., Messina was delivered up to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> king of Naples and his consort <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> Joan, who entered it in triumph. In a few years it returned to its former possessors. The year 1672 was remarkable for the revolt of the Messinians.—They threw off the Spanish yoke, and swore <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALLEGIANCE">allegiance</a> to Louis XIV., king of France. They were for some time vigorously assisted by the French; but before the Spaniards had gained the least advantage to excite any hopes of recovering so valuable a possession, Louis found himself necessitated from motives of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESERT">desert</a> his new subjects, and leave them to the mercy of their old incensed masters. The horror of being thus abandoned, and the chastisement inflicted by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, broke the fierce spirit of the Messinians; they were still stunned with the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-REMEMBRANCE">remembrance</a> and effects of this blow, when the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLAGUE">plague</a> in 1743 was introduced from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEVANT">Levant</a> and swept away more than half the inhabitants. From this chain of calamities, the opulence, trade, and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> of Messina, have been gradually sinking; and unless very favourable circumstances happen, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WILL">will</a> every year <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> lower. The number of its inhabitants does not now exceed 30,000. The following particulars are added from M. Houel, who visited this city since the late earthquakes, which completed its destruction. On the front of the cathedral there is a square, which, though not regular, is far from being <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a>. This was not the largest square in Messina before its overthrow; but it was the most elegant, the most splendidly adorned, and the best frequented. There stands in this square an equestrian statue of Charles II. of Spain, in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BRONZE">bronze</a>, which has been spared by the earthquake. It stands on a marble pedestal, in the middle of the square. Opposite to this statue is an elegant marble fountain, ornamented with a variety of figures, representing men and other animals, all of them spouting out water in great abundance; which used, in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>, to spread an agreeable and refreshing coolness over the square, that induced <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> to assemble here. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">Seven</a> streets terminated here. The cathedral forms a part of the square. It is dedicated to the blest Virgin; the occasion of which has been already mentioned. There is an anniversary feast celebrated in Messina, which is called the feast of the Letter. A lock of the Virgin’s <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>, which she sent to the Messenians at the same time with the letter, is carried through the city in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PROCESSION">procession</a> in a crystal vessel. She made also a present of her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> to the Messenian deputies. It is placed over the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TABERNACLE">tabernacle</a>. None but the canons of the cathedral are permitted to touch, or take up on their shoulders, the silver shrine in which the crystal vessel with the Virgin’s hair is deposited. Eight of those canons, with mitres on their heads, bear this shrine in the procession. The canopy suspended over it is supported by six senators in their robes. The picture and the hair are shown to strangers. This procession and the other <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> ceremonies of this festival are followed by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> races. The spirits of the people being already elevated by their religious exercises, they engage with amazing eagerness in these and the other diversions with which they are accompanied; a tumultuous joy reigns over the city; and the evening concludes with illuminations and fireworks. The ships in the harbour pay the citizens the compliment of entertaining them with a discharge of their guns on the occasion. Through a square called the Square of the Great <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HOSPITAL">Hospital</a>, runs a large and impetuous <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TORRENT">torrent</a>, the Porto delle Legni. It is precipitated from those lofty mountains which overlook this city on the south side. The channel which it has cut out for itself is at times entirely full. It would, on such occasions, overflow the square and other parts of the city, were it not confined by walls which have been built on both sides to prevent such accidents.—Another stream of a similar origin, called the Torrent of La Bocetta, runs through another part of the city; it is also confined within the walls to prevent it from overflowing. The Square of St John of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MALTA">Malta</a> is one of the largest in Messina. In the middle of this square is a fine marble fountain, ornamented with a variety of sculptured figures and jets d'eau. Beside the fountain there used to stand a large reservoir for horses to drink out of. In the time of the annual festivals, there used to be exhibited on the waters of the reservoir a galley, or rather a fictitious representation of a galley, with galley-slaves, soldiers, officers, and a commander on board, all in arms, and the galley properly equipped as a ship of war. This galley was decorated with great art; and by night the sails, and every other suitable part, were hung with lamps, which illumined it in a very splendid manner. Everything around was so artificially disposed, that when the fire-works were played off, the spectator was led to think, though he perceived only one galley, that the noise which he heard was produced by a naval <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMBAT">combat</a>; and that the other ships were concealed from his view by the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a> occasioned by the guns and fire-works. This, when properly conducted, was a noble spectacle. The senate repaired thither from the cathedral, attended with a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> and a numerous company. In one carriage sat six senators, the governor of the city, and sometimes the archbishop. It was exceedingly large, and drawn by six <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WHITE">white</a> horses very richly harnessed. Other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARRIAGES">carriages</a> followed, with the train who attended the governor and the senators. Almost all festivals owe their origin to some extraordinary event, or some singular story either true or false. It is said, that when the splendor with which the feast of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSUMPTION">Assumption</a> de la <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BARA">Bara</a> was celebrated at Messina, first began to attract foreigners to the city, on that occasion such crowds repaired thither as to alarm the inhabitants with the fears of a famine: But one year, when the number of strangers was greater than usual at the time of this festival, the magistrates were very much at a loss how to supply them with <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>; and at length, every other resource failing, no hopes of relief remained but from the kindness of the Blessed Virgin. Fervent prayers were addressed to their patroness; and next morning by day-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> three brigantines appeared entering the harbour with full sails. They proved to be loaded with corn. It was eagerly purchased; and the people of the city halted to appease their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HUNGER">hunger</a>. But when they came after refreshing themselves to pay the corn-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, neither ships nor merchants could be found. After their first emotions of surprise had subsided, they naturally concluded that such a reasonable supply must undoubtedly be a present from the Virgin, who, being pleased with the zeal of her Messenian votaries, and desirous to prevent the concourse of strangers who attended the festival from diminishing, had interposed in this miraculous manner to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-SAVE">save</a> them from the distresses of famine. A new festival was celebrated in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GRATITUDE">gratitude</a> to their generous benefactress. Three small vessels of silver were made, and dedicated to the Virgin in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of the event; and these are at present used as lamps in the cathedral. The senate likewise decreed, that the clergy should pay annually a small tax, to be laid out in constructing a small gallery to swim on the fountain, and in defraying the expenses of the fire-works. The profits of the clergy are so considerable on the occasion of the festival, that they may be supposed to pay the tax with great cheerfulness. In Messina, as in the other cities of Sicily, the women wrap themselves in a large <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> mantle above the rest of their dress. The stuffs are richer or plainer according to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-RANK">rank</a> and circumstances. People who are not rich enough to have fine cloaths of their own, hire them at so much an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>. There are women who make a livelihood by lending out their cloaths. The mantle covers the wearer from head to foot.—It reduces the old and the young, the ill-shaped and the handsome, pretty much to an equality in point of appearance. This must naturally appear very unfavourable to the influence of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>. But yet, on proper occasions, at church or in a public walk, the ladies of Messina find means to open and adjust the mantle so as to display all their beauties of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FACE">face</a> and shape, and to attract the affections of lovers, perhaps more powerfully than <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> their dress were suited to display their charms in a more ostentatious manner. Between Messina and the tower of Faro there stands a small church called the Madonna of the Grotto. It was anciently a temple of a round structure, and ornamented with columns like the temple of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> at Rome. Modern columns now supply the place that was occupied by the ancient. There are large niches in the rock adjoining to the temple, which are thought to be of equal antiquity. These contain no sculptured figures; but in Pagan times they might possibly contain some. Messina being situated between mount Etna and the gulph of Charybdis, and being likewise at no great distance from the volcanoes of Lipari and Stromboli, must have been in all ages liable to suffer by earthquakes. Such terrible events, however, appear to have been more unfrequent in ancient than in modern times, and have actually alarmed the present <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> oftener than any other. In the 1693 a fourth part of the cities of Sicily was destroyed by an earthquake. Messina merely felt the shock; all its buildings, however, suffered. In the year 1742 it suffered another equally violent. A plague which followed in 1743 retarded the repairs necessary after the earthquake. In the year year 1780 this city <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a>, for more than six months, to suffer from a new earthquake. Were the state of the elements, previous to these dreadful events, carefully examined, it might perhaps be found to undergo certain changes which might be considered as prognosticating them. The autumn of the year 1782 was unusually <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COLD">cold</a> and rainy. Fahrenheit's thermometer was often as low as 56 degrees. The succeeding winter was dry; and the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-MERCURY">mercury</a> never fell under 25 degrees; And, what is uncommon in that season, storms were now and then observed to arise from the west. The pilots in the channel observed that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIDES">tides</a> no longer rose at the usual periods, and the gulph of Charybdis raged with extraordinary fury. On the 4th of February 1783, the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> was heavy and calm; the sky obscured with thick <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a> seemingly all in a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FLAME">flame</a>. About half after twelve at noon, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> began to shake with a dreadful noise. The shocks continually increased, and became at length so violent as to open the ground, and to overturn in two or three minutes a considerable part of the buildings. A long white cloud appeared to the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west; and soon after another, very dark, in the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of the heavens. The latter in a moment spread over the whole horizon, and deluged the city with <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-RAIN">rain</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HAIL">hail</a>, accompanied with dreadful claps of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-THUNDER">thunder</a>. The inhabitants fled in the utmost terror to the fields and the ships in the harbour. From mid-day till five in the afternoon the earthquake continued almost without interruption. The shocks then became somewhat less frequent. The cries of the dying; the shrieks of those who were half-buried under the ruins; the wild terror with which others, who were still able, attempted to make their escape; the despair of fathers, mothers, and husbands, bereft of those who were dearest to them; then formed altogether a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> of horror, such as can but seldom occur in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the calamities of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-RACE">race</a>. Amid that awful scene, instances of the most heroic courage and the most generous affection were displayed. Mothers, regardless of their own safety, rushed into every danger to snatch their children from <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. Conjugal and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FILIAL">filial</a> affection prompted deeds not less desperate and heroic. But no sooner did the earthquake cease, than the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-POOR">poor</a> wretches who had escaped began to feel the influence of very different passions. When they returned to visit the ruins, to seek out the situation of their fallen dwellings, to inquire into the fate of their families, to procure food and collect some remains of their former fortunes—such as found their circumstances the most wretched became suddenly animated with rage, which nothing but wild despair could inspire. The distinction of ranks, and the order of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> were disregarded, and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> eagerly violated. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MURDER">Murder</a>, rapine, and lawless robbery, reigned among the smoking ruins. About one in the morning another shock of the earthquake was felt, which overturned most of the houses that were still standing. Most of those whom want, or avarice, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a>, still detained among the ruins, now shared the same fate with their friends whom the former shocks had buried under them. The succeeding day scarce alleviated the distress of this dismal night: the few wretches who still survived found themselves destitute of every <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a>. At length order was in some degree re-established; and in two days after every person was supplied at least with some small portion of the necessaries for subsistence. None yet thought of returning to take up their abode among the ruins. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMON">common</a> people fixed their residence on the plain of Porto Salvo, near the town of Salerno. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOBLES">nobles</a>, magistrates, and merchants, took up their abode on another plain, on the other side of the stream Porta de Legno; the soldiers at Terra Nuova. Some violent shocks which were again felt on the 7th of February and the 28th of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MARCH">March</a> completed the destruction of the city. The corn magazines, however, escaped without damage; and the public ovens and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AQUEDUCTS">aqueducts</a> were but little injured. From these facts it may perhaps be inferred, that had not the houses of Messina been, in general, hastily built at the first, and afterwards carelessly repaired, fewer of them would have been overthrown by the earthquake. The neighbouring villages having suffered but little, were the first to relieve the remaining inhabitants of Messina in their distresses. Maltese galleys for some days supplied necessaries to the poor and the sick with a generosity which merits the highest praise. They brought surgeons and whatever was needful for the cure of the wounded. The supplies sent by the king of France were refused, for what reason we know not. What money was needed for the support of the people was taken from the treasury of the city of Messina; for what the king of Naples sent was seized and spent by the garrison. It is said that not more than 800 or 900 persons perished by this earthquake. The sea during that convulsion of the land was slightly agitated in the harbour. Farther out the sea was more violently agitated; but none of the ships in the harbour were dashed to pieces. The waters rose so high as to be injurious in a very considerable degree to Pharo, as well as along the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SCYLLA">Scylla</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BAGNARA">Bagnara</a>. This earthquake was not of a momentary duration, like that by which <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LISBON">Lisbon</a> was destroyed, and like many others: for more than sixty days, from the 5th of February to the beginning of April, Messina continued to be shaken; and in that time felt more than 200 shocks. And ever after that period the alarm was again and again renewed. Not only the magistrates, the soldiers, and the people, but the priests likewise, with their tabernacle and altar, retired to the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARRACKS">barracks</a>. The nuns, too, deserted their cloister, and sought a retreat without the walls. Some of them confined themselves to the gardens of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONVENTS">convents</a>; others mixed indiscriminately with the people. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> damage which the public buildings within the city suffered was the fall of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DOME">dome</a> of the church of Purgatory. Only the walls were left standing; and even these had suffered considerably. One half of the steeple of the cathedral was beaten to the ground. The magazines of Porto Franco were likewise very much shattered. The fort of St Salvator, being built on an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> foundation, the side next the sea is there fallen <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DOWN">down</a>; but on the other side, where it is founded. founded on a rock, it has stood unmoved by all the shocks of the earthquake. On the 5th of February, when the earthquake was more violent than at any time afterwards, a strong smell of sulphur was felt. The earth was affected somewhat in the same way as if it had been borne up on a fluid; and seemed to reel with the shocks much like a ship tossed with the waves. This tremulous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> was felt all over Sicily; but towards <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PHAROS">Pharos</a> it became weaker. On the following days the sky was cloudy; the mountains of Sicily and the shores of Calabria continued covered with a thick fog like smoke. North and north-east winds raged with the most violent impetuosity. The disastrous year of this earthquake was scarce concluded, the chasms which it had opened in the ground were still yawning, and the poor inhabitants of the adjacent country still trembled with terror, when the elements again renewed their fury to ravage this miserable land. On Tuesday the 6th of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1784, about sunrise, the <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> began to blow softly from the north-east. The sea gradually swelled, rose beyond its <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a> with rapid impetuosity, overflowed the quay of Messina, and lashed with its billows the ruins of the Palazzata. It loosened and displaced many of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-STONES">stones</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MOLE">mole</a>, spread over the whole street, and attacked the pedestals of the statues which had been spared by the earthquake, and still stood firm among the ruins. The same furious wind which swelled the sea in so extraordinary a manner, ravaged the whole coast from Messina all the way to Syracuse.

MESSUAGE

Pages 432-432

MESSAGIUM, in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LAW">law</a>, a dwelling-<a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, with some <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LAND">land</a> adjoining assigned for its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>. By the name of messuage may a garden, shop, mill, cottage, chamber, cellar, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> the like, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a>.—In Scotland, messuage denotes what is called in England the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MANOR">manor</a> house, viz., the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> dwelling-house within any <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARONY">barony</a>.

META

Pages 432-432

in the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CIRCUS">circus</a>, was a pile of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-STONES">stones</a> of a pyramidal form, intended as a boundary of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-STADIUM">stadium</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> chariot-course.—When the meta was passed the seventh <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-RACE">race</a> was concluded. The greatest art and management were required in avoiding the meta, and yet going as near it as possible. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> they went too near, they were in the greatest danger of breaking the chariot to pieces; and if they took too <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LARGE">large</a> a circuit in the turn, they gave their rivals an opportunity of getting within them, besides losing a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of ground. The boundary of the Grecian stadium, or course, was called ἐπίστας τετράκοντα πόδια and ἐπίστας γεγαμένης; to which last name Horace probably alludes in calling <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, “ultima linea rerum.” The meta at Rome were first of wood, afterwards of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-STONE">stone</a>; but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Claudius made them of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, or rather gilded them. In the Roman circus there were two metas, one at the entrance of the course, and the other at the end of it. An <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-EGG">egg</a> was placed upon the top of the meta.

METACARPUS

Pages 432-432
or Metacarpium, (from μετά behind, and χάρπος, hand), in anatomy, that part of the hand between the wrist and the fingers. See Anatomy, no 55.

METAGITNION

Pages 432-432

the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of the Athenian year, answering to the latter <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">part</a> of our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> and the beginning of August, and so called from metagittia, a festival in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a>, which was kept in it. The Boeotians called this month panemus, and the Syracusans, carnius.

METAL

Pages 432-434

in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol12.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a simple, ponderous, shining, fixed, opake body, that fuses and becomes fluid by fire, and by <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COLD">cold</a> coagulates and hardens into a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MASS">mass</a>, capable of being distended under the hammer. See <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-METALLURGY">Metallurgy</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a>. Metal, in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HERALDRY">heraldry</a>. There are two <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-METALS">metals</a> used in heraldry, by way of colours, viz. <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> and silver, in blazon called <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> and argent. In the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> of arms these metals are represented by <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WHITE">white</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>, which are the natural colours of those metals. In engraving, gold is expressed by dotting the coat, &c., all over; and silver, by leaving it quite blank. It is a general rule in heraldry, never to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLACE">place</a> metal upon metal, nor <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> upon colour: so that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the field be of one of the metals, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> must be of some colour; and if the field be of any colour, the bearing must be one of the metals. Metals, Solution of. See Chemistry-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. On this subject Mr Keir has some curious observations in the Philosophical Transactions for 1793. He takes notice, that the word solution has two meanings; one expressive of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of dissolving, as when we say that “solution is a chemical operation;” and the other, when it is put for the substance dissolved in the acid, as “a solution of silver in the nitrous acid.” To avoid confusion, therefore, he uses the word solution to express the substance dissolved, together with its solvent; <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DISSOLUTION">dissolution</a> being the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TERM">term</a> made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of when the act of dissolving is meant. He continues the use of the terms phlogisticated and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEPHLOGISTICATED">dephlogisticated</a> to express certain states of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ACIDS">acids</a>, but without reference to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> of any kind. In dissolving metals, our author observes, that the properties of the several acids have been investigated with considerable success; and even one <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a>, viz. that of spirit of nitre and spirit of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AQUA">aqua</a> regis, is well known on account of its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of dissolving gold. A vast field, however, yet remains for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a> in the other acids, whether mixed together, or possessing various degrees of concentration, temperature, or phlogistication. Thus, though no two substances are more frequently in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of chemists than vitriolic acid and nitre, yet the properties of the mixture had not been investigated before Mr Keir made his experiments; and upon <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> he found, that this mixture possessed certain properties which neither the vitriolic nor nitrous acids singly possess. The results of his experiments on this subject are as follow. 1. In a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">long</a>-necked retort containing 1400 grains <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a>, 100 grains of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OIL">oil</a> of vitriol of the specific gravity of 1.844 were put along with 100 grains of pure nitre, and the salt dissolved in the acid by means of a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WATER">water</a>-bath. On applying a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, the silver began to dissolve, and the solution assumed a purple or violet colour; but no <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> was extricated. An end was put to the operation (by the rushing in of the water used in the pneumatic <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPARATUS">apparatus</a> applied to the retort) when 39 grains of silver had been dissolved. 2. To 100 grains of nitre previously dissolved in an equal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of vitriolic acid, 200 grains of standard silver were added; of which 92 grains were dissolved without the production of any air or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAS">gas</a>; but upon pouring in 200 grains of water into the retort, a violent effervescence took place, and 3100 measures of nitrous gas were thrown off; and on adding 200 grains more, a farther emission of 600 grain measures ensued; but no more was emitted on the addition of more water, nor did any farther dissolution of the metal take place than two grains. The same phenomena took place in various proportions, according to the different quantities of acid and metal made use of. On substituting tin for silver, none of the metal was dissolved or calcined by mixtures in the proportion of 200 grain measures of oil of vitriol to as much nitre, nor by 200 of the vitriolic acid to 150 of nitre; but with a proportion of 200 measures of the acid to 100 grains of nitre, the tin soon began to be acted upon, and dissolved through the liquor; but no gas was extricated till the digestion had been <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in boiling water for two hours. The tin was still only calcined, not dissolved; 8500 grain measures of nitrous gas were extricated, and 73 grains of the metal reduced to a white powder. On pouring into the retort 200 grains of fresh water, a new effervescence took place betwixt the water and white powder, by which 4600 grain measures of nitrous gas were thrown off. The <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of the menstruum was greatly promoted by augmenting the quantity of oil of vitriol, and adding water to the mixture. By this mixture quicksilver was calcined to a grey powder, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NICKEL">nickel</a> was also partly calcined and partly dissolved; but no other metal was much affected, tho' the surfaces of some of them were tarnished. The mixtures themselves were very apt to congeal, especially where there was a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LARGE">large</a> proportion of nitre; and their properties are much altered by the addition of water. Thus, in their concentrated state, they do not act upon <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-IRON">iron</a>; but by adding water, it acquires the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of acting upon that metal, and in different degrees according to the quantity of water added. Thus, by adding two measures of the compound acid to one of water, the liquor is rendered capable of calcining iron, and forming with it a white powder, but without any effervescence. An equal <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> of water produces effervescence; and with a larger proportion of water the iron acquires a yellow or <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> colour, such as phlogisticated nitrous acid acquires from iron, or communicates to a solution of martial vitriol in water. Dilution with water renders this compound acid capable of dissolving <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COPPER">copper</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ZINC">zinc</a>, neither of which it <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WILL">will</a> touch in its concentrated state. From this property of the compound acid not dissolving copper, but very readily silver, we have an easy method of separating the two metals from each other. This might be useful in many <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CASES">cases</a>; but is particularly so in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BIRMINGHAM">Birmingham</a>, where <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> numbers of copper vessels covered with silver are manufactured. Thus there are always a great <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTINGS">cuttings</a> or small bits called scraps, which are of no use but to separate the two metals from one another. The easiest method of doing this is an object of some <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>. Two methods have been generally practised for this purpose: one is by melting the whole mass of metal with <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, and separating them by means of eluation and testing; the other is by dissolving both metals in vitriolic acid, and then separating the solution of copper from the vitriol of silver. The disadvantage of the former method is, the quantity of lead and copper wasted; and of the latter, that of vitriolic acid. The virtues of a mixture of oil of vitriol and nitre were some <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a> ago communicated by Mr Keir to an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a> at Birmingham; and it is now generally used there to effect the separation of the two metals. The method of using it is very easy; nothing more being requisite than to put the pieces of plated metal into a glazed earthen <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAN">pan</a>, and to pour upon them some of the acid liquor, which may contain about one <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-POUND">pound</a> of nitre to eight or ten of oil of vitriol. Stir them about, and assist the action by an heat from 100 to 200 of Fahrenheit's <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-SCALE">scale</a>. When the liquor is nearly saturated, the silver may be precipitated in the form of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LUNA">luna</a> cornea by common salt; or it may be obtained in its metallic form by adding to the liquor some pieces of copper, and as much water as will enable it to act upon them. He is of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that the menstruum may be useful in all separations of silver from other metals. The name he seems to wish to impose upon it is aqua <a class="xref" href="../1815/vol0.html#article-REGINA">regina</a>. The following are the conclusions drawn from the experiments on these mixtures by our author. 1. A mixture of the vitriolic and nitrous acids dissolves silver plentifully. 2. It acts upon tin, and mostly calcines it, as well as <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-MERCURY">mercury</a> and nickel; having little or no action upon other metals. 3. The quantity of gas produced while the metal is dissolving, is greater, relatively to the quantity of the metal dissolved, when the proportion of nitre to the vitriolic acid is small, than when it is large; and when the metals are dissolved by mixtures containing much nitre with a small production of gas, the solution itself, or the metallic salt formed in it, yields abundance of gas when mixed with water. 4. Dilution with water renders the concentrated mixture less capable of dissolving silver, but more so of acting upon other metals. 5. This mixture of highly concentrated vitriolic and nitrous acids, acquires a purple or violet colour when phlogisticated, either by the addition of inflammable substances as fulphur, or by its action on metals, or by very strong <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IMPREGNATION">impregnation</a> of oil of vitriol with nitrous gas. 6. By means of this phlogistication the mixture acquired a property of dissolving, though in small quantities, copper, iron, zinc, and regulus of cobalt. 7. Water expels a vast quantity of nitrous gas from a concentrated mixture of vitriolic acid and nitre impregnated with it; but this fluid unites with a mixture of oil of vitriol and nitre without any considerable effervescence. By adding to the mixture of oil of vitriol and nitre a solution of common salt, a very powerful aqua regis is formed, capable of dissolving gold and platinum; and which, which, though perfectly free from all metallic <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, acquires at once a deep yellow colour. Dry common salt added to the concentrated mixture produces an effervescence, but no yellow colour. [Merged from <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PROCESS">PROCESS</a> VII, p.450] Silver and gold may be extracted from their ores by mercury. A new method of extracting the precious metals by means of amalgamation with mercury has lately been introduced into Germany. The <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATTRACTION">attraction</a> between these has indeed been known from the most remote antiquity: Vitruvius informs us, that by this means gold might be recovered from <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-EMBROIDERY">embroidery</a> and old cloths; and Pliny mentions the gilding of brafs and other metals by the same means. From time immemorial mercury has been made use of in the streaming for gold, in order to purify and collect together the gold dust which is dispersed in the sands; and almost all nations who practise this use the same process. The gold sand, after being washed, is triturated with quicksilver, and the superfluous metal separated by draining through <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>. By the miners it was used in a similar manner; the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-STONES">stones</a> containing gold being first pounded and then triturated in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILLS">mills</a> along with the mercury. But it was soon found, that in these mills there was a large quantity left behind in the residuum, so that it was necessary to subject what was left to the action of fire; on which account the mills were deemed unnecessary, and are now almost everywhere disused. The process of extracting gold and silver by amalgamation, however, was looked upon to be essentially deficient, by reason of an opinion which prevailed among the chemists, that mercury could not dissolve either of these metals except in their pure and perfect state; whence it was supposed, that a great quantity which fire could have extracted was left by the mercury. This opinion was supported by the most celebrated metallurgists, as Schlutter, Gellert, Wallerius, Silver and Kramer; whence it became generally believed, that amalgamation would never answer in great operations. But of late Baron Inigo Born has not only demonstrated that this can be done to great advantage, but has actually introduced it, notwithstanding that some difficulties were thrown in his way. The following is an account of the methods which have been practised for separating gold and silver from their ores by means of quicksilver. This process was introduced into some of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-MEXICO">Mexico</a> in 1566 by <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DON">Don</a> Pedro Fernandez de Velasco, and in 1571 into some of those of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PERU">Peru</a> by the same person; and from thence it quickly spread throughout all the mines in the south and <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east parts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, inasmuch that it is almost the only method used in that <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">part</a> of the world for extracting these metals. The richer ores, however, are purified by fusion with lead; and our author informs us, that formerly the poorer kinds of ores were certainly thrown away, and when the method of amalgamation was introduced into Peru, the old <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARROWS">barrows</a> were searched for the ores which had been rejected as useless, but were now put to the quicksilver. In the year 1588, Don Juan de Corduba, a Spaniard, applied to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-VIENNA">Vienna</a>, proposing to extract silver from its ores, whether <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-POOR">poor</a> or rich, by mercury, and in a short space of time. He made some experiments upon different kinds of ore, which on a small scale succeeded very well, but on attempting it with 20 quintals of it he failed; and as Lazarus Erker, who was employed to give in a report concerning it, disapproved of the method, it was not pursued any farther. The reasons alleged in Baron Born's book for this failure are, that he did not calcine his ore; that he did not use any salt; and that the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> was too cold; though this last circumstance might have been remedied had Corduba attended to it. Another Latin and anonymous account of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of amalgamation is preserved among the records of the aulic chamber. It is directed to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>, but the year in which it was written is not mentioned. According to the account given by the author of this <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, he had examined the mines of Guatemala in New <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, and made some useful regulations for them. He directs the ore to be calcined in furnaces like limekilns, the fire being kept up according to the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the ores, after which they are to be reduced to powder in mills or stamps. The pulverized matter is then passed through fine iron sieves, and put into earthen or copper vessels by 10 or 20 quintals at a time; more or less salt being mixed with it according to circumstances. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>-coloured ore requires 50 lb. to every thousand, and the darker somewhat more. To this mixture are to be added five pounds of dry tartar, two pounds of pulverized <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HORN">horn</a>, and three pounds of brick-dust. Some kinds of ores require but a small quantity of these additions. After the mixtures are put into the boilers, as much water is added as will make the whole of the confixture of paste moderately thick; the vessels must be exposed to sunshine, or kept in a place warmed artificially, adding more water when the matter begins to dry; and it must be stirred up three or four times a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>. At the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPIRATION">expiration</a> of three or four days, various colours appear upon the surface. After this 1 lb. of brimstone is to be added to every thousand pounds of ore, and the whole worked over again; but this addition is by the baron considered as quite superfluous. Lastly, 100 lb. of less of quicksilver is added, according to the nature of the ore; the whole mass is carefully worked over, and left at rest for 12 hours. A fire must next be kindled under the boiler, and the matter it contains triturated or stirred for two days together; keeping it always sufficiently diluted by a proportionable quantity of water. It is, lastly, allowed to rest for 12 hours, and then dried. When this operation is successfully performed, if the ores be rich, particles of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMALGAM">amalgam</a> will be seen in it: these are collected, washed out, and kept for further use, the leavings being carried to a place fit for washing over. This place ought to be on the slope of an hill, where a kind of pit is dug out and lined with brick and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MORTAR">mortar</a>, and ought to be large enough to contain 25 quintals. A stream of water is then made to run upon it, and the matter stirred without interruption. The superfluous water runs over the rim of the pit, and carries off the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHTER">lighter</a> stony and earthy particles, the heavy amalgam remaining at bottom. This is then to be mixed with the small clots already mentioned, which were taken out of the mass originally, and pressed through a cloth made of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a> or coarse <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>. The quicksilver, which comes through clean, is kept for farther use; the remainder distilled off in proper vessels, and the remaining silver melted into ingots. By this method it is said that even very poor ores are worked to advantage, the expense being very moderate. The following method of extracting gold from its ores is very much recommended by our authors: "The auriferous sand, which contains gold grains and gold-dust, is concentrated by washing; and without any calcination goes to the above mentioned washing-pit, which for this purpose need not be so large. On its upper part is fixed a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LAUNDER">launder</a>, about 12 feet long, covered in the bottom with a woollen cloth, in order to retain any part of the gold-dust which may be carried over with the water and stuff gently stirred in the pit. When the water carries off no more mud, but runs clear, the farther supply is to be stopped; the water in the pit is pumped or taken out with buckets; the coarser sand in the bottom is separated or scraped off by hands; and the finer heaviest sand at the bottom is mixed with quicksilver. Then it is squeezed through a piece of cloth; the quicksilver comes off without any gold, which separated from the sand remains as an amalgam, and is pure after the remaining quicksilver has been evaporated. The sand and heavier dust remaining on the launder is washed and treated in the same manner. "The auriferous ores and loadstones, however, which rise from different mines, are calcined like silver ores, more or less as the nature of their matrixes will <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a>. Then they are ground and sifted; and the auriferous stuff, thus prepared, is put into heaps, exposed to the sunshine, and worked and turned about for three or four days. It requires no salt. Afterwards sulphur, and at last quicksilver, are added and mixed with it. There is no occasion for fire under the vessel in which it is triturated, except in winter; and two days after, though not dried, it is immediately carried to the washing-pit, and treated like the amalgam of silver. "This method of extracting gold and silver is so certain and safe, that when other methods of amalgamation extract only one ounce of gold and silver, this produces three or four from the poorest ores in a shorter time and with less expense." P. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a> Acosta tells us, that at Potosi 6000 or 7000 quintals of quicksilver are annually consumed in the dressing of the ore, not to mention what is recovered from the leavings of the first washing. These leavings, called lamas, are burnt in particular furnaces in order to extract the remaining quicksilver; and there are upwards of 50 such furnaces near Potosi and Tarapaca. The ore refined there amounts, according to the best information, to the immense quantity of 300,000 quintals. Only about 2000 quintals of the quicksilver are recovered, which shows a loss of about two pounds of quicksilver on every quintal of ore. The ores are of different natures, and in proportion to the silver they contain require more or less quicksilver. That which contains most, requires naturally the greatest quantity of quicksilver; though some of the workmen pretend that there is a kind which contains very little silver, and yet requires a great <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of mercury; but whether this be owing to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> of the workmen, or to the mercury being absorbed by some other matter, is not generally known. The ore is first pulverized in mills, and then passed through iron or <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> sieves. The mills will grind, when properly regulated, 30 quintals in the space of 24 hours. The pulverized matter is put into heaps in the open air, and salt is mixed with it in the proportion of 5 to 50 quintals of the ore, in order to macerate and cleanse it of its impurities, that the quicksilver may the more readily amalgamate with the metal. Upon these heaps, and while they are stirring, the quicksilver is pressed through a cloth. Before the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of fire-places, the ore was repeatedly kneaded with quicksilver in wooden troughs, and formed into large round masses, which were left in that form for two days; after which they were worked again, until the metals appeared to be embodied together, which took from 9 to 20 days; but it was afterwards found that heat assisted the operation so far, that by means of proper ovens the same might be accomplished in five or six days. When the quicksilver has taken up the silver, and wholly separated it from its matrix the lead and the copper, the ovens are opened, the matter is taken out, and the quicksilver expelled and recovered in the following manner. The mixture is put into water troughs, and stirred therein by means of mills and water-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHEELS">wheels</a>, by which the earthy and extraneous particles are washed away, and the amalgam settles at the bottom. The sediment looks like sand. It is further washed over in flat plates, and perfectly cleansed; what goes off with the water is collected for further use under the name of relievers. When the amalgam is become clean and bright by this method, it is put into a cloth and squeezed out. The uncombined quicksilver silver runs off, and the remaining body of amalgam contains five parts of quicksilver and one of solid metal. It is made into masses named pinas, having the form of a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a> loaf, hollow within, and weighing about 100 pounds. They are exposed to a strong fire in order to expel the quicksilver, after being put into pots covered with earthen heads. The silver still appears in the form of amalgam, but is reduced to one sixth of the former <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>. Its texture is spongy, and the quality of the metal so fine, that the silversmiths cannot <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> it, neither can it be formed into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a>, without an alloy. Baron Born observes, however, that it is only cold amalgamation which produces silver of such uncommon fineness; by hot amalgamation it is generally alloyed with copper, which cannot be parted from it without cupellation. The most circumstantial account of the amalgamation of silver ore is that of Alonzo Barba. He divides the ores into two classes: 1. Those which are best treated by fire and fusion; and, 2. Such as are most fit for amalgamation. Those called pacos and tacana, may be amalgamated; but that none of their richer contents may be lost, it will be best to combine them with lead, and proceed by cupellation. The former of these ores has no lustre or brightness. It is said to be of a reddish-yellow, soft and friable; seldom rich in silver, and mostly valuable on account of its being easily got from the mine. Tacana is a rich silver ore, of a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> colour, sometimes of a grey or of an ash-colour; or a brown, rich, silvery <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>. 3. The plomo is too rich for pulverisation and amalgamation, and is therefore simply melted <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DOWN">down</a> with the tacana. This seems to be the same with the horn-silver ore; and is described as almost entirely consisting of native silver, of a black, grey, or greenish-white colour. Barba says that they found at Potosi some plomo of a cinnabar colour, which they had not seen anywhere else; but Baron Born thinks that here he has mistaken the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RED">red</a> silver ore for another <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>. Frezier affirms, that in what he calls the plomo ronco, the native silver appears upon rubbing or scratching it, and that it gives white and very pure silver by simple fusion without any amalgamation. In the imperial cabinet at Vienna, there is a specimen weighing about a pound, of black horn silver ore from Potosi, on the polished surface of which the virgin silver appears very plainly. 4. The machacado (virgin silver or gold grown in the matrix in the form of wire or <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>), is amalgated in the mortar. 5. The furoches (lead ores containing silver), are melted along with the rojicler and conchilo, two kinds of red silver ore. 6. The negrillos (grey copper and white silver ores) may be refined by amalgamation, though they are more fit for fire. Besides this classification into such as are fit for fire, and those for amalgamation, the ores require further to be sorted into such as require the addition of particular substances for their amalgamation. Vitriol is generally hurtful, especially when salt is added to the vitriolic ores; and it requires the addition of iron, tin, lead, and lime, in order to counteract its effects; but in some cases it is of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>, and promotes amalgamation. The calcination of vitriolic ores is of no service, but rather the contrary, as it disengages the vitriol, and brings on a vitriolic efflorescence. It may, however, be separated by washing till the water comes off tasteless and sweet. The amalgamation is disturbed by sulphur, bitumen, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANTIMONY">antimony</a>, only by the smoothness and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NEEDLE">needle</a>-like <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of the particles, which reduce the quicksilver to a kind of dust. The ores mixed with these always run into reguli, and must therefore be put into a strong calcining fire; if melted without calcination, they would run entirely into dross and scoria. The finer the ores are pounded so much the better; and after putting the powder through a fine sieve, the coarser part goes again to the mill: they ought to be previously burnt, in order to assist the operation of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GRINDING">grinding</a>. The best method of obtaining fine powder is by washing over; but as this is very apt to pack and turn clammy, it ought to be mixed with sand.
