The ancient metrocomiae had each its choripiscopus or rural <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEAN">dean</a>, and here was his see or residence. See METROPOLIS and CHORIEPISCOPIUS.

METRONOMII

Pages 643-643

the name given by the Athenians to five officers in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CITY">city</a> and ten in the piraus, whose duty it was to inspect all sorts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> except those of corn. The piraus was the greatest mart in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATTICA">Attica</a>.

METROPOLIS

Pages 643-645

the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>; or the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CITY">city</a>, and as it were mother of all the rest. The <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TERM">term</a> METROPOLIS is also applied to archiepiscopal churches, and sometimes to the principal or mother-<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of a city. The Roman empire having been divided into 13 dioceses and 120 provinces, each <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> and each province had its metropolis or capital city, where the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PRIMATE">primate</a> had his residence. To this civil <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> was afterwards adapted, and the bishop of the capital city had the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of affairs, and the pre-eminence over all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> of the province. His residence in the metropolis gave him the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of metropolitan. This erection of metropolitans is referred to the end of the third century, and was confirmed, by the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of Nice. Metulum A metropolitan has the privilege of ordaining his suffragans; and appeals from sentences passed by the suffragans are preferred to the metropolitan. Metropolis (anc. geog.), a town of Acarnania, a little to the south of Stratos.—Another, of Lydia; situated between Colophon and Priene, near the Cayster.—A third, of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PHRYGIA">Phrygia</a>; sacred to the mother of the gods, who was here worshipped.—A fourth Metropolis of Epirots, a district in Thessaly, to the east of Gomphi, and the last town of that district. Metropolis, the people. Metulium (anc. geog.), a considerable city of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LIBURNIA">Liburnia</a>, at the siege of which Octavius Caesar was wounded. Said to be the metropolis, and situated on two eminences, intersected by a valley (Appian.) Now generally thought to be Metting in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CARNIOLA">Carniola</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 16. N. Lat. 46. 5. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METZ">Metz</a>, an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, and strong town of France, and capital of the territory of Mefflin, with a citadel, a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, and a bishop's see, whose bishop assumes the title of a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of the empire. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> church is one of the finest in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> called Collin and the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of the governor are worth seeing. The Jews live in a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">part</a> of the town by themselves, where they have a synagogue. The sweetmeats they make here are in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> esteem. It is seated at the confluence of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Moselle and Seille. E. Long. 6. 16. N. Lat. 49. 7. Metzu (Gabriel), an eminent painter, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a> in 1615. His subjects were usually taken from low <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>; but they were all designed after <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, and surprisingly well represented; such as women selling fish, fowls, or hares; sick persons attended by the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a>; chemists in their laboratories; dead <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAME">game</a>, painters rooms, shops, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a> hung with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINTS">prints</a> and pictures; all which subjects he composed well, and finished them with <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> neatness, as he likewise did his portraits. He spent a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a> on his pictures, which has occasioned their scarcity and dearth at this time; and besides, it is confidently said, the Dutch prevent their being carried out of their own country, as much as possible. So that those paintings of Metzu, which are sometimes seen in the collections of our kingdoms, are either obtained by chance, or purchased at large prices. Though it ought also to be remembered, that the value set upon the works of this <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MASTER">master</a> throughout <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FLANDERS">Flanders</a>, has induced several painters to endeavour at imitating and copying his works, which having gradually circulated abroad and being a little mellowed by time, are now called originals. He died in 1658. Mevania (anc. geog.), a town of the Cispennine Umbria; seated at the confluence of the Tina and Clitumnus, on the Via Flaminia, famous for its herds of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WHITE">white</a> cattle brought up there for sacrifice; the white <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> said to be owing to the waters of the Clitumnus (<a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>). Mevania was the country of Propertius. Mevaneses, the people. Now said to be Bevagna, in the territory of the Pope. Meulen (Anthony Francis Vander), painter of battles, &c. was born at Brussel in 1634; and was a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> Snyers, a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>-painter of considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a>. Some of his compositions happening to be carried to <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, were shown to M. Colbert; who soon discerned the abilities of Vander Meulen, and by his generous offers induced him to leave his native city and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> at Paris. Here he was employed by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XIV. and had an appointment of 2000 livres pension, beside being paid for his <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a>. He attended that monarch in most of his expeditions in the field, and designed on the spot the sieges, attacks, encampments, and marches, of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KING">king</a>'s armies, also the views of those cities and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> memorable by any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of success; and from those sketches he composed the paintings, which were intended to perpetuate the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-REMEMBRANCE">remembrance</a> of those <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> exploits. He died in 1690. The principal works of this master are at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VERSAILLES">Versailles</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MARLY">Marly</a>; but many of his easel pictures are dispersed through England, France, and Flanders. Meursius (John), a learned and laborious writer, born at Lofdun, near the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HAGUE">Hague</a>, in 1579. He early discovered a fondness for polite literature and the sciences; and went to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LAW">law</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-ORLEANS">Orleans</a> with the son of Barneveldt, whom he accompanied in his travels. In 1610 he was made professor of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> at Leyden, and afterwards Greek professor. In the following year, the magistrates of the United Provinces proved how high their <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> was of his abilities, by fixing on him to write the history of his country. Meursius married in the year 1612. His wife, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANNA">Anna</a> Catharina Bilberuccia, descended from a very ancient and noble family in Angermond a city of Pomerania, possessed many amiable qualities, and rendered his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> life remarkably happy, while he discharged the duties of his professorship with an assiduity equal to his abilities. At the same time the republic of letters did not lose the advantages to be derived from his labours; for during the fourteen years of his residence at Leyden, the works which he published were more numerous than those which had been presented to the world by the whole body of professors from the original foundation of the university in 1575. Meursius's writings had now disseminated his reputation in every part of Europe; nor had the fame of his diligence and talents as a professor spread with less rapidity. In so high a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-RANK">rank</a>, indeed, did he stand among his literary contemporaries, that Christian IV. king of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a> conferred on him the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of historiographer <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a>, and invited him to undertake the professorship of history and politics in the academy of Sora, which was founded by King Frederick II., although the revival of its honours and dignities may be dated from this <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, when it seemed to be again founded under the auspices of Christian IV. Meursius and his family left Leyden in the year 1635. On his arrival at Sora, he was received with the most friendly tokens of regard by his Majesty and the Danish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>, and more particularly by <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHANCELLOR">Chancellor</a> Rovenkrantz, on whom he has bestowed very ample praises in one of his letters. Here he resided, equally beloved and admired, for above twelve years. His pupils were not very numerous, but his exertions never relaxed. Those houses likewise which were not devoted to the duties of his professorship, he employed in revising the works of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, and in philological disquisitions. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> was not much impaired by the infestations of application; but in the year 1638 he had a violent attack of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, from which disorder he had had suffered severely before. In a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> to Vossius he thus describes his melancholy condition: "The state of my health during the whole of the last winter has been truly deplorable. My sufferings from the stone have been really dreadful. I have voided so many, that the repeated discharges brought on a wound which emitted blood for above four months. I was next attacked by a tertian fever, which increased constantly, and produced an universal laxitude of body, a dejection of spirits, and a total loss of appetite. But, thank heaven, I have now in some <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> recovered my strength, and gotten the better of these complaints." He recovered from this attack; but in the following year the disorder returned with redoubled violence, and brought on a consumption which terminated his existence on the 20th <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> of September 1639. He left behind him a son who was named after him, and one <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a>. So mild were the dispositions of Meurhuis, that in all his writings he constantly avoided literary disputes. He was sometimes unavoidably drawn into them; but constantly endeavoured to promote a reconciliation, rather than widen any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREACH">breach</a>, by his replies to the attacks of his adversaries. In his friendships he was firm and affectionate. Of his domestic life, whatever is known has been gathered from his letters. The same easy tranquillity seems to have attended him in every situation. In his family he was particularly fortunate. In his son, to whom he gave his own name, he seemed to behold his own youth renewed. The same application, the same eagerness in the pursuit of knowledge, marked the conduct of this promising young <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MAN">man</a>; who did not long survive his father, but died soon after he had recommended himself to the notice of the learned world by his publications. They were only three in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>; but displayed so much <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> learning, that they have been assigned to the father, John Meurhuis, by Labbe Beughem and others. This mistake was occasioned as much by the similitude of their names, as by the nature of their works, and their manner of treating philological subjects. His works may be divided into four classes, of which each might form a separate volume <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they were ever to be republished. Meurhuis himself indeed, in one of his letters to Vossius, proposes such a division. From that epistle, and from another which the younger Meurhuis sent to G. I. Vossius, who strongly advised him to republish the whole of his father's writings, and from the collections of his posthumous works which have appeared from Struvius, Grochuphius, Molker, and some others, a catalogue of his works might be formed. Some affluence <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WILL">will</a> also be derived from the indexes published in their respective works, by Hankins, Deffelius, Wetenius, and Bartholinus. The <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> which Meurhuis recommends for publishing his works, is to insert in the first volume all that he has written relative to <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>; in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, his historical pieces; in the third, his miscellaneous dissertations; and in the fourth, the various authors which he published, with his notes and corrections. Before we conclude, one mistake with respect to this great scholar, which prevails very generally, must be corrected. A scandalous and indecent work, which is intitled *Meurhii elegantiae Latini sermonis*, and has *Aloisia Sigae Satyrae Sotadicae* annexed to it, is very falsely attributed to Meurhuis; nor indeed are the *Satires* with more reason assigned to Aloisia Sigae, who was a Spanish lady, eminent for her piety and virtue. The real author of these infamous productions was Wettenius, an advocate at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COPENHAGEN">Copenhagen</a>, who probably assumed the name of Meurhuis, in order to shield himself from the disgrace which would naturally have attended the writer of such a performance. To insure the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-SALE">sale</a> of his books, however, might have been the principal view of Wettenius. At any rate, such a conclusion may be fairly deduced from the disguised title, and from his desire that the world should affix it to a character so distinguished and respectable in almost every branch of various literature.

MEWING

Pages 645-645

the falling off <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> change of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>, feathers, skin, horns, or other parts of animals, which happens in some annually, in others only at certain stages of their lives; but the generality of beasts mew in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>. An old <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HART">hart</a> casts his horns sooner than a young one, which is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> in the months of February and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MARCH">March</a>, after which they begin to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BUTTON">button</a> in March or April; and as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> grows strong, and the season of the year puts forth the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, to their heads grow, and are furred full by the middle of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JUNE">June</a>. It is to be observed, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> a hart be gelt before he has a head, he <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WILL">will</a> never have any; and if he be gelt after he has a head, he will never <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> his horns; again, if he be gelt when he has a velvet-head, it will always be so, without fraying or barnilling.

MEXICO

Pages 645-691

a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of the Spanish empire in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, once a celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, the most powerful and civilized in the New World. In former times the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> now distinguished by the name of the *Vale of Mexico*, was called *Atlanac*, into which the rest of it being divided into the kingdoms of *Mexi*-Mexico was to, *Acolhuacan*, *Tlacopan*, and *Michuacan*; the republics anciently of *Tlaxcallan*, *Cholollan*, *Huexotzinco*, and some other states. Of these the most westerly was Michuacan, which to the east and south had Mexico; on the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NORTH">north</a> the country of the Chichemecas, and some other barbarous nations; on the west the lake of Chapallan, and some independent tribes. It had four considerable cities; the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> being seated on the eastern shore of a beautiful lake named *Pascuaro*. The kingdom of Tlacopan lay betwixt Mexico and Michuacan, and was of very small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>; its capital was seated on the western border of a lake called *Tezcuco*, four miles westward of that of Mexico. Acolhuacan was the most extensive as well as the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a>. It was bounded on the east by the republic of Tlaxcallan; on the south by a province of Mexico named Chalco; on the north by the country of the Huaxtecas; and on the west by other states of Mexico, terminating at the lake Tezcuco. Its length from south to north was somewhat more than 200 miles, and its breadth about 60; it was very populous, and had a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> many cities. On the eastern <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of the lake of Tezcuco was situated the capital of that territory, 15 miles to the eastward of that of Mexico; and no less celebrated for its antiquity than the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-POLITENESS">politeness</a> and civilization of its inhabitants. Tlaxcallan, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-OR">or</a> Tlascal, a celebrated republic, had Acolhuacan to the west; the republics of Cholollan and Huexotzinco to the south; and some of the Mexican states on the north and east. It was but of small extent; not reaching more than 50 miles in length and 30 in breadth. Its capital stood on the side of a great mountain, about 70 miles to the eastward of Mexico. The kingdom of Mexico, though the most <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MODERN">modern</a>, came at last to be the most extensive of the whole. On the south and south-west it extended as far as the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PACIFIC_OCEAN">Pacific Ocean</a>; on the east it was bounded by the republics of Tlacopan and Michuacan; on the north by the country of the Huexotzinco; and on the north-west by the country of the Chichemecas; the whole being comprehended between the 14th and 21st degrees of north latitude, and between 27° and 28° of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a>, computed from the meridian of Ferro. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the origin of the nations on the eastern continent is obscure, that of the inhabitants of the western continent is much more so; and indeed, till very lately, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of every one of the American nations, till the arrival of the Spaniards, has been either treated as entirely fabulous, or very slightly touched upon by historians. By the industry of the Abbé Francisco Clavigero, however, we are now furnished with an account of the ancient kingdoms <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> enumerated; more full and authentic than could have been expected, considering the difficulty there must have been of procuring materials. According to this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>, it is undeniable that Mexico was first peopled from the more northerly parts of the continent, which for many ages had been filled with inhabitants. Some have supposed, from the traditions of the natives, and the discovery of very <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> skeletons in many parts of New <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, that this country was first inhabited by giants; but though similar conjectures and discoveries have been made in other countries, we are by no means warranted from thence to conclude that the whole human <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-RACE">race</a> were formerly of an immense size; it being most probable, as our author observes, that the gigantic race were but a few individuals who lived at different times and in different nations. The Toltecs are the most ancient Mexican <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATION">nation</a> of which we know anything. They were expelled, as we are told, from their own country (supposed by Clavigero to have been Tollan, to the northward of Mexico) in the year 472; and for some <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIME">time</a> led a migratory and wandering <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. In whatever <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLACE">place</a> they determined to reside for any considerable time, they erected houses and cultivated the ground. Thus their migrations were extremely slow, and it was not till 104 years after they set out that they reached a place about 50 miles to the eastward of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Mexico, where they settled for 20 years, giving to their new place of residence the name of Tollantzinco. From thence they proceeded about 40 miles farther to the west, where they built a city called, from the name of their country, Tollan, or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TULA">Tula</a>. The Toltecs, during their journeys, were conducted by a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of chiefs; who, by the time they arrived at Tollantzinco, were reduced to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a>, and, after their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FINAL">final</a> settlement, the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> was changed into a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MONARCHY">monarchy</a>; but by what means, or on what account, we are not told. Their first <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KING">king</a> began his reign in 667, and their monarchy lasted 384 years, during which time they reckon just eight princes. We are not, however, to imagine that each of their kings lived <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LONG">long</a> enough to make up this space. It was a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> among them that the name of the king should be <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> for 52 years, and no longer, from the time he ascended the throne. If he died within that <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, the government was carried on in his name by a regency; if he survived, he was obliged to resign his authority. During the four centuries that the Toltec monarchy continued, they had increased very considerably in number, and had built many cities; but when in the height of prosperity, almost the whole nation was destroyed by a famine occasioned by drought; and a pestilence, probably the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of the former. "According to Torquemada (says our author), at a certain festival-<a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-BALL">ball</a> made by the Toltecs, the foul looking <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEVIL">devil</a> appeared to them of a gigantic size, with immense arms, and in the midst of the entertainment he embraced and suffocated them; that then he appeared in the form of a child with a putrid head, and brought the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLAGUE">plague</a>; and, finally, at the persuasion of the same devil, they abandoned the country of Tula." These stories, according to Clavigero, are taken from the symbolical representations or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIEROGLYPHICS">hieroglyphics</a>, by which this piece of history was represented, and which the Spanish author has taken literally. Be the cause what it <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WILL">will</a>, however, it is certain that the surviving Toltecs abandoned their country, and dispersed themselves among the surrounding nations, where they were well received, on account of their superior knowledge and civilization. They were succeeded by the Chichemecas, a much more barbarous people, who came from an unknown country called Amaquemecan, where they had for a long time resided; but of which no traces or <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-REMEMBRANCE">remembrance</a> can be found among any of the American nations known to Europeans; so that Clavigero supposes it must have been very far to the northward. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTIVE">motive</a> which the Chichemecas had for leaving their own country is not known. They were eighteen months on their journey, and took possession of the defolate country of the Toltecs about a hundred years after the former had left it. They were much more uncivilized than the Toltecs; but, however, had a regular form of monarchical government, and in other respects were less disgusting in their manners than some of the neighbouring nations. The last king who reigned in Amaquemecan before the departure of the Chichemecas, had left his dominions between his two sons Auchcauhli and Xolotl, and the latter conducted the new colony. Having proceeded from the ruins of Tula towards Chempoalla and Tepepolio, Xolotl sent his son to survey the country. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> crofted the borders of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a> and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> which surround the vale of Mexico; then ascending to the top of a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> one, he viewed the whole country, and took possession of it in the name of his father, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOOTING">shooting</a> four arrows to the four winds. Xolotl being informed by his son of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the country, chose for the capital of his kingdom Tepepolio, about six miles to the northward of the city of Mexico, and distributed his people in the neighbouring territory; but as most of them went to the northward, that <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PART">part</a> obtained the name of the coun-try. try of the Chichemecas, in distinction from the rest. Here a review of the people was taken, and their number, according to Torquemada, was more than a million. In <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONFIRMATION">confirmation</a> of this the historian adds, that in his time there were still remaining twelve piles of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-STONES">stones</a> they threw to ascertain their numbers; but Clavigero thinks it improbable that so large an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> should set out on so long an expedition, or that so small a district could maintain so many hunters. Xolotl finding himself peacefully settled in his new dominion, sent one of his officers to explore the sources of some of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> of the country. While performing this task he came to the habitations of some Toltecans, who it seems had still kept together, and were likely once more to become a nation. As these people were not inclined to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WAR">war</a>, and greatly esteemed for their knowledge and skill in the arts, the Chichemecas entered into a strict <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a> with them, and Prince Nopaltzin, who had first surveyed the country, married a Toltec princess. The consequence of this alliance was the introduction of the arts and knowledge of the Toltecans among the Chichemecas. Till now the latter had subsisted entirely by hunting, and such <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> and roots as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> spontaneously produced. They were clad in the skins of wild beasts, and, like these beasts, they are said to have sucked the blood of the animals they caught; but after their connection with the Toltecans they began to sow corn, to learn the art of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DIGGING">digging</a> and working <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-METALS">metals</a>, to cut stones, manufacture cotton, and, in every respect, to make great improvements. When Xolotl had reigned about eight years in his new territories, an embassy of five persons arrived from a distant country not far from Amaquemecan, expressing a desire of coming with their people to reside in the country of the Chichemecas. The king gave them a gracious reception, and assigned them a district; and, in a few years after, three other princes, with a great army of Acolhuans, who were likewise neighbours of Amaquemecan, made their appearance. The king was at that time at Tezcuco, to which place he had removed his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COURT">court</a>; and here he was accosted by the princes, who, in a submissive and flattering manner, requested him to allow them a place in his happy country, where the people enjoyed such an excellent government. Xolotl not only gave them a favourable reception, but offered them his two daughters in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>, expressing his concern that he had no more, that none might have been excluded from the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> alliance. On the third prince, however, he bestowed a noble virgin of Chalco, in whom the Toltec and Chichemecan blood were united. The nuptials were celebrated with extraordinary pomp; and the two nations, after the example of the sovereign, continued to intermarry. As the Acolhuans were the more civilized nation of the two, the name of Chichemecas began to be appropriated to the more rude and barbarous part, who preferred hunting to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a>, or who chose a life of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> in the mountains to the restraints of social laws. These barbarians associated with the Otomies, another savage nation who lived to the northward, occupying a tract of more than three hundred miles in extent; and by their descendants the Spaniards were harassed for many years after the conquest of Mexico. As soon as the nuptial rejoicings were over, Xolotl divided his territories into three parts, assigning one to each of the princes. Acolhuatzin, who had married his eldest <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a>, had Azcapazalco, 18 miles to the westward of Tezcuco; Chiconquauhtli, who married the other, had a territory named Xaltocan; Xolotl and Tzontecomatl, who married the lady of inferior <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-RANK">rank</a>, had one named Coatlichan. The country continued for some time to flourish, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> increased greatly, and with it the civilization of the people; but as these advanced, the vices of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUXURY">luxury</a> and ambition increased in proportion. Xolotl found himself obliged to treat his subjects with more severity than formerly, and even to put some of them to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. This produced a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSPIRACY">conspiracy</a> against him, which, however, he had the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOOD_FORTUNE">good fortune</a> to escape; but while he meditated a severe <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a> on the conspirators, he was seized with the distemper of which he died, in the fortieth year of his reign, and in a very advanced <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>. His corpse was adorned with various figures of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> and silver, and placed in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a> made of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GUM">gum</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COPAL">copal</a> and other precious substances, where it remained five days, until the lords summoned to the funeral attended. The body was then burnt, and the ashes deposited in an urn of the hardest <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-STONE">stone</a>. This urn was kept exposed in the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> for forty days, during which time the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a> attended with lamentations; after which it was carried to a cave in the neighbourhood, with similar demonstrations of grief. Xolotl was succeeded by his son Nopaltzin, who at the time of his accession is supposed to have been about sixty years of age. In his time, the tranquillity of the kingdom, which had begun to suffer disturbance under his father, underwent much more violent shocks, and civil wars took place. Acolhuatzin, the only one of the three princes who remained alive, thinking the territory he possessed too narrow, made war upon the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LORD">lord</a> of a neighbouring province named Tapotzotlan, and deprived him of his territory. Huetzin, son to the late prince Tzontecomatl, lord of Coatlichan, fell in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-LOVE">love</a> with the granddaughter of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a>, a celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>, but was rivalled by a neighbouring lord, who determined to support his pretensions by force of arms. Huetzin, however, got the better, defeated and killed his adversary, and then possessed himself of the lady and his estate. This was followed by a rebellion of the whole province of Tolantzinco, so that the king himself was obliged to take the field. As the rebels were very numerous, the royal army was at first defeated; but having at last received a strong reinforcement, the rebels were overcome, and their ringleaders severely punished. The king did not long survive the restoration of tranquillity to his dominions. He died in the thirty <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SECOND">second</a> year of his reign, and ninety-second of his age, leaving the throne to his eldest son Tlotzin. We are not informed of any particulars relating to this prince farther that he was of an excellent disposition, greatly beloved by his subjects, and, though addicted to peace, yet affiluous in exercising his people in the art of war. He reigned thirty-six years, and died of a very painful <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>. Quinatzin, the son and successor of Tlotzin, proved a vain and luxurious prince. His accession to the throne was celebrated with much greater pomp than prince. any of his predecessors. Xolotl had removed his court from Tenayuca to Tezcuco; but being disgusted with this last place, on account of the conspiracy formed against him there, he had returned to Tenayuca.—There the court continued till the reign of Quinatzin, who removed it back to Tezcuco. In his passage thither, he caused himself to be transported in an open chair or litter, carried on the shoulders of four of his <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> lords, while four others held an umbrella over his head. Before his time the kings had been accustomed to walk upon their feet like other people; but this example, once set, was quickly followed by all the lords and great people in the kingdom, who now strove to out-do one another in expensive and ostentatious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a>. The reign of Quinatzin, though tranquil at first, was soon disturbed by dangerous revolts and rebellions. These first broke out in two states, named Maztillen and Totopoe, situated among the northern mountains. The king, having collected a great army, marched without delay against the rebels, and challenged their leaders to come <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DOWN">down</a> and fight him in the plain.—This challenge being accepted, a furious engagement ensued, in which, though great numbers fell on both sides, no decisive advantage was gained by either party. Frequent engagements took place for the space of forty days, until at last the rebels, perceiving that their own numbers were daily diminishing, without any possibility of being recruited like the royal army, made a final surrender to the king, who punished the ringleaders with great severity. Tranquility, however, was not yet restored: the rebellion spread to such a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, that the king was obliged not only to take the field in person, but to employ six other armies, under the command of faithful and experienced generals, to reduce the rebels. Those proved so successful in their enterprises, that in a short time the rebellious cities were reduced to obedience, and the kingdom enjoyed the blessings of peace during the long reign of Quinatzin, who is said to have sat on the throne for no less than sixty years. He was succeeded by his son Techotlatla; but as the affairs of the Acolhuans now began to be connected with those of the Mexicans, it will be proper to give some account of that people. The Mexicans, called also the Aztecas, dwelt till the year 1600 in a country called Azilan, situated to the north of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CALIFORNIA">California</a>, as appears by the route they pursued in their journey; but how far to the northward we are not certainly informed. Betancourt makes it no less than 2700 miles, and Boturini says it was a province of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>. The cause of their <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MIGRATION">migration</a> is said to have been as follows: Among the Aztecas was a person of great authority, named Huizilin, to whose <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> every one paid the utmost deference. He had conceived a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>, for what reason we know not, to persuade his countrymen to change their residence; and to effect this he fell upon the following stratagem. Having heard, while meditating on his scheme, a little <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BIRD">bird</a> singing on the branches of a tree, the notes of which resembled the word <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-TIBUR">Tibur</a>, which in the Azteca <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> signified "let us go," he took that opportunity to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> upon the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a> of the people. With this view, he took along with him a respectable person, and made him attend to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a> of the bird. "What can it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> (says he), but that we must leave this country, and find ourselves another? Without doubt it is the warning of some secret <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a> who watches over our welfare: let us obey, therefore, his <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-VOICE">voice</a>, and not draw his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANGER">anger</a> upon us by a refusal." Tecpaltzin, for that was the name of his friend, readily agreed to the interpretation; and both of them being persons of great influence, their united persuasions soon gained over to their project the bulk of the nation; and they accordingly set out. This account, though it has somewhat the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FABLE">fable</a>, is what the Mexicans themselves give; and is certainly more worthy of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> than that of the Spaniards, who maintain that the Aztecas set out by the express command of the devil. But whatever was their motive, it is certain that they began their migration about the year above-mentioned. Torquemada says, that in all the hieroglyphic paintings which record this migration, there is delineated an arm of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, or a great river, which, however, Clavigero takes to be a representation of the universal deluge. Boturini supposes it to have been the gulf of California, over which, he thinks, they transported themselves; but our author controverts this opinion, because there are no remains of the buildings they constructed, during their migration, in California as there are in other places. If there really was any river of consequence which they crossed, he says it must have been the Colorado, or <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol18.html#article-RED_RIVER"><a class=</a>"xref" href="vol0.html#article-RED">Red</a> River, which discharges itself into the gulf of California, in lat. 32°. 30'. Having crossed this beyond the lat. of 35°, they proceeded towards the south-east, as far as the river Gila, where they stopped for some time; and on the banks of that river there are remains of the great edifices they constructed. From thence having resumed their course towards the S.S.E., they proceeded to lat. 29°, and stopped again at a place upwards of 250 miles distant from the city of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIHUAHUA">Chihuahua</a>, towards the N. N. W. This place is now known by the name of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CASA">Casa</a> grandi, on account of a very large <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> still extant, and universally attributed to them by the traditions of the country. It is constructed on the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of those of New Mexico, that is, consisting of three floors with a terrace above them, and without any entrance to the under <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a>. The door for entrance opens to the second floor; so that a scaling <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LADDER">ladder</a> is necessary; and the inhabitants of New Mexico build in this manner, in order to be less exposed to the attack of their enemies; putting out the scaling ladder only for those to whom they give admittance into their houses. No doubt the Aztecas had the same motive for raising their edifice on this plan, as every mark of a fortress is to be observed in it, being defended on one side by a lofty mountain, and the rest surrounded by a wall about seven feet thick, the foundations of which are still existing. In this there are stones as big as mill-stones; the beams of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> are of pine, and well finished. In the centre is a little <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> mount, apparently constructed with a design to keep <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> on, and observe the enemy. Some ditches have been formed in this place, and several <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-KITCHEN">kitchen</a> utensils found, as earthen pots, dishes, and jars, with some looking-glasses made of a stone called itztili. The Aztecas having staid here as long as they thought thought proper, crossed the mountains of Tarahu- mara, directed their course southward, and stopped again for three years at Culiacan, a place situated on the gulf of California, in 24 degrees north latitude. Here they formed a wooden image of a god called Huitzilopochtli, whom they imagined to be their tute- lar deity, and made a chair of reeds and rushes to transport it, calling this vehicle the chair of God. Four priests were chosen, to carry the image on their shoulders, whom they called the servants of God; and the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of carrying it they name teomama, which fig- urines "to carry God on one's back." The Aztecas, when they left their original habita- tions, were divided into six tribes; but here the Mex- icans were left with their god by five of them, viz. the Xochimilcas, Tepanecas, Chalcafe, Tlauhicus, and Tlacalans. The cause of this separation is not known. The tribes just mentioned pretend that it was done at the express command of God; but there can be little doubt that it was occasioned by some disagreement among themselves. This is rendered farther probable, when we consider that on their journey towards Tula, the remaining tribe was divided into two violent fac- tions, which alternately persecuted one another; nei- ther did they afterwards construct any more edifices. However, they always travelled together, in order to enjoy the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> of their imaginary God. At ev- ery place where they stopped an altar was erected to him; and at their departure they left behind them all their sick, and probably also some others to take care of them, or such as were not willing to endure the fatigue of farther journeys. They stopped in Tula <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NINE">nine</a> years, and eleven more in the neighbouring parts. At last, in 1216, they arrived at Zumpango, a con- siderable city in the vale of Mexico, where they were received in a very hospitable manner by the lord of that district. He not only assigned them proper ha- bitations, but became very much attached to them; and even demanded from among them a wife for his son Ihuicatl. This request was complied with; and from this marriage all the Mexican kings descended. The Mexicans continued to migrate from one place to another along the lake of Tezcuco. Xolotl, who was then on the throne of the Acolhuans or Chiche- mechas, allowed them to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> in whatever places of his dominions they thought proper; but some of them finding themselves harassed by a neighbouring lord, were obliged, in 1245, to retire to Chapaltepexi, a mountain on the western borders of the lake, scarce two miles distant from the site of Mexico. This took place in the reign of Nopaltzin; when, as has already been observed, disturbances began to take place in the Acolhua dominions. The Mexicans, however, did not find themselves any more secure in their new place of residence than formerly; they were perse- cuted by the neighbouring lords, and obliged to take refuge in a number of small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, named Acolco, at the southern extremity of the lake of Mexico. Here for 52 years they lived in the most miserable manner that can be imagined; subsisting on fish, in- sects, roots, &c., and clothing themselves with the leaves of the amoxtl, which abounds in that lake. In this miserable plight the Mexicans continued till the year 1314, when they were all reduced to a state of the most <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SLAVERY">slavery</a>. This was done by the king of a petty state named Colhuacan; but there are different accounts of the manner in which it was effected. Some say that this prince, unwilling to allow the Mexicans to maintain themselves in his ter- ritories without paying tribute, made war upon them, subdued and enslaved them. Others affirm, that pre- tending compassion for their miserable situation, he offered them a more commodious place of residence. The Mexicans accepted the offer with great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>; but had scarcely set out to take possession of their new place of residence when they were attacked by the Colhuans, made prisoners, and carried off for slaves. After some years a war broke out between the Col- huans and Xochimilcas; in which the latter gained such advantages, that they were obliged to employ liberty in conferring their slaves to assist them. They accordingly ordered them to prepare for war, but without furnishing them with arms necessary for a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> enterprise; so that piece of the Mexicans were obliged to content themselves with long lances, having their <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-POINTS">points</a> hardened in the fire; they also made knives of the stone itztli, and shields of reeds woven together. They agreed among them- selves not to waste their time, as was usual, in making prisoners, but to content themselves with <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> off one <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-EAR">ear</a> of their enemies, and then leaving them with- out further injury. They adhered punctually to this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a>; and rushing furiously upon the Xochimil- cas, cut off an ear from as many as they could, killing those who struggled to such a degree, that they could not effect their purpose. In short, so well did the Mexicans acquit themselves in this engagement, that the Xochimilcas not only abandoned the field, but were obliged to take refuge among the moun- tains. After the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>, the Colhua <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> pre- sented themselves before their general with the pris- oners they had taken; for it was by the number of these, not of the enemy left dead on the field, that they judged of their valour. The Mexicans had taken only four, and these they kept concealed for the abominable purpose of sacrificing them. The Colhuans, there- fore, seeing no trophies of their valour, began to re- proach them with cowardice; but the Mexicans, pro- ducing their baskets of ears, desired them to judge from these how many prisoners they might have taken, had they not been unwilling to retard their victory by taking up time in binding them. Notwithstanding the valour displayed by the Mex- icans in this engagement, it doth not appear that their haughty masters were in the least mollified or inclin- ed to afford them easier terms than before. Having erected an altar to their god, they demanded of their lord something precious to offer in sacrifice to him; but he disdainfully sent them a dirty cloth, including the filthy carcase of a vile bird. This was carried by Colhua priests; and without any <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> laid upon the al- tar. The Mexicans, with apparent unconcern, re- moved this filthy offering, and put in its place a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-KNIFE">knife</a> made of itztli, and an odoriferous <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HERB">herb</a>. On the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> of consecration, the Colhua prince failed not to at- tend with his nobility; nor with a view to do <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> to the festival, but to make a mockery of the Mexicans. Their derision, however, was soon changed into hor- ror, when the Mexicans, after a solemn dance, brought forth the four Xochimilcan prisoners they had taken; and, after having made them dance a little, cut open their breasts with the knife which lay on the altar, and plucking out their hearts, offered them, while yet warm and palpitating with life, to their diabolical idol. This horrible sacrifice had such an effect upon the spectators, that both king and subjects desired the Mexicans immediately to quit their territories and go where they pleased. This order was instantly obeyed; the whole nation took their rout towards the north, until they came to a place named Acatzinatlan, situated betwixt two lakes, and afterwards named Mexicoctzinco; but for some reason or other, being discontented with this situation, as indeed they seem very often to have been, they proceeded to Iztacalco, still nearer to the site of Mexico. Here they formed the image of a little mountain of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, and danced round it a whole night, singing their victory over the Xochimilcas, and returning thanks to their god for having freed them from the yoke of the Colhuas. Clavigero is of opinion, that by this mountain they represented Colhuacan, as in their pictures it was always represented by a hunch-backed mountain; and this is the literal signification of the name. Having stayed two years in Iztacalco, they came to a place on the lake where they found a nopal or opuntia growing in a stone, and over it the foot of an eagle. All the Mexican historians say that this was the mark given them by their oracle of the place where they were finally to settle. Here, then, they put an end to their wanderings; and, as soon as they had taken possession of the spot, an altar was erected to the god, or rather devil, whom they worshipped. The altar was consecrated in a manner conformable to the cruel <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> which these people had adopted. Having at that time no prisoners among them, one of their number went out in quest of some animal for a victim; but happening to meet with a Colhuaua, a quarrel ensued; and the Mexican proving victorious, bound his enemy, brought him home, and presented his heart to the idol. Around this altar they now began to build their habitations; which, like the celebrated city of Rome, consisted at first of a parcel of miserable rush huts; as they were then furnished with no better materials. Their city, if such it might be called, was named Tenochtitlan, and afterwards Mexico, which name afterwards prevailed; and, according to Clavigero, signifies the place of Mexitli or Huiztilopochtli, their god of war; and in this respect also the founding of Mexico was similar to that of Rome, the latter being protected by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MARS">Mars</a> their god of war, as the Mexicans were by Mexitli. The city of Mexico was founded in the year 1325, in the most commodious situation we can imagine, viz. on a small <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> named Tenochtitlan, in the middle of a great lake, without ground to cultivate for their subsistence, or even room sufficient to build their habitations. Their life was therefore as miserable here for some time as it had been when they were on the islands at the end of the lake, and they were reduced to the same shifts to maintain themselves. To enlarge the boundaries of their island, they drove palisades into those parts of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WATER">water</a> which were most shallow, terracing them with stones and turf, and uniting to their principal island several other smaller ones which lay in the neighbourhood. To procure for themselves afterwards stones, wood, &c. for constructing their habitations, as well as clothing and other necessaries, they instituted a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> with the people who dwelt on the borders of the lake, supplying them with fish, water-fowl, and other more minute inhabitants of the lake and marshes, which they contrived to render eatable; and in return for all this they received the necessaries above-mentioned. The greatest effort of their industry, however, was the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> of floating gardens, by means of bushes and mud of the lake; and these they brought to such perfection that they produced maize, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-PEPPER">pepper</a>, chia, French beans, and gourds. For thirteen years that the Mexicans had to struggle with <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> difficulty, they remained at peace; but factions sooner did they begin to prosper and live comfortably, than the inveterate enmity betwixt the two factions formerly mentioned broke out in all its fury. This produced a separation; and one of the parties took up their residence on a small island at a little distance to the northward, which, from an heap of sand found there, they at first named Xaltitlan, but afterwards Tlatoaneco, from a terrace constructed by themselves. This island was afterwards united to that of Tenochtitlan. About this time the Mexicans divided their city into four parts, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> which still subsists; each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> having now its tutelar saint, as it had formerly its tutelar god. In the midst of their city was the sanctuary of their great god Mexitli, whom they constantly preferred to all the rest. To him they daily performed acts of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADORATION">adoration</a>; but instead of making any progress in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a>, they seem to have daily improved in the most horrible barbarities, at least in their religion. The dreadful sacrifices made of their prisoners already mentioned, could only barbarity be exceeded by that which we are now about to relate. Being now on a more respectable footing than formerly, they sent an embassy to the petty king of Colhuacan, requesting him to send them one of his daughters, that she might be consecrated the mother of their protecting god. The unsuspecting prince, intoxicated with the thoughts of having his daughter made a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a>, readily complied with their desire.—The unfortunate princess was conducted in great triumph to Mexico; but no sooner was she arrived, than she was sacrificed in the shocking manner above related; and, to add to the horror of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEED">deed</a>, the body was flayed, and one of the bravest young men of the nation dressed in her skin. Her father, ignorant of this dreadful transaction, was invited by the Mexicans to be present at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APOTHEOSIS">apotheosis</a> of his daughter, and went to see the solemnity, and to worship the new divinity. He was led into the sanctuary, where the young <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MAN">man</a> stood clothed in the bloody skin of his daughter; but the darkness of the place prevented him from seeing what was before him. They gave him a center in his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, and some copal to begin his worship; but having discovered by the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FLAME">flame</a> of the copal the horrible spectacle, he ran out in a distracted manner, calling upon his people to revenge the injury; but this they were not able to do at that time nor ever after. Historians are unanimous, that this sacrifice was performed at the express command of the devil; and indeed in this instance, their credulity seems pardonable; though Clavigero, with more reason, attributes it to his priests. In the year 1352 the Mexican government was changed from an aristocracy to a monarchy. At first they were governed by 20 lords, of whom one had an authority superior to the rest. This naturally suggested the idea of monarchy; and to this change they were also induced by the contemptible state in which their nation still continued, thinking that the royal <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> would confer upon it a degree of splendor which otherwise it could not enjoy; and that by having one leader, they would be better able to oppose their enemies. Proceeding, therefore, to elect a king, the choice fell upon Acamapitzin, a man of great estimation among them, and descended from Opochtili a noble Aztec, and a princess of the royal family of Colhuacan. As he was yet a bachelor, they attempted to negotiate a marriage, first with the daughter of the lord of Tacuba, and then of the king of Azcapozalco; but these proposals being rejected with disdain, they applied to Acolmiztli lord of Coatlichan, and a defendant of one of the three Acolhuian princes; who complied with their request, and the nuptials were celebrated with great rejoicings. In the meantime, the Tlatelolcos, the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> rivals of the Mexicans, resolved not to be behind them in anything which had the least appearance of augmenting the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> of their state. They likewise, therefore, chose a king; but not thinking proper to choose him from among themselves, they applied to the king of the Tepepanecs, who readily sent them his son; and he was crowned first king of Tlatelolco in 1353. In this the Tlatelolcos seem to have had a design of humbling their rivals, as well as rendering themselves more respectable; and therefore it is probable, that they had represented the Mexicans as wanting in that respect due to the Tepepanec monarch, as having elected a king without his leave, though at the same time they were tributaries to him. The consequence of this was, that he took a resolution to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> their tribute. Hitherto they had paid only a certain number of fish and waterfowl; but now they were ordered to bring also several thousands of fir and willow <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> to be set in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a> and gardens of Azcapozalco, and to transport to the court a great floating garden, which produced vegetables of every kind known in Anahuac. This being accomplished with great difficulty, the king commanded them next year to bring him another garden, with a duck and swan in it both sitting upon eggs; but so, that on their arrival at Azcapozalco the brood might be ready to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HATCH">hatch</a>. This was also done; and the prince had the satisfaction of seeing the young birds come out of the eggs. The third year they were ordered to bring a live stag along with a garden. This was more difficult than any of the former tasks; because they were obliged, in order to hunt the stag, to go to the mountains of the continent, where they were in danger of falling into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of their enemies; however, this also was accomplished, and the desire of the king gratified. In this manner the Mexicans were oppressed for no less than 50 years. They freed themselves, however, from all their difficulties by vigorous exertions, absurdly ascribing to the protection of that malevolent being whom they worshipped the glory of every deliverance. Acamapitzin governed this city, which at that time comprehended the whole of his dominions, for 37 years in peace. His queen being barren, he married another wife, but without abandoning the first; and these two, instead of being rivals to one another, lived together in the utmost <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a>; the first wife taking upon herself the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> of educating Huitzilihuitlel, the son of the second. He had, besides, several children by other women, and one named Itzcoatl, who afterwards proved one of the best and most renowned kings who sat on the throne of Mexico. He is said also to have conquered four considerable cities; but Clavigero thinks he must in this only have been an auxiliary, it being very improbable, that while he could scarce maintain his own territories, he should think of foreign conquests. Acamapitzin died in 1389, greatly lamented by the Mexicans, and his death was followed by an interregnum of four months. As the deceased monarch had formally resigned his authority into the hands of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOBLES">nobles</a>, it was necessary that a new <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-ELECTION">election</a> should take place; and when this was done, the choice fell upon Huitzilihuitlel, the son of Acamapitzin. As he was still unmarried, it was resolved, if possible, to procure him an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> and advantageous <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MATCH">match</a>. With this view, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEPUTATION">deputation</a> of nobility was sent to the king of Azcapozalco, requesting, in very humble terms, an alliance with one of his daughters. The expressions made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of by these ambassadors are said by our author to have been particularly elegant in the Mexican language; but it is difficult to understand how a speech made among a people ignorant of the art of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> could be particularly recorded at the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a> of some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HUNDREDS">hundreds</a> of years after. They are as follow: "We beseech you, with the most profound respect, to take compassion on our <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> and your <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a> Huitzilihuitlel, confined among the thick rushes of the lake.—He is without a wife, and we without a queen.—Vouchsafe, Sir, to part with one of your jewels or most precious feathers. Give us one of your daughters, who may come to reign over us in a country which belongs to you." This piece of oratory had such an effect upon the king, that he granted their request, and a Tepepanec princess was conducted in great triumph to Mexico, the marriage was solemnized with the utmost joy. Though this princess brought him a son the first year of their marriage, the king, in order to strengthen himself by fresh alliances, married also the daughter of another prince, by whom he had Montezuma Ihuicamina, the most celebrated of all the Mexican kings. We must now return to the history of the Acol-Rei, who at this time were governed by Techotlalala the son of Quimatzin. For 30 years this prince enjoyed an uninterrupted tranquillity. This was interrupted by the revolt of Tzompan, prince of Xaltocan, and the last of the family of Chiconquahutli, one of the three original Acolhuian princes, who had drawn into his conspiracy the sovereigns of six other states. The king, out of respect to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of the rebel, offered to <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-PARDON">pardon</a> him if he would lay down his arms; but Tzompan, confident of his strength, rejected the offer with contempt. The king was therefore obliged to send an army against him. in which the Tepanecans and Mexicans served as auxiliaries. The war lasted only two months; Tzompantli was defeated and put to death, along with several others of the principal rebels. The Mexicans, who had behaved with great valor, returned in triumph to their city, while Teotlalco took several very prudent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> to strengthen his government, prevent rebellions in future, and to augment the splendor of his throne. In consequence of the renown acquired in this war by the Mexicans, and the advantages resulting from the alliance with the king of Azcapotzalco, that people now began to be held in much higher estimation by their neighbors than before. They extended their commerce, and in consequence of that, came to wear cotton instead of the threads of the wild-palm, which had formerly constituted their whole dress; but this gleam of prosperity was soon overcast, and they had to encounter a more intractable and formidable enemy than any that they had yet met with. This was Maxtlaton prince of Coyoacan, and son to the king of Azcapotzalco. Being of a cruel and revengeful temper, for which he was dreaded even by his father, he resolved to resent the indignity which he pretended to have been done to him by the marriage of his sister to the king of Mexico. The true cause of his displeasure, however, was his fear that the Tepanecan <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> might devolve on his sister's son by Huitzilhuitl; and to prevent this, he took the barbarous method of sending assassins to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MURDER">murder</a> his nephew. The king of Mexico was not then able to resent the injury; for though, by his marriage with the Tepanecan princesses, the oppressive tribute was taken off, and the Mexicans had only to pay a couple of ducks annually, by way of acknowledging the Tepanecan superiority, yet the one nation was far from being in a condition to cope with the other. The barbarity of Maxtlaton was not unknown to his father; but it is certain that he did not reflect it; and indeed there is great reason to suppose that he took part with his son in most of his wicked enterprises. As the Mexicans advanced in wealth and power, so did their rivals the inhabitants of Tlatelolco. Their first king died in 1399, leaving his subjects greatly improved in civilization, and the city much enlarged and beautified. The rivalry which subsisted between the two cities had indeed greatly contributed to the aggrandizement of both. The Mexicans had formed to many alliances by marriage with the neighboring nations, had so much improved their agriculture, and floating gardens on the lake, and had built so many more vessels to supply their extended commerce and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a>, that they were enabled to celebrate their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECULAR">secular</a> year, answering to A.D. 1402, with greater magnificence than they had ever done since they left their original country of Atzlan. All this time Teotlalco continued to reign in Acolhuacan; but being now very far advanced in years, and finding his end approach, he called to him his son Ixtlilxochitl, and recommended to him to beware of the ambitious disposition of the king of Azcapotzalco, as he was apprehensive that he might attempt something against the peace of the empire. His suspicions were verified; for on the death of Teotlalco, which happened in 1406, the king of Azcapotzalco, without making the usual submissions to the new king, to whom he was a feudatory, set out for his own territories, with a view to stir up the other feudatory princes to rebellion. Having called to him the kings of Mexico and Tlatelolco, he told them, that Teotlalco, who had long tyrannized over that country, being dead, he designed to procure freedom to the princes, so that each might rule his own territory entirely independent of the king of Acolhuacan; but for this purpose he needed their assistance, and trusted to their well-known spirit to take part with him in the enterprise. He informed them likewise, that in order to ensure success, he would find means to unite other princes in the confederacy. The new king of Acolhuacan, in the mean time, was employed in settling the affairs of his kingdom, and endeavouring to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> the good will of his subjects. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-COMBINATION">combination</a> against him was soon discovered; but though Ixtlilxochitl was desirous of heading his army in person, he was dissuaded from doing by his courtiers; so that the conduct of the war was committed to his generals. To weaken the enemy, they ravaged the territories of six revolted states; but notwithstanding this, and the superior <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a> of the royal army, the war was carried on by the rebels with great obstinacy, their armies being constantly recruited by fresh troops in proportion to their losses. At last, after three years of a ruinous war, the king of Azcapotzalco, finding that his resources would at last fail him, sued for peace; but with a design of accomplishing by treachery what he had not yet been able to do by force. His adversary, equally reduced with himself, consented to a peace; though he knew very well that the Tepanecan prince intended to observe it no longer than suited his purpose. In the year 1409 died Huitzilhuitl king of Mexico-Chimalpopoca, who likewise left the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of electing a successor to the nobility. They made choice of his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> Chimalpopoca; and from thence it became an established <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-LAW">law</a> to choose one of the brothers of the deceased king, or if he had no brothers to elect one of his grandsons. While the new prince was endeavouring to secure himself on the throne, the treacherous Tezozomoc used all means in his power to strengthen the party he had formed against the king of Acolhuacan. In this he was attended with such success, that the unfortunate prince found himself reduced to the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of wandering among the neighboring mountains, at the head of a small army, accompanied by the lords of Huexolta and Coatlichan, who remained always faithful to him. The Tepanecans distressed him to such a degree, by intercepting his <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>, that he was forced to beg them of his enemies. One of Díaz and his grandsons was sent to Otompan, a rebel state, to request them to supply their king with the provisions he stood in need of, and to exhort them to abandon the cause of the rebels, which they had espoused. No task could be more dangerous; yet such was the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MAGNANIMITY">magnanimity</a> of the young prince's disposition, that he readily set out on the journey; nor was he deterred by the information he got that there were in the place certain Tepanecans who had come on purpose to publish a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PROCLAMATION">proclamation</a> from Tezozomoc. He went boldly to the most public place of the town, and in presence of those Mexico who published the proclamation made known his request. This heroism, however, did not meet with the success it deserved. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROPOSITIONS">propositions</a> were derided from the moment they were made; but the people did not offer any farther insult, until one of the meaner sort threw a stone at him, exciting others of the same stamp to put him to death. The Tepanecans, who had hitherto continued silent, perceiving their opportunity, joined in the general cry to kill the prince, and began also to throw stones. The prince attempted first to defend himself, and afterwards to escape by flight; but both being equally impossible, he fell under a shower of stones. The Tepanecans exulted in this act of treachery, and soon after cut off Ixtlioxochitl himself, after having treacherously persuaded him to a conference with two of their captains. This perfidious act was committed in sight of the royal army, who were too weak to revenge it; the royal corpse was saved with difficulty; and Nezahualcoyotl, heir apparent to the crown, was obliged to shelter himself among the bushes from the fury of his enemies. Tezozomoc having now in a great <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> gained his point, proceeded to pour down his troops upon those cities and districts which had remained faithful to the late unfortunate monarch. The people made a most desperate <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>, and killed vast numbers of their enemies; but at last being themselves reduced by the calamities of war, and in danger of total extermination, they were obliged to quit their habitations and fly to other countries. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TYRANT">tyrant</a>, then, finding himself superior to all his adversaries, gave Tezcuco in fief to Chimalpopoca king of Mexico, Huexotla to Tlacacotl king of Tlatelolco; placing faithful governors in other places, and appointing Azcapozalco, the capital of his own territory, the royal residence and capital of Acolhuacan.
